frame.systemSummary: Atcraft is one system for running an architectural-hardware manufacturing business end to end: what you make and what it is built from, what customers have ordered, what has to be bought or made to cover it, what is on the shelf, what has been checked, packed and sent, and what is owed either way. Everything in it hangs off two things — an item master that every other document points at, and a stock ledger in which every single movement of material is written down with a reason and a name against it. Because of that, the stock figure on the screen is not an estimate that somebody keys in and corrects later; it is the arithmetic of documents your own people have raised, and every one of those documents can be traced back to who raised it, who approved it, and why. The rest — sales orders, MRP, purchase orders, goods receipts, quality inspections, production orders, job work, packing, dispatch, invoices and payments — is the paperwork of the business, arranged in the order the work actually happens.
frame.whatItReplaces: Almost every business of this size runs on a stock register in a spreadsheet, a purchase file, a WhatsApp group for the shop floor and the accountant's own books — four records of the same facts that agree with each other only until somebody is on leave. The everyday cost is not the typing; it is that nobody can answer a plain question in one place: is this order covered, why did we buy 200 of those, who passed that lot, where did the twelve missing pieces go. What changes is that each of those facts now has exactly one home and one moment at which it is recorded. Stock changes only when a document is posted — a receipt, an issue, a production booking, a dispatch — never by editing a number, so the register cannot quietly drift. An order that cannot be covered from stock is not a discovery made at picking time; the shortfall is on the screen the moment the order is confirmed. What you give up is the freedom to fix things afterwards: an approved purchase order cannot be edited, a sealed carton cannot be unsealed, a posted movement cannot be deleted. Corrections happen the way they do in a ledger — by another entry, with a reason, that stays visible.
frame.signIn: Open the address your administrator gave you and sign in on the Sign in screen with your email address and password. If your account has two-factor authentication switched on, the screen then asks for the six-digit code from your authenticator app; there is a "Back to password" link if you started with the wrong account. Get the password wrong too many times in a row and the screen holds you off with a visible countdown before it will try again — wait it out rather than reloading. There is a "Forgotten your password?" link below the button. The first time you sign in with a password an administrator issued for you, the system will not let you go any further: it takes you straight to "Choose a new password", explains that a temporary password is in use, and asks for a new one. The new password must be at least twelve characters and contain a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol; a live checklist beside the box shows what is still missing, and the server additionally refuses very common passwords and anything containing your own email address. Setting it signs out every other device you were signed in on. Only when that is done does the rest of the application open. Afterwards, your own account lives on Profile & sessions, reached from your name at the top right: change your password there, switch two-factor authentication on or off, and see every device currently signed in as you — with a Revoke button beside each one, which is what to use the day a phone is lost.
frame.navigation: The menu down the left is deliberately not an alphabetical list of features; it is the order the work happens in, from demand through to accounts. Overview is the dashboard. Sales holds sales orders, customers and dealers. Inventory holds stock balances, the stock ledger, reservations, transfers and adjustments, warehouses and storage locations. Engineering holds items, bills of material, routings and the item masters (categories, units, conversions, attributes, brands, manufacturers and price lists). Planning holds MRP. Procurement runs requisitions, purchase orders, goods receipts, RFQs, quotations, purchase returns, vendors and transporters. Manufacturing holds production orders, production planning, assembly, work orders and job work. Quality & Dispatch holds quality control, the QC check sheets, packing and dispatch. Finance holds ledgers and outstanding, vendor invoices, payments and the chart of accounts. Insights holds reports, the audit trail and documents. Administration holds users and roles, and the organisation record. Two things about the menu are worth knowing. First, you only see the sections your job needs — a storekeeper does not see Finance, because every screen in it would only refuse them; if a colleague describes a screen you cannot find, it is a permission question for your administrator, not a fault. Second, some entries carry a small number: open sales orders, requisitions waiting, purchase orders waiting for approval, jobs in progress, job work sitting at a vendor, inspections pending, consignments running late. That number is the day's queue. Along the top there is a box that searches items by code or name, a bell for notifications with the unread count on it, a light/dark switch, and your own name, which opens Profile & sessions and Sign out.

endToEnd.title: Record what you sell
endToEnd.what: New item. Give it a code and name, choose its base unit (required — an item cannot exist without one), and tick what it is allowed to do: sold, purchased, manufactured, used as a component, sold as a spare. These are independent ticks, not a single type, because a rose handle really is bought, used in a kit and sold as a spare all at once.
endToEnd.effect: Nothing moves. This creates the record every later document points at, so the code you choose here is the code that will appear on the customer's order, the vendor's order and the stock ledger.

endToEnd.title: Say what it is built from
endToEnd.what: Create the bill of material for the finished item, one line per component, with the quantity per unit made and a scrap percentage where waste is normal. Then open it and use Submit for approval, and then Approve — a draft cannot be approved directly, because a structure nobody put forward has not been reviewed by anybody.
endToEnd.effect: Nothing moves. It fixes the multiplication that everything downstream relies on: 100 kits x 2 handles = 200 handles. Approval is the moment that number becomes the plant's answer rather than one engineer's.

endToEnd.title: Take the customer's order
endToEnd.what: New order. Name the customer, the warehouse it will ship from, the date they want it, and one line per item with quantity and price.
endToEnd.effect: Creates an obligation and nothing else. The order is still a draft: no stock is set aside and nothing is promised until the next step.

endToEnd.title: Confirm it
endToEnd.what: Confirm, with a reason. The order's own document number (SO/2526/00012 and the like) is the heading of the page and is what to quote on the phone.
endToEnd.effect: This is the step that binds. The customer's credit headroom is checked, and whatever stock exists is reserved line by line. A reservation does not move any stock out of the warehouse — the on-hand figure is unchanged — it lowers what is available to anybody else. Where there is not enough, the panel says which lines are short and by how much, and links to MRP. A partly covered order is completely normal here, not an error.

endToEnd.title: Work out what the shortfall needs
endToEnd.what: Start a run: how many days ahead to look, and which warehouses to count. It runs in the background — you are not holding a screen open while it thinks — and the list shows it moving to Completed.
endToEnd.effect: Nothing moves. The run explodes every bill of material behind the order book, nets off what you already hold and what is already on order, and consolidates a part used in several places into one requirement rather than one per place it appears.

endToEnd.title: Act on what it found
endToEnd.what: Read the shortage list, tick the rows you accept and Convert them; ignore the ones you do not want, with a reason. Requires the right to convert MRP suggestions.
endToEnd.effect: Nothing moves yet, but the work is now real: a buy suggestion becomes a purchase requisition, a make suggestion becomes a production order, and a job-work suggestion becomes a job work order. A suggested transfer can only be ignored, not converted.

endToEnd.title: Order the bought parts
endToEnd.what: Raise the purchase order against an approved vendor, then on the order Submit, Approve and Send — three separate acts, each with a reason. A vendor can only be approved once bank details and a tax identity are on file, and only by somebody other than the person who entered them, because approval is what unlocks payments to a bank account.
endToEnd.effect: Money is committed. Once the order is approved it can no longer be edited — the vendor has been sent it. If it is wrong, cancel it and raise another; the cancelled one stays on the record.

endToEnd.title: Receive the goods
endToEnd.what: Receive against the order, entering received and accepted quantities line by line, then Post receipt. The goods land in the warehouse the purchase order named — the receipt does not let you redirect a delivery.
endToEnd.effect: This is where purchased material becomes your stock. The balance goes up, and a ledger line is written for every movement with its reason. Anything that needs incoming inspection is received onto QC hold instead of into free stock, so it counts as owned but cannot be issued yet. Until a receipt is posted it is material in the building that the system does not yet own — which is exactly what the list is showing you.

endToEnd.title: Inspect what was held
endToEnd.what: Open the pending inspection, record the readings against the check sheet it was raised on, and decide: accepted, rejected, rework, hold or scrap — the quantities must add up to the whole lot inspected. Recording readings and deciding are separate rights, so the person measuring need not be the person signing.
endToEnd.effect: Deciding is a stock movement, not a note. Accepted quantity moves from QC hold into free stock; rejected moves to damaged and raises the return; scrap is written off. Rework and hold move nothing and stay in the pool to be decided again. One reading on a critical parameter out of specification rejects the lot whatever else passed.

endToEnd.title: Make the finished goods
endToEnd.what: On the production order: Release, which explodes and freezes the components and holds the stock for the job; Issue material, which is the storekeeper handing material to the floor; Record production as output comes off; then Complete and Close. Only the steps the order's current state allows are shown — a released job has no Approve button because it cannot be approved again.
endToEnd.effect: Components leave the warehouse when they are issued, and finished goods enter it when production is recorded. Completing books the last output and automatically issues the components marked for backflush, in proportion to what was actually made. From Start onwards the job can no longer be cancelled.

endToEnd.title: Check the promise is now covered
endToEnd.what: Return to the order and read the allocation panel, or look at Inventory > Reservations for the same facts across every order.
endToEnd.effect: Nothing moves. It tells you whether the finished goods now in stock have been picked up against this customer's lines, or whether something is still short.

endToEnd.title: Pack it (where a packing order exists)
endToEnd.what: Open the packing order, Add carton, put the goods in, and Seal carton — sealing is confirmed and cannot be undone, because a taped box is a physical fact. Then Complete packing and Hand over to dispatch. The packing list PDF is generated in the background and appears when it is ready.
endToEnd.effect: Sealing issues the carton itself out of stock, so boxes are accounted for and paid for once. The goods being packed do not move here — they leave at dispatch, and posting them in both places would take the same stock out twice. Packed quantities are worked out from what is in the cartons; they are never typed in, and the system refuses to pack more than was ordered.

endToEnd.title: Send it
endToEnd.what: Create dispatch: the customer, the sales order it is against, the warehouse, the lines and quantities, and the transport details — transporter, vehicle, driver, LR number, e-way bill, promised delivery date. Then Mark ready when it is staged at the gate, and Dispatch when it goes.
endToEnd.effect: Mark ready moves no stock — it says the consignment is packed and waiting. Dispatch is the step that ships: the reservation the sales order was holding is consumed and the finished goods leave the warehouse in one movement. Shipping 40 of a line of 100 is ordinary — the order becomes partly dispatched and the balance of 60 stays open for the next consignment.

endToEnd.title: Follow it to the customer's door
endToEnd.what: On the tracking board, Mark in transit when the carrier collects, add tracking events as you learn them, and Confirm delivery on arrival. If it arrives past the promised date the system will not accept the confirmation without a reason for the delay.
endToEnd.effect: No stock or money moves — this records what the receiver did. Late consignments are called out on the board in red with the number of days, and can be filtered on directly, because that is the list somebody has to work through every morning.

endToEnd.title: Settle the money, and be able to prove all of it
endToEnd.what: Vendor invoices are entered against what was received and paid on Payments; customer outstanding and the ledgers sit under Ledgers & Outstanding, with the chart of accounts behind them. Reports covers the statutory and management views, and the Audit trail shows every create, approval, rejection and status change with who did it, when, and the reason they gave.
endToEnd.effect: Money is recorded, and the whole journey above becomes reconstructable from one screen: the order, the plan, the purchase, the receipt, the inspection, the job, the consignment.

roles.forWhom: The owner, or the one or two people trusted to set the system up and keep it running.
roles.canDo: Everything the business does: every screen, every approval, every master list, plus creating users, assigning roles and maintaining the organisation record. The only thing held back from it is platform-level company management, which belongs to whoever hosts the system. Give this out sparingly — an administrator can approve their own work, which is exactly what the separate approval roles below exist to prevent.

roles.forWhom: The person who answers for the factory floor.
roles.canDo: Everything a production supervisor and a QC inspector can do, and on top of that the sign-offs: approving and cancelling production orders, approving allocations and moving reserved stock from one order to another, closing job work, and approving bills of material.

roles.forWhom: The person who holds the keys to the store.
roles.canDo: Warehouse work: receiving goods against purchase orders, issuing material to jobs, taking material back, transfers between warehouses, adjustments and physical counts. They see stock, the ledger and items. They do not price anything, do not approve anything and do not see finance.

The whole procurement cycle — vendors, requisitions, RFQs, quotations, purchase orders, returns — plus the approvals a buyer cannot give themselves: approving requisitions, and approving, rejecting or cancelling purchase orders. Can also start an MRP run. Reads the brand and manufacturer lists, because parts are often sourced by maker.

roles.forWhom: The buyer who does the day's procurement work.
roles.canDo: Raises and prices everything — vendors, requisitions, RFQs, quotations, purchase orders — and sends an approved order to the vendor. Deliberately cannot approve any of it. That gap is the control: the person who chooses the supplier and the price is not the person who commits the money. Reads the brand and manufacturer lists, because parts are often sourced by maker.

Runs released work: creates and releases production orders, manages work orders, issues material to jobs and takes it back, records production, runs assembly, and sends and receives job work. Sees BOMs, routings, work centres, machines, stock and reservations. Cannot approve a production order or close job work — that is the plant manager's.

Sees the inspection queue, records readings and records the accept, reject, rework, hold or scrap decision, with the stock movement that follows from it. Sees the receipts, jobs and job work the inspections came from, and can attach photographs and certificates. Cannot write the check sheets themselves.

Packing and sending: building and sealing cartons, completing packing orders, creating consignments, releasing them, and confirming delivery. Sees transporters, sales orders, stock and items. Does not price, approve or invoice anything.

Maintains customers, raises and amends sales orders, and confirms them — which is what reserves stock and reports the shortfall. Sees prices, brands, stock, reservations, dispatches and sales invoices. Cannot buy, make or ship.

Ledgers, customer and vendor outstanding, vendor invoices, sales invoices, recording payments, GST reporting, stock valuation and item costs. Sees purchase orders and receipts so an invoice can be matched to what actually arrived. Runs and exports reports. Does not raise operational documents.

roles.forWhom: The person who decides what gets made and bought, and when.
roles.canDo: Runs MRP, reads the shortage list and converts suggestions into requisitions and production orders. Sees bills of material with their costs, routings, stock, reservations, the order book, and items with their brands. Can allocate and reallocate reserved stock between orders. Cannot approve a purchase order or release a job.

Creates and maintains items, item categories, the finish/size/colour attributes, brands and manufacturers, bills of material with their costs, and routings; can mark a BOM obsolete. Sees work centres and machines. Uploads drawings and specifications. Cannot approve a BOM, and touches nothing transactional.

roles.forWhom: An external auditor, or an internal reviewer during a review.
roles.canDo: Reads everything and changes nothing, including the full audit trail, and can export reports. The safe role to hand to somebody who needs to look.

roles.role: Vendor roles (Owner, Manager, Dispatch Manager, QC Contact)
roles.forWhom: Staff at your suppliers, if you open the vendor portal to them.
roles.canDo: A narrow window onto their own records only — their purchase orders, their consignments, their documents — and the system additionally confines them to that one vendor and, for a vendor manager, to the item categories you assign. A vendor owner can also raise their invoices and see payments; a vendor dispatch manager records consignment and courier details; a vendor QC contact sees inspection outcomes on their own supplies.

frame.configurable: Your own staff maintain the lists the business genuinely owns, without anyone from the software side being involved: item categories, units of measure and the conversions between them, the finish, size and colour attributes, brands and manufacturers, price lists, warehouses and the storage locations inside them, vendors, customers and dealers, transporters, work centres and the machines in them, the QC check sheets, and users and roles — including new roles of your own if the built-in ones do not match how you split the work. Branches, plants, departments and the accounting calendar are yours too, on the Organisation screen. What you cannot edit is the vocabulary the system computes with: the statuses a document can be in (draft, pending approval, approved, released, dispatched and so on) and the item groups (raw material, component, semi-finished, finished good, consumable, packing material, spare, scrap, service). That is deliberate, and it is what makes the rest trustworthy. The rules that protect you — an approved purchase order cannot be edited, a job cannot be released without its components held, a lot on QC hold cannot be issued — are written in terms of those statuses; if a status could be renamed or a new one added from a settings screen, the rule attached to it would quietly stop applying. Item groups are for reporting and for setting sensible defaults on a new item, and nothing in the system is allowed to decide what you may do based on them; the ticks on the item itself — can be sold, can be purchased, can be manufactured, can be a component, can be a spare — are the ones that decide, and those you set freely, item by item. So the practical rule is: if it is a name, a rate, a place, a person or a specification, you maintain it; if it is a step in a lifecycle, it is fixed, and the way to change how a lifecycle behaves is a change to the software, discussed and released like any other.
frame.gettingHelp: When a screen refuses something, it tells you which of four things happened, and each has a different next step. If the message is about stock — not enough available — the quantity you asked for is promised elsewhere or has not arrived; check the reservations and the allocation panel on the order, and either free some up or plan for it. If it says the action is not allowed in this state, the document has moved past that point: a purchase order that has been approved cannot be edited, a production order that has started cannot be cancelled, a sealed carton cannot be reopened. The remedy is always to raise the next document rather than to undo the last — cancel and re-raise, adjust, return, or issue again — and that trail is a feature, not a nuisance. If it says you are not permitted, the account is right and the rights are not; note the screen and the button and ask your administrator, who can adjust your role on Users & Roles. If it says something changed since you opened it, someone else saved the same record while you were working — refresh the screen, look at what they did, and redo your change on top of it. Anything asking for a reason genuinely needs three characters or more, and that sentence is kept in the audit trail, so write the reason a colleague would need in six months, not "ok". Two habits pay for themselves: check the Audit trail before asking anyone what happened to a document, because it names who did what and when with the reason they gave; and if the message says something went wrong on the server, it carries a short reference code — send that code with your description, because it is what lets the fault be found in the logs immediately instead of being guessed at.

chapters.groupIntro: This chapter covers the way in and the reference lists the rest of the system draws on. It starts with signing in and the first-time password change, then the dashboard an owner opens each morning and the left-hand menu that maps the whole business. The larger part of it is Item master data, where the classifications, units, conversions, finishes, brands, manufacturers and price lists live - the vocabulary every other screen picks from, and the one area the client is expected to maintain without help. It closes with the company's own structure of branches, plants and departments, the notification inbox, and the two screens where a person looks after their own account.
chapters.groupTitle: Getting in, and the lists everything else uses

screens.title: Signing in
screens.purpose: The only screen anyone sees before they are signed in. It takes the email address the account was created with and its password, and - if that person has switched on two-factor protection - a six-digit code from their authenticator app afterwards. Everything else in the system is closed until this succeeds, and every action taken after it is recorded against the name that signed in, which is why accounts are personal and not shared between a shift.
screens.whoUses: Everyone with an account, at the start of every shift.

keyActions.how: Type the email address and password, then press Sign in.
keyActions.note: Pressing Enter in the password box does the same thing.

keyActions.how: The eye button at the right-hand end of the password box shows what has been typed.
keyActions.note: Useful on a shop-floor keyboard; it hides again on a second press.

keyActions.how: After a correct password, if two-factor is switched on for the account, type the six digits from the authenticator app and press Verify and sign in.
keyActions.note: Back to password returns to the first step if the wrong account was used.

keyActions.action: Ask for a password reset link
keyActions.how: Forgotten your password? below the Sign in button. Give the email address, and the company code only if the same address is used for more than one company. Press Send reset link.
keyActions.note: The reply is always the same - if an account exists for that address, a link has been sent. It never says whether the address is registered, because either answer would tell a stranger who works here.

keyActions.how: The control at the top right of the sign-in card.
keyActions.note: It is here as well as inside the application, because a night shift should not have to sign in to a bright screen first.

flow: Open the address the ERP is published at.
Type the email address and the password.
Press Sign in.
If asked, type the six-digit code from the authenticator app and press Verify and sign in.
The dashboard opens - unless the password was issued by an administrator, in which case Choose a new password opens instead.
rules: Five wrong passwords in a row lock the account for fifteen minutes. This stops someone working through a list of guesses; the person themselves only has to wait, or ask an administrator for a reset.
Several attempts in quick succession also make the button count down - Try again in 30s - rather than accepting more. The countdown clears itself; the page does not need reloading.
A successful password reset through the emailed link also lifts a lock, because whoever opened the mailbox has proved the account is theirs.
The reset link is time-limited and arrives by email only. Nobody in the business, including an administrator, can read an existing password - a reset always replaces it.
screens.permission: None. This is the only screen anyone can reach without an account.
screens.notes: This screen is not in the list of routes I was given, but the chapter has to cover signing in and the deck needs a screenshot of it. The forgotten-password screens live at /forgot-password and /reset-password if separate screenshots are wanted; the reset screen carries the same live password checklist described under Your account.

screens.title: Dashboard
screens.purpose: The first screen after signing in, and the one an owner reads before deciding what the day is about. It answers four questions at a glance - what have we sold that is not yet out of the door, what is our stock worth, what is waiting on somebody's signature, and what is late. Below the figures it shows the documents waiting on a decision from the person reading it, and the last few things anyone in the company did. Nothing on this screen is edited; every tile and every line is a doorway into the screen that owns that work.
screens.whoUses: The owner and every manager. A storekeeper or an operator sees a shorter version of it, because a tile that leads somewhere they may not go is not shown at all.

keyActions.action: Open the work behind a figure
keyActions.how: Click any of the tiles - Open sales orders, Stock value, POs awaiting approval, Production in progress, QC pending, Dispatches in transit, Overdue deliveries, Overdue sales orders.
keyActions.note: Each one lands on the list screen for that figure, not on a report of it.

keyActions.action: Deal with something waiting on you
keyActions.how: Needs your attention lists up to six documents raised for your roles. Click one to open the document and decide it there.
keyActions.note: A line marked Not yours to decide is in your team's queue but needs a different right to sign off - opening it will show no approve button. That is a colleague's to take.

keyActions.action: See what the company has been doing
keyActions.how: Recent activity shows the last eight recorded actions. Click one to open that record; Audit trail at the top right of the panel opens the full history.
keyActions.note: Only shown to someone entitled to read the audit trail.

keyActions.how: Refresh, at the top right of the page.
keyActions.note: The figures are recalculated about once a minute, so pressing it twice in quick succession will show the same numbers - that is the system being economical, not stuck.

flow: Sign in; the dashboard opens by itself.
Read the eight figures across the top - the two red ones are overdue work and are the ones that need a decision today.
Work down Needs your attention and clear anything waiting on your signature.
Glance at Recent activity to see what the rest of the company has done since you last looked.
Move into the day's work from the left-hand menu.
rules: The stock value is taken from a summary that is rebuilt on its own schedule, not recalculated as you watch. The tile prints how old it is - "On-hand at valuation, 20 minutes ago" - so an out-of-date figure is visible rather than disguised.
The purchase-order tile shows the money as well as the count, because six orders worth a lakh and six worth a crore are not the same queue.
Overdue deliveries and Overdue sales orders are counted against the date that was promised, not against the date the paperwork was raised.
A tile is only shown if the account may also open the screen it leads to. A dashboard that is emptier than a colleague's is a difference in permissions, not a fault.
The greeting uses the signed-in person's first name, and the line under it says when the figures were computed.
screens.permission: The figures need the right to see the dashboard. The approvals panel appears for anyone holding an approval right of any kind; the activity panel needs the right to read the audit trail. An account with none of the three is told plainly that its dashboard is empty and to ask an administrator.
screens.notes: This screenshot should be taken as the owner, so the tiles are all present. Worth capturing the whole window rather than the page alone - it is the natural place in the deck to point at the left-hand menu and the header. The menu is grouped in the order work actually flows: Overview, Sales, Inventory, Engineering, Planning, Procurement, Manufacturing, Quality & Dispatch, Finance, Insights, Administration. Every person sees only the entries they may use. The header carries a search box that opens the item list on whatever is typed, the light/dark control, a bell with the unread count on it, and the name menu holding Profile & sessions and Sign out. On a desktop the menu can be narrowed to icons with the arrow at its foot; on a phone it becomes a drawer behind the menu button. There is no chart on this page - two chart panels were removed because the figures behind them are no longer produced, so do not promise one in the deck.

screens.title: Item master data
screens.purpose: The vocabulary the whole system picks from: how items are classified, what they are measured in, how those measures relate to one another, the permitted finishes, sizes and colours, the brands products are sold under and the manufacturers that make them, and what things sell for. Nothing here is a transaction - no stock moves, no money is posted - but almost every document elsewhere chooses from these lists, so an hour spent getting them right saves an argument at every goods receipt afterwards. This is the screen to reach for whenever the answer to "can we change that ourselves?" is yes.
screens.whoUses: The owner, or whoever is trusted with the item master - often the same person who creates new items.

keyActions.how: The tabs across the top: Categories, Units, Conversions, Attributes, Brands, Manufacturers, Prices.
keyActions.note: The tab is part of the web address, so a colleague can be sent straight to the unit conversions rather than told to open Masters and click the third tab.

keyActions.how: Each tab has its own search box and filters, above its table.
keyActions.note: Switching tabs clears them deliberately - page four of the category tree means nothing in the price list.

flow: Open Item Masters from Engineering in the left-hand menu.
Pick the tab for the list being maintained.
Search or filter down to the rows in question, or press the New button at the top right of that tab.
rules: Which tabs appear depends on what the account may read. Units and Conversions are governed by one right, so they always appear and disappear together.

Brands and Manufacturers can be sorted by clicking the Code or Name heading - and brands by Position as well. The other five lists cannot: each arrives in the order that makes sense for it - categories in tree order, prices by validity - and the search box and filters are how a row is found.
Every list shows fifty rows at a time by default and pages through the rest.
screens.permission: Opening the screen at all needs the right to read at least one of its lists: categories, units, attributes, brands, manufacturers or prices. Each tab is then shown or hidden on its own read right, and the create, edit and delete buttons on its own change right - so a person can be given the ability to read every list and change only one of them.
screens.notes: Two things the deck assembler should know. First, the screenshot of /masters will show the Categories tab, because that is the first tab an owner sees. Second, and worth telling the client: every tab's read right opens this screen and its sidebar entry on its own - an account that may only maintain brands, say, gets in and sees only the Brands tab. On a system installed before brands and manufacturers existed, the administrator roles receive those four rights automatically and every other role is granted them from Settings -> Roles.

screens.title: Categories
screens.purpose: How the item master is classified - hardware, hinges, locks, and whatever nesting the business actually uses. Categories sit inside one another, and reports group on them, which is what makes a sensible tree worth building once and leaving alone. The list arrives in tree order with each level indented under its parent, so the shape of the classification is visible without opening anything.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the item master.

keyActions.how: New category at the top right. Give it a code and a name, choose the parent it sits under or leave it at the top level, add a description if it helps.
keyActions.note: The code is what reports group on and cannot be changed afterwards - agree it before saving.

keyActions.action: Add one underneath an existing category
keyActions.how: The three-dot menu at the end of a row, then Add a sub-category.
keyActions.note: The parent is filled in for you, and can still be changed in the form.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Show sub-categories. The button that appears in the toolbar - Inside HDW - clears the drill-down again.
The pencil at the end of the row. Change the name or description, or pick a different parent.
keyActions.note: Moving one moves everything beneath it, and the dialog warns before you save.

keyActions.action: Stop offering a category on new items
keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Available on new items and save.
keyActions.note: This is the gentle option: items already classified under it keep their classification, and the category stays in the tree.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Retire category, then confirm.
keyActions.note: This removes it from the tree and from every picker, and there is no undo on this screen.

flow: Open the Categories tab.
Use Top level only to see the trunk, or search for the branch in question.
Press New category, or the three-dot menu on a row and Add a sub-category.
Fill in the code, the name and the parent, and save.
The new row appears in the tree, indented under its parent.
rules: A category's code cannot be changed once it exists, because historical reports group on it and a changed code would silently split a year's figures in two.
Moving a category moves its whole subtree in one go, and every level below it is renumbered at the same time. The move is refused if it would push the tree past eight levels deep.
A category cannot be moved beneath one of its own descendants - the branch would be cut off from the tree - so its own subtree is not offered in the parent list.

Retiring is refused while the category still has sub-categories, or while items are still assigned to it. Move or retire the children first, and reassign the items. The reason is that silently reassigning items would change how every past report groups them.
Searching or filtering shows only the matching rows, so an indented row may then appear beneath something that is not its parent. Clear the search to read the tree properly.
screens.permission: Reading needs the right to view categories; creating, editing and retiring need the right to manage them. Without the change right the list is fully readable and no New, pencil or Retire appears.

screens.title: Units of measure
screens.purpose: What quantities are counted in - pieces, boxes, kilograms, metres. Each unit belongs to one measurement family, and each family has exactly one base unit that everything else in it resolves through. The decimal places on a unit decide how finely a quantity may be stated on a document, which is how you stop somebody booking 3.7 hinges.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the item master. In practice this list is set up once and barely touched.

keyActions.how: New unit at the top right. Give it a code and a name, choose the measurement family, set the decimal places, and mark it as the family's base unit if it is the first one.
keyActions.note: Nought decimal places for anything only ever counted whole, such as pieces.

keyActions.action: Rename a unit or change its precision
keyActions.how: The pencil at the end of the row.
keyActions.note: The code and the family are shown but cannot be edited.

keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Available on new items and save.
keyActions.note: Refused while items still measure in it - change those items first.

keyActions.action: See which unit a family resolves through
keyActions.how: The Base badge in the Measurement family column.

flow: Open the Units tab.
Press New unit.
Enter the code and name, pick the measurement family, set the decimal places.
Tick Base unit of this family if this is the family's first, reference unit.
Save. The unit is immediately available on item forms.
rules: A unit's code and its measurement family are fixed once created. Moving a unit from Weight to Count would orphan every conversion in both families, so it is refused - create a new unit instead.

A family must always keep exactly one base unit. The tick box is locked on the unit that is currently the base; to change it, promote another unit to base instead. Trying to create a second base for a family is refused, and names the one that already holds the job.

A unit cannot be deleted, and this is deliberate: removing one would strand every quantity ever recorded in it. Retirement, through the Available on new items box, is the way out - and even that is refused while active items are still measured in it.
The measurement families available are Count, Weight, Length, Area, Volume and Time.
screens.permission: Reading needs the right to view units; adding and editing need the right to manage them. The same right covers the Conversions tab, so the two always appear together.

screens.title: Unit conversions
screens.purpose: How two units of the same family relate - one box is twelve pieces, one kilogram is a thousand grams. This is the most consequential small screen in the system: a conversion entered backwards does not fail, it quietly multiplies or divides every quantity derived from it, at every goods receipt, every bill of material and every stock valuation. Everything about the screen is built to make the direction unmistakable before anything is saved.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the item master, usually alongside the units themselves.

keyActions.how: New conversion at the top right. Choose the From unit, then the To unit, then type the factor - how many To units make one From unit.
keyActions.note: Kilograms to grams is 1000, not 0.001. The panel below the form spells the equation out in words as you type, in both directions, before you save it.

keyActions.how: Check a conversion at the top right. Type a real quantity, pick the two units, press Convert.
keyActions.note: The answer comes from the server and is the same answer any document would get - it is not a second sum done on this screen, which could only agree with its own mistake.

keyActions.how: The bin icon at the end of the row, then confirm.
keyActions.note: There is no edit. To correct a factor, remove the row and enter it again.

flow: Open the Conversions tab.
Press New conversion.
Pick the From unit. The To list then offers only units of the same measurement family.
Type the factor and read the sentence in the panel below - "1 BOX = 12 NOS, and therefore 1 NOS = 0.083333 BOX".
Save, then press Check a conversion and convert a realistic quantity to confirm the direction.
rules: The factor always answers one question: how many of the second unit make one of the first. Read it any other way and every quantity derived from it is wrong.

A pair is stored once and works in both directions, so there is no reverse row to enter. Entering the reverse as well is refused - two rows could disagree, and whichever the system found first would win.

A conversion may only relate two units of the same measurement family. Kilograms to pieces is not a unit conversion at all - it is a weight that belongs to a particular item - and it is refused, which is why the second list only ever offers the first unit's own family.
A conversion cannot be edited, only removed and re-entered. Changing a factor in place would silently re-value stock that was already booked through it.

Once a conversion is removed, a document quoting one of the two units can no longer be resolved into the other: the system refuses the document rather than guessing a factor. Have the replacement ready before removing one.

If a company has more units than one page can hold, a conversion pointing at one of the later ones shows as "Unknown unit" with a warning above the table. The factor and its direction are still correct.
screens.permission: Reading needs the right to view units; adding and removing need the right to manage them. Check a conversion needs only the read right, so anyone who can see the list can verify a factor.

screens.title: Finishes, sizes and colours
screens.purpose: The company's own vocabulary for how a product is finished, how big it is and what colour it is. Until recently these were typed by hand on each item, which meant "Brushed", "brushed" and "Brushed Steel" were three different finishes and no report could group by finish at all. They are proper records now: whoever maintains this list decides what the business is allowed to say, and everybody filling in an item form chooses from it rather than typing.
screens.whoUses: The owner, or whoever decides the product vocabulary - typically the same person who signs off new items.

keyActions.action: Add a finish, a size or a colour
keyActions.how: New value at the top right. Choose which of the three it is, give it a code and a name, and set its position in the list.
keyActions.note: As soon as it is saved it appears in the Finish, Size or Colour box on every item form and every variant - nothing else has to be done.

keyActions.how: The pencil at the end of the row, change the Name, save.
keyActions.note: Entirely safe. Items point at the record, not at the words in it, so a corrected spelling appears against every item using it at once.

keyActions.how: The pencil, then change Position in the list. Lower comes first; values sharing a position fall back to their code.
keyActions.note: This is what sizes need - 12mm, 25mm and 50mm is the order a person expects and is not the order they sort in.

keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Offered on forms and save.
keyActions.note: Refused while any item or variant still carries it - see the rules.

keyActions.action: Look at one attribute at a time
keyActions.how: The two boxes above the table: the first chooses Finish, Size or Colour, the second chooses Offered or Retired. The search box finds a code or a name.

flow: Open the Attributes tab.
Filter to the attribute being extended - Finish, say.
Press New value.
Enter a short code (ANTIQUE-BRASS) and the name as it should read on forms (Antique Brass).
Set the position if the order on the form matters, and save.
Open any item form: the new finish is now in the Finish list.
rules: Which of the three an entry belongs to is fixed once created. Moving a value from Finish to Colour would silently retarget every item pointing at it, so it cannot be done - retire it and create a new one under the right attribute.
The code is fixed once created too, and must be unique within its own attribute. Two finishes cannot share a code; a finish and a colour may.

Renaming is free and is the whole point of the list. Because items reference the record rather than the text, correcting a spelling here corrects it everywhere - on items, on variants and in every report that groups by it.

There is no delete. A value can only be retired, and retiring is refused while any item or variant still carries it. Change those items first. The reason is direct: an item would otherwise be showing a value its own edit form could no longer offer, and the next person to save that item would drop it without noticing.
A retired value stays on the items that already have it - it simply stops being offered to anyone filling in a new one.
The item form shows these boxes to anyone entitled to read the values. Adding to the list is a separate right, so an item clerk can choose a finish without being able to invent one.
screens.permission: Reading the list needs the right to view item attributes; adding, renaming and retiring need the right to manage them. Without the change right the list is fully readable with no New button and no pencil.
screens.notes: This is the newest part of the screen and the one the client asked for, so it deserves a full page in the deck. For the screenshot, filter to Finish - a list of real finishes reads far better than a mixture of all three. The Offered/Retired filter is labelled in those words rather than Active/Inactive, which is worth matching in the caption.

screens.title: Brands
screens.purpose: The names the business sells its products under - the house brand, a premium line, and any partner brand whose goods it resells. A brand is a record of its own rather than words typed on each item, so every item carrying it is found with one filter and a corrected spelling reaches every item at once. A brand may name the manufacturer that owns it. It is classification and nothing more: no price, discount, approval or permission anywhere in the system depends on which brand an item carries.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the product data - usually the person who maintains the item master.

keyActions.how: New brand at the top right. Give it a code and a name, and optionally the manufacturer that owns it, a position in the list and a description.
keyActions.note: As soon as it is saved it appears in the Brand box on every item form and in the brand filter on the item list.

keyActions.action: Correct a name or change the owner
keyActions.how: The pencil at the end of the row.
keyActions.note: Safe: items point at the brand record, not at its words, so the new name shows everywhere at once. The code is locked.

keyActions.action: Choose the order brands are offered in
keyActions.how: The pencil, then change Position in the list. Lower comes first.
keyActions.note: Put the house brand first, whatever its code sorts as.

keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Offered on item forms and save.
keyActions.note: Refused while any item still carries the brand - move those items first.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu at the end of the row, then Retire brand. Give a reason and confirm.
keyActions.note: Refused while any item still carries the brand, and the dialog shows exactly why. The reason is kept on the audit trail.

keyActions.how: The status box and, for someone who may read manufacturers, the Owner box above the table; the search box finds a code or a name. Click the Code, Name or Position heading to sort.

flow: Open the Brands tab.
Press New brand.
Enter a short code (ATCRAFT-PRO) and the name as it should read on forms (ATCRAFT PRO).
Choose the owning manufacturer if there is one, and a position if the order on the form matters.
Save, then open any item form: the brand is now in the Brand list.
rules: The code is unique within the business and fixed once created. A retired brand's code is never reused either, because it still appears in the history of the items that carried it.
A brand has at most one owner - the manufacturer whose brand it is - recorded for reference only.
A brand cannot be switched off or retired while any item, active or inactive, still carries it. Move the items to another brand first; the refusal says so.
Retiring is final: a retired brand disappears from every list and picker, and nothing on this screen brings it back.
Nothing in the system decides anything from a brand. Prices, discounts, approvals and stock all ignore it; it exists to classify, filter and report.
screens.permission: Reading the list needs the right to view brands; adding, editing and retiring need the right to manage them. The Owner column and filter also need the right to view manufacturers - without it a recorded owner reads 'Not in the active list'.
screens.notes: The demonstration data carries three brands - ATCRAFT, ATCRAFT PRO and a fictional partner brand on the bought-in lock cylinders - so the screenshot shows real rows.

screens.title: Manufacturers
screens.purpose: Who actually makes a part. That is often not who sells it to you: a lock cylinder is routinely bought from a distributor while being made by someone else, which is why a manufacturer is a list of its own and not a vendor. The business's own works belong here too, as the maker of everything made in-house. An item records its maker and the maker's own part number, and each supplier link records which maker's part that supplier delivers - so a recall notice or a warranty claim can be traced to the right goods.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the product data, and the buyers who source parts by maker.

keyActions.how: New manufacturer at the top right. Give it a code and a name, and optionally its registered legal name, its country (India unless changed), website and notes.
keyActions.note: It is then offered on the item form, as a brand owner, and is shown against the supplier links that name it.

keyActions.how: The pencil at the end of the row.
keyActions.note: The code is locked; everything else can change.

keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Offered on forms and save.
keyActions.note: Refused while items, supplier links or brands still name it.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Retire manufacturer. Give a reason and confirm.
keyActions.note: When it is refused, the dialog names what is in the way - items, supplier links or brands.

keyActions.how: The status box above the table; the search box finds a code, a name or a legal name. Click the Code or Name heading to sort.

flow: Open the Manufacturers tab.
Press New manufacturer.
Enter the code and the trading name; add the legal name and website if they help.
Save. The maker is now offered on the item form and as a brand owner.
rules: The code is unique within the business, fixed once created, and never reused after the manufacturer is retired.
A manufacturer cannot be switched off or retired while any item, supplier link or brand still names it. The refusal says which.
A manufacturer is not a vendor. Nothing is ordered from, received from or paid to a manufacturer; those are vendor matters.
A manufacturer's part number is free text, kept exactly as the maker writes it; the system never interprets it.
Nothing in the system decides anything from a manufacturer: it is recorded for traceability and reporting.
screens.permission: Reading the list needs the right to view manufacturers; adding, editing and retiring need the right to manage them.
screens.notes: The demonstration data carries the company's own works and two fictional outside makers - a lock-cylinder maker and a spring and fastener maker - whose parts arrive through the demonstration fastener distributor.

screens.title: Price lists
screens.purpose: What an item sells for, to whom, in what quantity, and from when. A price is four things at once - a channel, an optional variant, a quantity slab and a dated window - and holding all four is what lets the system answer "what does this cost today?" with one number rather than a judgement. Sales order entry reads this list, so a rate agreed with a dealer takes effect the moment it is entered here, without anybody retyping it on an order.
screens.whoUses: The owner, or whoever sets prices - and it is read by anyone raising a sales order.

keyActions.how: The Item box at the top of the tab. Type part of a code or name and choose from the list.
keyActions.note: A price list belongs to one item, so nothing is shown until an item is chosen.

keyActions.how: New price at the top right. Choose the channel - Sale, Dealer or Distributor - whether it applies to every variant or one, the currency, the amount, the quantity it applies from, and the dates it is valid between.
keyActions.note: Leave the end date empty for a price that runs until it is superseded. Applies from quantity of nought means it applies at any quantity.

keyActions.how: The pencil at the end of the row.
keyActions.note: The amount, the quantity slab, the dates and the notes can be changed. The channel, the currency and the variant cannot.

keyActions.action: Take a price out of use without losing it
keyActions.how: The pencil, then clear Active and save.
keyActions.note: An inactive row is ignored when a price is worked out, and stops blocking a new row that would otherwise clash with it. It stays visible and on the record.

keyActions.how: The bin icon at the end of the row, then confirm.
keyActions.note: It disappears from the list and from price resolution. If the record matters, turn Active off instead.

keyActions.how: The boxes above the table filter by channel, by variant and by status.

flow: Open the Prices tab and choose the item.
Read the existing rows - Valid to shows "Until superseded" for an open-ended price.
If a price is being replaced, edit the row it replaces and give it an end date first.
Press New price, choose the channel, enter the amount and the date it takes effect from.
Save. The new rate is used by sales order entry from that date.
rules: Two active prices may not overlap on channel, variant, quantity slab and dates all at once. A save that would overlap is refused and names the row it clashes with - close that one first. This is what keeps "the price today" a single answer instead of a choice between two.

The channel, the currency and the variant are what a price is, and cannot be changed after it is saved. Quotations already raised on it would otherwise stop making sense. To move a price to another channel, close this row and add a new one.
An end date, once set, cannot be removed. Add a new row for the period that follows instead.
Amounts are held in the currency stated on the row and shown in it; nothing on this screen adds two currencies together.
screens.permission: Reading needs the right to view prices; adding, editing and removing need the right to manage them. Choosing an item needs the right to search the item master as well - without it the tab says so plainly and can still be opened from a link that already names an item.
screens.notes: This tab looks empty until an item is chosen, so the screenshot must be taken with an item selected and a few price rows visible - ideally one Sale row and one Dealer row on the same item, which is what makes the channel column mean something.

screens.title: Organisation
screens.purpose: Who the company legally is, where it operates from, how it is divided, and where its costs are charged. The company record carries the name, GST and PAN numbers and the registered address that appear on documents, and the bank details and terms printed on every invoice. Branches are GST registrations and billing addresses. Plants are the manufacturing sites that warehouses, production orders and people belong to. Departments group people and nest inside one another, and each may name a default cost centre. Cost centres - where money is charged - have their own tab and their own page in this handbook. This is set up once at the start and then touched rarely - usually when a new site opens, a registration changes or the bank account does.
screens.whoUses: The owner and whoever administers the system. Nobody else needs to open it.

keyActions.how: The Company tab. Change the name, legal name, GSTIN, PAN, CIN, contact details, address, currency, financial-year start month or time zone, then Save.
keyActions.note: Without the right to change it, the same details are shown as a plain list rather than a form nobody can submit.

keyActions.action: Record the bank details printed on invoices
keyActions.how: The Company tab, the Bank & invoice card below the company details. Bank, branch, IFSC, account name, account number and the invoice terms, then Save bank details.
keyActions.note: Saved on its own, never as a side effect of correcting the address above, and every change is kept in the audit trail with the account number masked. The IFSC is checked for its shape - four letters, a zero, then six letters or digits - and spaces in it or in the account number are dropped, so both can be typed as they are printed on a cheque leaf.

keyActions.how: The Branches tab, then New branch. Code, name, GSTIN, address, GST state code, contact details, and the Head office and Active boxes.
keyActions.note: The code is printed on documents and cannot be changed later.

keyActions.how: The Plants tab, then New plant. Code, name, the branch it belongs to, and its address.
keyActions.note: Warehouses and production orders are placed against a plant, so add the plant before the warehouses.

keyActions.how: The Departments tab, then New department. Code, name, the plant it sits at, the department it sits under, the head of department and its default cost centre.
keyActions.note: Departments nest, so a shop-floor section can sit under Production without being a plant of its own.

keyActions.action: Retire a branch, plant, department or cost centre
keyActions.how: The three-dot menu at the end of the row, then Retire. Type a reason and confirm.
keyActions.note: The reason is required, and it is kept. A record that vanished for no stated reason is exactly what makes an audit trail useless six months later.

flow: Open Organisation from Administration in the left-hand menu.
Fill in the Company tab first - it is what appears on documents.
Add the branches: one per GST registration.
Add the plants under their branches.
Add the departments, nesting them as the business is actually organised, and name a head for each.
rules: A branch, plant or department code cannot be changed once created, because it appears on issued documents and in past audit records.
There can only be one head office, and the head office cannot be retired. Nominate another branch as head office first.
A branch cannot be retired while people are still assigned to it, or while it still has plants or warehouses. Reassign those first.
A plant cannot be retired while people are assigned to it, or while it still has departments or warehouses.
A department cannot be retired while it still has sub-departments, or while people are assigned to it.

A department's default cost centre is offered only to people who may see cost centres, and while a department names it that cost centre cannot be switched off. Someone who edits the department without that right leaves the default exactly as it was.
Retiring never deletes history: the record stops being offered on new documents, and everything that already refers to it keeps its history and stays readable.

The bank details are optional. Anyone who may read the company record sees them in full - they are printed on every invoice the company sends - and only someone who may change the company record can change them.
screens.permission: Each tab has its own read right - company, branches, plants, departments, cost centres - and its own change right. A tab the account may not read is not shown at all; a tab it may read but not change is fully readable with no New, Edit or Retire. The bank card follows the company rights.
screens.notes: One thing to flag to whoever administers the system: opening this screen at all requires the right to view the company record or the right to view cost centres. An account given only the branch or plant right will not reach the screen, so grant the company view right alongside. The accounts team, who keep the cost centres, reach the screen on that right alone. The Financial years and Cost centres tabs are on this same screen but are described separately, because each is a different job.

screens.title: Cost centres
screens.purpose: Where money is charged. A cost centre is a shop, a process or a sales zone - die-casting, machining, plating, the West zone - and centres nest, so Machining can sit under Production. Production orders, job-work orders, stock adjustments and vendor invoices can each name one, a department names one as its default and a work centre names the one its machine hours are charged to. When a vendor invoice is approved its purchase cost reaches the ledger split by cost centre, and the Cost centre statement reads the ledger back per centre and account.
screens.whoUses: The accountant, who keeps the list. Buyers, planners and the production team, who name a cost centre on the documents they raise.

keyActions.how: Organisation, the Cost centres tab, then New cost centre. Code, name, type (Production, Service, Administration or Selling), the parent it sits under, and optionally the plant, the head and a description.
keyActions.note: The type only groups the centre on reports - nothing else depends on it. The code is printed on the statement and cannot be changed later.

keyActions.action: Charge a document to a cost centre
keyActions.how: The Cost centre box on the production order, job-work order, stock adjustment and vendor invoice forms. A vendor invoice line has its own box, which defaults to the invoice's.
keyActions.note: Optional: left empty, the document is unallocated. The box is shown only to people who may see cost centres; for everyone else a new document is raised unallocated and an amended one keeps the centre it had.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu at the end of the row, Edit, clear Active and save.
keyActions.note: Refused while an active sub-centre, a department default or a work centre still uses it. Documents that already name it keep it.

keyActions.action: Retire a cost centre for good
keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Retire. Type a reason and confirm.
keyActions.note: Refused while anything at all names it - a sub-centre, a department, a work centre or any document - so stopping it being offered is usually the right step instead. Posted ledger history keeps its centre either way.

keyActions.action: See the spending by cost centre
keyActions.how: Reports, then Cost centre statement, with a date range.
keyActions.note: Each row is one cost centre and one ledger account over the period.

flow: Open Organisation from Administration in the left-hand menu, then the Cost centres tab.
Add the top-level centres first - Production, the service functions, Administration, Sales.
Add the centres beneath them - one per process under Production, one per zone under Sales.
Give each department its default cost centre on the Departments tab, and each work centre its own on the Routing screen.
From then on, name the cost centre on each production order, job-work order, adjustment and vendor bill as it is raised.
rules: A cost centre is optional everywhere. A document without one is unallocated; nothing is ever charged to a default centre behind anybody's back.

The statement reads the posted ledger, and today the postings that carry a cost centre are approved vendor invoices - and their reversals. A production order, job-work order or stock adjustment records its cost centre on the document, where it is kept for reporting, but posts nothing to the ledger by itself.
Only income and expense postings carry a cost centre. Tax, payables, stock and bank balances never do.

A vendor invoice line is charged to its own cost centre, else to the invoice's, else nowhere - decided when the invoice is approved, so changing the invoice's centre moves every line that names none of its own.
A new posting needs an active cost centre. An invoice whose centre was switched off after it was entered is refused at approval until it is changed.
Centres nest at most six levels deep, the same limit as departments, and an active centre cannot sit under an inactive one.
Reversing a posted journal keeps its cost centre - even one retired since - so a reversal cancels out on the statement as well as on the account.
The code cannot be changed once created, and a retired centre's code cannot be reused.
screens.permission: Reading the list needs the right to view cost centres, which on its own also opens the Organisation screen. Adding, changing, switching off and retiring need the right to manage them. The accounts role holds both; the purchase, production and planning roles can view, so they can name a centre on their documents.
screens.notes: The demonstration data carries an example tree for an architectural-hardware works: Production with die-casting, machining, buffing and polishing, plating/PVD (job-worked), assembly and packing beneath it; Quality Control, Stores, Maintenance and Administration; and Sales with a North and a West zone. Every one of them says it is an example - the breakdown is to be confirmed with Atcraft, not taken as a rule.

screens.title: The accounting calendar
screens.purpose: The financial years every posted document is dated against. Opening the year is a two-minute job at the start of April; closing one is the moment the books for that year stop moving. It sits on the Organisation screen because it belongs to the shape of the company rather than to any one department, but it is the only place in this chapter where an action cannot be undone by the person taking it.
screens.whoUses: The owner and the accountant.

keyActions.how: Open a year at the top right. Give it a code, a start date and an end date, mark it current if it is, and add a note if there is anything to record.
keyActions.note: Do this before any document is posted into the new year.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Edit. Only available while the year is still open.
The three-dot menu, then Close year. Type a reason and confirm.
keyActions.note: Read the confirmation: after this nothing further can be posted into that year.

keyActions.how: The three-dot menu, then Reopen year, with a reason.
keyActions.note: Only a platform administrator sees this, and only they can do it - the system refuses it for anybody else even if they reach it another way.

flow: Open Organisation, then the Financial years tab.
Press Open a year and enter the code and the dates.
Mark it as current so new documents fall into it.
At the end of the year, once everything has been posted and reconciled, use Close year with a reason that says why the books are being closed.
rules: Two years may not cover overlapping dates. A year whose range overlaps another open one is refused.
Closing a year is one-way from this screen. Nothing further can be posted into it, and only a platform administrator can reopen it - that restriction is what makes a filed period trustworthy.
Closing a year also clears its Current marker, because a closed year is history and would otherwise keep occupying its dates.
Reopening is for correcting a genuine error, and the reason given is recorded against the year. When a year is reopened its dates are checked against the other open years again.
screens.permission: Reading the calendar and opening, editing or closing a year go with the general settings rights rather than a right of their own. Reopening a closed year is restricted to a platform administrator.

screens.title: Notifications
screens.purpose: Everything the system wants a particular person to know about: approvals waiting on them, receipts posted, quality decisions taken, stock below its reorder level, jobs that failed. It is the counterpart to the bell in the header - the bell says how many are unread, this screen is where they are read and dealt with. The second tab decides which events reach a person at all, and by which route, so that somebody who wants goods receipts in the app but not in their inbox does not have to choose between all of it and none of it.
screens.whoUses: Everyone, for their own notifications. Nobody sees anybody else's.

keyActions.how: The Inbox tab opens on Unread only. Each card shows the event, how long ago, and a short description.
keyActions.note: Unread items are listed first, then the newest.

keyActions.action: Go to the record behind a notification
keyActions.how: The Open... link at the foot of the card.
keyActions.note: Not every notification points at a document; those without a link are for information.

keyActions.how: Mark read at the right of the card.
Mark all as read, at the top right.
keyActions.note: It reports how many it marked and how many are still unread, because the count can exceed what one screen holds.

keyActions.action: Look back at something already read
keyActions.how: Change the first filter from Unread only to Everything.
keyActions.note: Also filter by severity, or by event type.

keyActions.how: Load more at the foot of the list.
keyActions.note: The list arrives thirty at a time and keeps growing as you press it.

keyActions.how: The Preferences tab. Tick or clear In app and Email against each event, then Save preferences.
keyActions.note: Discard abandons the changes. A row marked "Using the default for this event" has never been changed by you.

flow: Click the bell in the header, or open Notifications.
Work down the unread cards, opening the record behind anything that needs action.
Mark all as read once the list has been dealt with.
Once, at the start: open Preferences and switch off the emails for events you would rather see only in the application.
rules: Repeated events are folded into one card with a count on it - "11 times" - rather than arriving as eleven separate lines, so a machine that stops repeatedly does not bury everything else.

The unread count on the bell and the count on this screen are the same figure and cannot disagree. Past a certain number the count stops being exact and shows as "99+" - that is a floor, not a precise figure.
Email goes to the address on your own profile. Changing where email arrives means changing the account's address, which is an administrator's job.

The events that can raise a notification include approvals pending, granted and rejected, purchase orders and production orders running late, job work overdue, dispatch delayed, a sales order at risk, stock below reorder level, stock shortages, allocation changes, QC inspections pending and QC failures, goods receipts posted, payments due, MRP runs finishing, reports being ready, and background jobs finishing or failing.
screens.permission: Everything here needs the right to see notifications, and everything shown is your own. The bell in the header is hidden entirely from an account without that right, rather than shown as a bell that could never fill up.
screens.notes: For a good screenshot the demo account needs some unread notifications; a freshly seeded system may show "Nothing unread", which is an honest but dull picture. Consider capturing the Preferences tab as well - it is the part the client will actually be asked about.

screens.title: Your account
screens.purpose: Where a person looks after their own sign-in: their password, the extra protection of an authenticator code, and the list of devices currently signed in as them. It is reached from the name menu at the top right of every screen. Nothing here touches anybody else's account, and nothing here needs a permission - taking away somebody's ability to change their own password would lock them into a session they could not get out of.
screens.whoUses: Everyone, for themselves.

keyActions.how: The card at the top shows your last sign-in, whether two-factor is on, your roles, your account type, and how many permissions you hold.
keyActions.note: Permissions are checked on every request, so a change an administrator makes takes effect at once rather than at your next sign-in.

keyActions.how: The Change password card. Type the current password, then the new one twice, then Change password.
keyActions.note: The checklist below the box ticks off each requirement as you type: at least twelve characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol.

keyActions.how: Two-factor authentication, then your current password, then Set up two-factor. Type the secret shown into an authenticator app, then confirm with the six-digit code it produces.
keyActions.note: From then on, signing in asks for a code after the password.

keyActions.how: The same card, with both your current password and a current code from the app.
keyActions.note: Both are asked for on purpose - a stolen phone or a stolen password alone should not be enough to remove it.

keyActions.action: See where you are signed in
keyActions.how: Active sessions lists each device, its address, when it was last used and when it expires. Your own is badged This device.
Revoke at the end of its row.
keyActions.note: Revoking the one marked This device signs you out of the tab you are in.

keyActions.how: Sign out everywhere, at the top right of the sessions card.
keyActions.note: Use this if you think somebody else has your password. It signs out this device too.

flow: Open the name menu at the top right of any screen and choose Profile & sessions.
To change a password: type the current one, then the new one twice, watching the checklist tick off.
Press Change password.
Every other signed-in device is signed out; the one you are using stays signed in.
rules: Changing your password signs out every other device holding your account. That is the point of it - if the reason for changing was that somebody else knew it, leaving their session alive would defeat the change.
The new password must be different from the old one.

Beyond the five rules shown on screen, the system also refuses passwords that are common or that contain your own email address. Those cannot be shown as a live checklist, so they arrive as a message when you press the button.
Changing your password also clears any lock left over from earlier failed attempts.
An administrator can issue a new password for somebody who is locked out, but nobody can read an existing one.
screens.permission: None beyond being signed in. Everyone can read and change their own account, and only their own.
screens.notes: A vendor-portal account or a platform administrator is labelled as such on the details card; ordinary staff read as Internal staff. Resetting somebody else's password happens on the Users screen, which belongs to another chapter.

screens.title: Choose a new password
screens.purpose: The screen a person lands on the first time they sign in with a password an administrator created for them. It is deliberately bare - no menu, no dashboard, nothing but the password form and a way out - because until that temporary password is replaced the rest of the system stays closed. The reason is simple and worth telling staff plainly: whoever set up the account knows that password, so until it is changed the account is not yet the person's own, and anything done under it could not fairly be attributed to them.
screens.whoUses: Every new joiner on their first sign-in, and anyone whose password an administrator has just reset.

keyActions.how: Type the temporary password in Current password, then your own new one twice, and press Change password.
keyActions.note: The same live checklist as on the account screen: twelve characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol.

keyActions.how: Sign out instead, at the foot of the card.
keyActions.note: The same screen will appear at the next sign-in - it cannot be skipped.

flow: Sign in with the address and temporary password the administrator gave you.
This screen opens instead of the dashboard.
Type the temporary password, then choose your own and repeat it.
Press Change password.
The application opens at the dashboard, and every other device signed in as you is signed out.
rules: While the account is in this state, every other address in the system redirects back here. This is not a banner that can be ignored.
The new password must differ from the temporary one - re-entering the administrator's password is refused.
Changing it clears the flag and signs out every other device, keeping the one being used.
The same thing happens whenever an administrator resets an existing person's password, not only on a first sign-in.
screens.permission: None beyond being signed in. It is the only screen an account in this state may open.
screens.notes: This is the same password form as the one on Your account, wrapped in a smaller shell - one task seen twice, so the deck should say so and not repeat the field-by-field description. If a single screenshot has to serve both, take it here: it shows the warning about the temporary password, which is the part a new joiner needs to read.

chapters.groupIntro: This part of the system holds the engineering record: what the business makes and buys, and how each made item is put together. Everything else — purchasing, stores, production, job work, quality, despatch and billing — points back to a row that was created here, so a mistake in this chapter travels everywhere. The item master is the single register of every part, product, consumable and service; the bill of materials states what goes into a product and in what quantity; the routing states the sequence of operations it passes through, on which work centre and machine. The screens are deliberately strict: a bill or a routing that has been approved cannot be quietly altered, because orders have already been placed and jobs already released against it.
chapters.groupTitle: What We Make, and How It Is Built
