screens.title: Item Master
screens.purpose: This is the single register of every distinct thing the business deals in — raw brass, castings, a finished mortice handle, a carton, a consumable, even a service. Every other screen in the ERP reaches back to a row here, so the code and name entered on this screen are what a storekeeper reads on a bin card, a buyer quotes to a vendor and a customer sees on an invoice. The list is designed to stay usable when the master runs into tens of thousands of parts: the search and every filter are answered by the server, and only one page of rows is ever sent to the screen. There is one item master, not separate lists for purchased and manufactured parts, because the same part is very often both.
screens.whoUses: Whoever maintains product data — usually the owner or a senior engineer for new products, and a storekeeper or buyer looking a part up during the day.

keyActions.action: Find an item by code or name
keyActions.how: Type into the search box above the grid.
keyActions.note: The search looks through the entire item master, not just the rows on screen. It needs at least two characters — a single letter would force the system to read every row and would be too slow to be useful, so it is ignored.

keyActions.action: Narrow the list to one category, group, brand or status
keyActions.how: Use the drop-downs in the toolbar: category, item group, brand (offered to someone who may read brands), and Active only / Inactive only.
keyActions.note: Choosing a category also brings in everything filed under its sub-categories. The status control offers only the two real states — there is no 'show everything' option.

keyActions.action: Find items by what they are allowed to do
keyActions.how: Open the Capabilities button in the toolbar and tick one or more of Purchasable, Manufacturable, Sellable, BOM component, Assembly component, Spare part, Job work.
keyActions.note: Several may be ticked at once and they are combined, so 'purchasable AND manufacturable' is a real question the list can answer. The count of active ticks is shown on the button.

keyActions.how: Press Clear, which appears next to the filters as soon as one is set.
Click the code, or click anywhere on the row.
Press New item at the top right, fill the form and press Create item.
keyActions.note: Only visible to someone with the right to create items.

keyActions.action: Change how many rows are shown, or the sort order
keyActions.how: Use the page-size selector at the foot of the grid (25, 50, 100 or 200 — it opens at 50) and click the Code or Name column heading to sort.

flow: Press New item.
Enter the code and the name. The code is normalised by the system, so RM-001 and 'rm 001' cannot become two separate items.
Choose the item group — raw material, component, semi-finished, finished good, consumable, packing material, spare, scrap or service.
Optionally choose a category, a finish, size and colour, a brand and a manufacturer from the lists the business maintains, and type the manufacturer's own part number.
Choose the base unit — the unit stock is counted in. Optionally set a different purchase unit and sale unit; both start as 'Same as base'.
Enter the HSN code and the GST rate.
Choose the production type — Make, Buy, Make or buy, or Job work — and enter lead time in days, reorder level, and standard cost if you are entitled to see costs.
Tick every capability the item genuinely has. At least one must be ticked.
Press Create item.
rules: An item code is unique within the business and cannot be changed after the item is created, because it is printed on labels and quoted on documents that have already left the building. If a code is wrong, create the correct item and retire the wrong one.

The nine capabilities are independent, on purpose. One item may be purchasable, manufacturable and sellable at the same time — a handle bought from a trader in season and made in the workshop out of season is one part, not two.
At least one capability must be ticked. An item that can do nothing is unusable by every other screen and is almost always a slip of the keyboard, so the system refuses to save it.

The production type and the capabilities must agree: Make needs 'Manufacturable', Buy needs 'Purchasable', Make or buy needs both, and Job work needs 'Job work'. Otherwise planning would raise a suggestion to make something no production order can be created for.
The item group is a reporting classification only. It never decides what an item is allowed to do — the capabilities do that, and nothing re-reads the group afterwards.

A purchase or sale unit must be convertible to the base unit, and the conversion must already be defined under Masters. This is checked when you save, so the problem surfaces at the desk rather than at a goods receipt with the vendor's lorry at the gate.
GST rate cannot exceed 100 percent and lead time cannot exceed 3650 days.

An optional default bin must belong to the item's default warehouse. Receipt and material-issue pickers prefill it only in that warehouse; you can clear or choose a different bin. Reassign the default before retiring its bin.
screens.permission: Anyone who may view items can open this screen. New item appears only for someone with the right to create items. The Standard cost column is shown only to someone with the right to see item costs — the figure is withheld by the system itself, not merely hidden. The category and unit pickers need the separate rights to view categories and to view units; without them those drop-downs simply come up empty. The brand filter, and the Brand and Manufacturer boxes on the form, need the rights to view brands and manufacturers; without them the boxes offer only 'None', and editing an item keeps whatever brand and maker it already records.
screens.notes: Two honest gaps worth knowing before the screenshot is taken. (1) The grid deliberately carries no stock or reorder-level column — stock for one item is answered on that item's Stock tab, and putting it in a list of 50 rows would mean a separate stock look-up per row. (2) Nothing in the application deactivates an item, so the 'Inactive only' filter will normally return an empty list; items leave service by being retired, not deactivated. There is no delete on this screen. On a fresh system the capability icons on each row will look sparse, because the create form starts with every capability unticked rather than pre-ticking the ones usual for the chosen group.

screens.title: The Item Record
screens.purpose: Everything the business knows about one item, gathered into six tabs so that a question about stock, a question about which products use the part, and a question about who supplies it are all answered from the same place. Each tab loads only when it is opened, so the record appears immediately and the heavier questions are asked only when someone actually asks them. This is also where an item is edited and, at the end of its life, retired.
screens.whoUses: Everyone: a buyer checking a supplier and a last purchase price, a storekeeper checking what is on the shelf and what is reserved, an engineer checking which products would be affected by a change.

keyActions.how: Overview tab — code, name, group, category, the three units, production type, lead time, HSN and GST, reorder and safety levels, shelf life, whether stock is batch or serial tracked, sale and dealer price, the finish, size and colour, and the brand, the manufacturer and the manufacturer's part number.
keyActions.note: The panel beside it lists all nine capabilities as separate Yes/No lines, never as a single classification.

keyActions.how: Press Edit in the header and change what is needed: the sale and dealer prices (only for someone with the price-management right), the planning figures (minimum order, reorder quantity, safety stock, shelf life, default bin), and whether stock is batch or serial tracked.
keyActions.note: The code is locked. Changing batch or serial tracking while the item holds stock anywhere is refused — clear the balance first. A shelf life needs batch tracking.

keyActions.action: See the finish, size and colour variants of this item
keyActions.how: Variants tab.
keyActions.note: A variant shares this item's bill of materials, planning figures and capabilities and differs only in its identity, its price and cost difference against the parent, and its barcode. Anything that needs its own bill of materials is a new item, not a variant.

keyActions.how: Variants tab: New variant, or the pencil at the end of a variant's row. Pick at least one of finish, size or colour, and the price difference against the parent (negative allowed).
keyActions.note: Adding needs the right to create items, editing the right to update them. The code is locked after creation. The cost difference is shown only to someone who may see costs.

keyActions.action: See stock of this item everywhere
keyActions.how: Stock tab — four totals across the whole business (on hand, reserved, available, and owned but elsewhere), then a row per warehouse showing on hand, reserved, QC hold, damaged, in transit, at job work and available.
keyActions.note: 'At job work' is stock the business still owns but which is sitting at an outworker. It is the quantity people forget when a part reads short.

keyActions.action: See which products use this part
keyActions.how: Where used tab — every bill of materials that lists this item as a component, with the parent's code, the bill and its version, the status, and the quantity per.
keyActions.note: This is the impact check before changing or retiring a part. Obsolete bills are left out, because the question is what a change would break now.

keyActions.how: Prices tab — channel (sale, dealer, distributor), price, the quantity the slab starts at, and the dates it is valid between.
keyActions.note: Read only here. Prices are added and changed under Masters, on the Prices tab.

keyActions.action: See the suppliers of this part
keyActions.how: Vendors tab — vendor, the vendor's own code for the part, the maker's part number it delivers (with the maker's name), lead time, minimum order, order multiple, last purchase price and date, and which one is preferred.
keyActions.note: The last purchase price is written by goods receipts and cannot be typed here.

keyActions.action: Link, edit, prefer or unlink a supplier
keyActions.how: Vendors tab: Link vendor, or the star, pencil and bin icons at the end of a link's row. The star makes that source the preferred one.
keyActions.note: All four need the right to update items.

keyActions.how: Press Retire in the header and confirm.
keyActions.note: Only offered to someone with the right to delete items, and only while the item has not already been retired.

keyActions.how: Variants tab, then the bin icon at the end of the variant's row.

flow: Open the item from the Item Master list.
Read the Overview to confirm it is the right part.
Before changing anything structural, open Where used to see which products would be affected.
Press Edit, make the change, and Save changes.
To take a part out of service: open Where used and Stock first, then press Retire, read the warning the dialog puts up, and confirm.
rules: Retirement is final. A retired item stops appearing on every list, picker and lookup in the application, this page stops opening, and nothing anywhere brings it back. If the item might be needed again, do not retire it.

Nothing is erased when an item is retired. Ledger entries, bill-of-materials lines and documents already issued keep their reference to it, so history and old paperwork still resolve the code and name.

Retirement is not blocked by stock or by use in a bill of materials — but the confirmation goes and looks before you commit, and tells you how much stock will be left stranded and how many bills still list the part. That is a decision for you to take, not a rule the system will enforce.
No reason is recorded for a retirement, because the system does not ask for one: the audit trail records the act and your name against it.
A retired finish, size or colour cannot be assigned to an item, but an item that already carries one keeps it. Master data is tidied going forward, never by rewriting what was already recorded.
A variant's finish, size and colour combination is freed the moment it is retired, so an identical variant can be created again under a new code.

A brand or manufacturer that has been switched off cannot be newly given to an item, and neither can be switched off while items still carry it - so the brand an item shows is always one the business still offers.
screens.permission: Viewing needs the right to see items. Edit appears for someone with the right to update items; Retire, both for the item and for a variant, needs the right to delete items — deliberately a different right, because deactivating is reversible and retiring is not. The Stock tab needs the right to view inventory, Where used the right to view bills of materials, and Prices the right to view prices; without them the tab shows a polite note instead of the data. Standard cost and the variants' cost difference are shown only with the right to see item costs.
screens.notes: Several things on this screen are read-only and the deck should say so rather than leave the reader hunting for a button. Variants cannot be created or edited anywhere in the application — only listed and retired. Supplier links cannot be created or edited anywhere. Prices are maintained under Masters, not here. Sale price and dealer price appear on the Overview but there is no field for them on the item form, so on a system without seeded data they will read zero. The 'Valuation' line on the Overview will show a dash: the field was removed from the system and the screen still asks for it. Batch and serial tracking are shown but cannot be changed from any screen. There is no activate/deactivate control. The Where used tab lists direct parents only, so its Level column always reads 1.

screens.title: Bills of Material
screens.purpose: The register of every bill of materials in the business — one row per version, not one per product. A single handle legitimately carries a superseded version 1, a live approved version 2 and a version 3 being drafted for next season, and this list shows all three rather than hiding them behind whichever is current. A bill only starts driving planning and production once it has been approved, and only one approved bill per product can be the default one planning reaches for.
screens.whoUses: The engineer or product-development person who writes bills, and the person who approves them.

keyActions.how: Type the bill's code into the search box, or sort by clicking the BOM code, Version, Status, Effective from or Approved column headings.
Two drop-downs in the toolbar: status (Draft, Pending approval, Approved, Obsolete) and type (Production, Assembly, Phantom, Alternate).
keyActions.note: Press Clear to drop both filters at once.

keyActions.how: Click the BOM code, or click anywhere on the row.

keyActions.action: Jump to the product a bill is for
keyActions.how: Click 'Open item' in the Item column.
Press New BOM at the top right.
keyActions.note: Only visible with the right to create bills of materials.

keyActions.action: See at a glance which bill planning will use
keyActions.how: Look for the green Default badge and the Approved status on the same row.

flow: Press New BOM.
Search the item master for the product this bill produces.
Choose the type — Production is the normal one — and a revision letter.
Enter the output quantity: how many units one run of this bill yields. Choose the base unit.
Set Effective from, and leave Effective to empty for an open-ended version.
Tick 'Make this the default bill for the item' if this is the bill planning should use once it is approved.
Add the component lines: search the item master for each component, enter the quantity per, the scrap percentage, and tick Optional where the component is a configurable extra.
Add a note if the revision needs explaining, then press Create BOM. The bill is created as a draft, and its code and version number are issued by the system.
rules: A bill can only be written for a product that is flagged 'Manufacturable' on the item master. If it is refused, open the item and enable that capability first.
A component must be flagged 'BOM component' and must be active. A part cannot be a component of itself.
A bill needs at least one component line. The system will not accept an empty structure.

Quantities on a line must be stated in the component's own stock unit. This is not a convenience — components are added up across every level of every structure, so a line entered in boxes under one parent and in numbers under another would produce a total that looks plausible and is wrong.
The version number is issued by the system, not typed. Two engineers creating a bill for the same product at the same moment therefore cannot be given the same number.
Only one approved bill per product may be the default. Approving a new default automatically stands the old one down in the same step, so the slot is never occupied twice.
An Alternate bill must name the bill it stands in for, and that bill must be for the same product.
screens.permission: Viewing needs the right to see bills of materials. New BOM needs the right to create them. Nothing on this list changes a bill's status — that is done inside the bill.
screens.notes: The Item column can only show a link reading 'Open item', not the product's code and name: the list rows the system returns carry the product's identity but not its part number. The bill's own code is the identity this grid can honestly show, and the product's code and name do appear once the bill is opened.

screens.title: One Bill of Materials
screens.purpose: One version of one product's structure, shown four ways: the components the bill itself states, the full multi-level requirement for a real order quantity, the costed roll-up, and the other products that use the same parent item. This is where a bill is submitted, approved, rejected, retired or copied forward. The tab that earns its place is Exploded requirements — it walks every level below the product, and a part reached through several sub-assemblies comes back as one line with the quantities added together, which is the number a buyer actually needs.
screens.whoUses: The engineer who wrote the bill and the senior person who approves it; a planner or buyer reading the exploded requirement before a run.

keyActions.how: Structure tab — line number, component, quantity per, scrap percentage, the operation the line is assigned to, and whether each part is made or bought.
keyActions.note: This is one level only, exactly as the bill was written, for the bill's own output quantity. Optional lines and substitutes are marked.

keyActions.action: Work out what a real order needs
keyActions.how: Exploded requirements tab, type the order quantity into 'Quantity to explode'.
keyActions.note: The list redraws about half a second after you stop typing. Three tiles above it say how many distinct components came back, how many of those were merged from more than one branch, and how many levels were traversed.

keyActions.action: See which sub-assemblies a merged part came from
keyActions.how: On the Exploded requirements tab, click the last column of a row marked 'appears in N sub-assemblies'.
keyActions.note: A screw used twice in one handle and four times in a lock body appears as a single line for six, and this is where you see the two branches that were added together.

keyActions.how: Cost tab — material cost, operation cost, total, and cost per unit, with a line-by-line breakdown showing where each rate came from.
keyActions.note: If any part in the structure carries no cost, a warning names them and says plainly that the total is a floor, not the full cost.

keyActions.action: See which other products use this one
keyActions.how: Where used tab.
Press Submit for approval, type a reason, confirm.

keyActions.action: Approve or reject a submitted bill
keyActions.how: Press Approve or Reject, type a reason, confirm.
keyActions.note: Rejecting sends the bill back to draft with your reason attached — it does not destroy anything.

keyActions.action: Make a change to an approved bill
keyActions.how: Press Copy as new version, give the reason, an effective-from date, and choose whether the operations are carried across too.
keyActions.note: The version you were looking at is left exactly as it was, and you are taken straight to the new draft.

keyActions.how: Press Mark obsolete, type a reason, confirm.

keyActions.action: Throw away a draft that was never released
keyActions.how: Press Delete draft, type a reason, confirm.
Edit draft on a DRAFT bill: the component grid and the operations grid arrive prefilled, and Save replaces both wholesale
keyActions.note: A bill someone else saved first answers with a conflict - reload it and re-apply the change. A draft approved without operations takes the item’s default routing as its operation steps.

flow: Open the bill from the Bills of Material list.
Check the Structure tab against the drawing.
Open Exploded requirements and type the quantity of a typical run, to see the full requirement and check nothing is missing or doubled.
Open Cost and see whether the roll-up is complete or whether parts are missing a cost.
When it is right, press Submit for approval and give the reason.

A second person opens the same bill and presses Approve, with their own reason. The bill becomes available to planning and production and, if it was marked default, replaces the previous default in the same step.
Later, when the design changes: press Copy as new version, edit the new draft's components, and take it through submission and approval again.
rules: An approved bill cannot be edited. Production orders, purchase orders and costings already raised against it must keep resolving to the structure they were planned against — so a change is a new version, created with Copy as new version, and the old version stays exactly as the paperwork remembers it.

A bill of materials cannot be approved by the person who wrote it. Approval is evidence of a second person's judgement, and a bill approved by its own author is not evidence of anything. Someone holding the top administrator role is the only exception.
A bill with no mandatory component lines cannot be submitted, because approving it would release a structure that produces nothing. Optional lines and substitutes do not count towards this.
Every status change — submit, approve, reject, mark obsolete, delete draft — requires a reason of at least three characters, and the reason is recorded against your name.

Marking a bill obsolete keeps the record. Planning stops choosing it and every order already raised against it still resolves. If it was the default for its product, it stops being the default, which frees the slot for a replacement.

Deleting is only offered on a draft, and it destroys the record — the draft, its lines and its operations all go, and only the audit entry survives. It is safe only because a draft has never been released to anything that could point at it. A draft that other alternate structures point at is refused even so.
Below the top level, the explosion only follows bills that are approved and in date. A draft's explosion therefore shows its own lines and then only the approved sub-assemblies underneath.

A phantom sub-assembly is dissolved on the way through: it never appears as a component of its own, its parts appear directly instead. The screen names any phantom it passed through, so nothing looks lost.

Optional components and substitute lines are shown on the structure but do not create a requirement of their own — a substitute is a replacement for another line and would double the count, and an optional extra is demanded by the order that selects it.
Structures are followed down at most twenty levels.
screens.permission: Viewing needs the right to see bills of materials. Submit for approval needs the right to update them; Approve and Reject need the right to approve them; Mark obsolete and Delete draft both need the right to make bills obsolete — deliberately not the editing right, because destroying a structure is closer to retiring one than to changing it. Copy as new version needs the right to create bills. The Cost tab needs the separate right to see bill-of-materials costs.
screens.notes: The important gap in this chapter: there is no way to edit a draft bill's lines once it has been created. The create dialog is the only place components are entered. In practice a wrong draft is deleted and re-created, or copied as a new version and the copy edited — except that the copy cannot be edited either. This is worth flagging to the client. Second: the bill's operations cannot be entered anywhere in the application, so the Operations count in the header will read zero and the 'Operation cost' on the Cost tab will read zero for any bill created through these screens; operation times and rates live on the Routing screen instead. Third: Mark obsolete and Delete draft are never both on screen at once, because the statuses that permit them do not overlap. Fourth: the Where used tab lists direct parents only.

screens.title: Routings, Work Centres and Machines
screens.purpose: How a product is made, as opposed to what it is made of. A routing is the ordered list of operations a product passes through — cut, machine, buff, plate, assemble — each one performed at a work centre and, where the choice matters, on a named machine. Because the hourly rate and the length of the working day belong to the work centre rather than to the operation, all three registers live on one screen as three tabs: change a centre's rate and every routing that uses it is re-costed at its next reading.
screens.whoUses: The production engineer who writes the process, the maintenance planner who keeps the machine register, and the supervisor who records a breakdown.

keyActions.action: Find a routing and see its operations
keyActions.how: Routings tab, then click the row. A panel opens showing the sequence, the operation, the work centre, setup and run minutes, queue and move minutes, the hourly rate, the process charge and the cost per unit — plus the routing's total time, lead time and cost per unit.
keyActions.note: Money columns come from the system's own costing, computed fresh each time. If the costing cannot be read, the money columns are left blank rather than shown as zero — a costing nobody computed is not the same as a costing of nothing.

keyActions.how: Routings tab, New routing.
keyActions.note: Needs the right to manage routings.

keyActions.how: Routings tab, pencil icon at the end of the row.
keyActions.note: The pencil is offered only on a draft. An approved routing shows no pencil, because the system would refuse the change anyway.

keyActions.action: Approve a routing, or retire one
keyActions.how: Open the routing, then Approve (on a draft) or Mark obsolete (on an approved one) at the foot of the panel; type a reason and press Confirm.

Work centres tab — code, name, capacity per hour, rate per hour, setup charge, hours per day and status, and the cost centre the centre's hours are charged to. New work centre to add one, pencil to edit.
keyActions.note: The cost centre box and column are shown only to someone who may see cost centres; anyone else who edits the work centre leaves its cost centre as it was. While a work centre names a cost centre, that cost centre cannot be switched off.

keyActions.how: Machines tab — code, name, type, capacity, rate, condition, last and next service dates. New machine to add one, pencil to edit.
keyActions.note: Sort by 'Next service' to read the grid the way a maintenance planner reads it.

keyActions.action: Record a breakdown or a service
keyActions.how: Machines tab, the spanner icon on the row. Choose the new condition, type a reason, and revise the next-service date at the same time.
keyActions.note: Condition is a recorded change with a reason, not a field on the edit form — a machine out of action stops being offered for work, and that should never happen quietly.

keyActions.how: Routings by status; machines by condition (Available, Running, Maintenance, Breakdown, Retired).

keyActions.action: Put an operation on a machine
keyActions.how: The Machine picker on the operation row, listing the workable machines of that row’s work centre
keyActions.note: The choice is cleared when the work centre changes and unavailable for outsourced steps, which run on the vendor’s equipment. The routing panel shows the machine beside the work centre.

flow: Make sure the work centres exist first, on the Work centres tab, each with its hourly rate, setup charge and working hours per day. Operations are costed at the centre's rate, so a routing cannot be costed before its centres exist.
Add machines to those centres if a particular machine changes the run time.
On the Routings tab press New routing.
Enter the routing code and name, and search the item master for the product it makes.
Set Effective from and, if the process is time-limited, Effective to. Tick 'Default routing for the item' if this is the process planning should use.

Add the operations in order: code, name, work centre, setup minutes, run minutes per unit, queue minutes, move minutes and any flat process charge. Tick 'Job work' where the step goes outside and 'QC' where it must be inspected.
Press Create routing. It is saved as a draft and the version number is issued by the system.
A second person opens the routing and presses Approve with a reason. From that point it is available to planning and production and can no longer be edited.
rules: A routing can only be written for a product flagged 'Manufacturable' on the item master, and that item must be active.
A routing needs at least one operation. Approving one with no operations would release a process that describes no work, so it is refused.
Every operation runs on a work centre. A machine is optional, but if one is named it must belong to that work centre and must not be retired.
An approved routing cannot be edited — production orders and planning runs already reference it. A change means a new routing version.
A routing may not be approved by the person who created it, unless they hold the top administrator role. Approval is a second person's judgement.

Work centres and machines are checked again at the moment of approval. A routing can sit in draft for weeks, and the centre it plans work at may have been closed or the machine scrapped in the meantime; releasing it to the floor without re-checking would push that problem onto the shop.
Only one approved routing per product can be the default. Approving a new default stands the old one down in the same step.

Setup time is paid once per batch and run time for every unit — which is exactly why a larger batch costs less per piece. Queue time and move time lengthen the job but are charged nothing, because nobody is working on the part while it waits in front of a machine or travels between cells.
The rate is the work centre's, never the operation's. Changing a centre's hourly rate re-costs every routing that uses it, at the next time the cost is read.

Lead time is rounded up to whole days, and calculated against the shortest working day among the centres involved. If grinding runs sixteen hours and plating only eight, plating is what the job waits for — taking the longer shift would promise a date the plant cannot hit.

A machine's condition moves in fixed steps. A machine that is running must be stopped before planned maintenance begins, so the job's end is recorded before the downtime starts; a breakdown can be reported from either working state. Retiring a machine is final — production entries still name it, so the record survives, but it can never take work again.
The code of a routing, a work centre or a machine cannot be changed after it is created.
A working day must be more than zero hours and no more than twenty-four.
screens.permission: Three separate rights, not one. Seeing each tab needs the corresponding view right — routings, work centres, machines — and a person who holds none of the three sees a note saying so instead of the screen. Creating and editing routings, and approving or retiring them, need the right to manage routings. Adding and editing work centres needs the right to manage work centres. Adding and editing machines, and changing a machine's condition, needs the right to manage machines. So a machine fitter is not shown the routing form, and a maintenance planner is not hidden from the machine form.
screens.notes: This screen is a set of tabs with dialogs, not a list-and-detail pair like Items and BOM — a routing opens in a panel over the list, so screenshots should be taken with the panel open. Points to flag. (1) Editing a draft routing replaces its whole operation list; the form loads the existing operations from the server first for exactly that reason, and a message says so while it is loading. (2) There is no 'copy as new version' button for routings, although the rule that an approved routing needs a new version is enforced — in practice the client must create a new routing under a new code. (3) There is no way to delete or abandon a draft routing from the screen. (4) The work centre edit form carries a note saying 'use activate or deactivate on the centre itself', but no such control exists on the screen, so a work centre cannot be taken out of use from the application. (5) The Item column on the routing list can only offer an 'Open item' link, because the list rows do not carry the product's code. (6) Costing figures on the routing panel are shown at a quantity of one unit.

chapters.groupIntro: This part of the system answers two questions that run the whole factory: who has committed to buy from us, and what does that oblige us to make or buy. It begins with the accounts themselves — direct customers, OEM buyers, dealers and distributors, each with the credit terms that decide whether an order can be accepted at all — and moves to the sales order, which is where a customer's intention becomes a firm commitment. Confirming an order is the moment that matters: it checks the account's credit standing, then reserves whatever stock is on hand against each line, and reports honestly on whatever it could not cover. What it could not cover is the input to planning. The last two screens are the planning run itself, which takes the confirmed order book, nets it against stock, against orders already placed with suppliers and against work already on the floor, explodes the bills of materials for whatever has to be manufactured, and proposes what to buy, make and send out for job work — proposals a person accepts, never orders it places on its own.

screens.title: Sales orders
screens.purpose: The order book. Every commitment the business has made to a customer sits here, from a draft keyed in five minutes ago to one that is half despatched. It is where a new order is raised and where an existing one is found. It is also the honest picture of demand: an order that is confirmed here is an order the planning engine will plan against.
screens.whoUses: The sales desk and whoever owns the order book — typically a sales executive raising orders and the owner reviewing what has been promised.

keyActions.how: New order, top right. A dialog collects the customer, the warehouse it ships from, the required date and at least one line, then creates the order as a draft and opens it.
keyActions.note: The button only appears for someone with the right to create sales orders. An order cannot be created empty — it needs at least one line in the same step.

keyActions.how: Click the order code, or anywhere on the row.
Customer box in the toolbar; type to search and pick.
Status dropdown — draft, confirmed, allocated, partly despatched, despatched, invoiced, closed or cancelled.
Required from / Required to date boxes.
keyActions.note: This windows on the date the customer needs the goods, not the date the order was keyed in. It is the same date planning works to.

keyActions.how: Tick Urgent only.
Tick Open only.
keyActions.note: "Open" means confirmed, allocated or partly despatched — exactly the orders that still represent unmet demand and exactly what a planning run picks up.

keyActions.how: Search box — matches the order code and the customer's own PO number.
Clear, which appears once at least one filter is set.
Open an order, choose Dispatch, review the prefilled order lines and lower quantities if needed. Record vehicle/LR/tracking evidence, then create the consignment.
For a confirmed or partially dispatched order with a shortage, choose Allocate available stock on Allocation. The scheduled sweep also checks waiting orders every fifteen minutes.
Order detail lists its dispatches and invoices. Once the order is INVOICED, Close order completes it.

flow: Filter to what you are looking at — a customer, a delivery window, or just the open orders.
Read the Required column: an order that is still open and past its date shows in red with the number of days it is late.
Watch for the amber Approval badge beside a status. That order carries a price below cost and cannot be confirmed until somebody signs for it.
Click the order code to open it.
rules: Fifty orders are shown at a time and you page through them; the whole book is never loaded into the browser.
A required date that has already passed is flagged red only while the order is still open — on a despatched or closed order it is history, not a problem.

Priority is a rank from 1 to 9 (5 is normal), and urgency is a separate flag. The two are shown separately because they mean different things: priority decides who gets scarce stock first, urgency is a marker for the desk.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to see sales orders can open this list. The New order button appears only for someone who may create them. The standard Sales Executive role has both.
screens.notes: There is no customer name column — the order row carries a customer reference, not a name, so the customer is offered as a filter instead. Worth saying in the caption so the client does not read it as an omission. A screenshot with a mix of statuses, one red late date and one Approval badge will carry the whole page. Reserved / Dispatchable now / Short are live figures. Closed reservations do not permit shipment; short confirmed orders may dispatch their reserved part.

screens.title: One sales order
screens.purpose: The whole of one order: who it is for, what was promised, what it is priced at, how the tax falls, and — once it is confirmed — exactly how much stock is being held for each line and how much is not. This is the screen where an order is completed, approved if it needs approving, confirmed, and if necessary cancelled. Everything the customer would see on an acknowledgement is calculated here and shown here.
screens.whoUses: The sales executive who raised the order; whoever holds the authority to approve below-cost pricing; the owner deciding whether to confirm.

keyActions.how: Edit, top right. Opens the same form the order was created with.
keyActions.note: Only on a draft, and the customer and order date are locked even then — an order cannot be moved to another account.

keyActions.how: Add line, top right, or the Add line button on the empty Lines table.
keyActions.note: Draft only. Leave the unit price empty and the system prices the line from the customer's own price list. When the item has finish, size or colour variants, pick the variant too — the line is priced with its difference.

keyActions.how: Pencil or bin icon at the end of the line's row.
keyActions.note: Draft only. Removing a line renumbers the rest and the totals are recalculated.

keyActions.how: Approve pricing, which only appears when a line was priced under the item's cost, or discounted above the company threshold, and nobody has signed for it yet.
keyActions.note: Needs the right to approve sales orders, and it may not be the person who raised the order.

keyActions.how: Confirm, top right, then confirm again in the box that explains what confirming does.
keyActions.note: Draft only. This is the step that runs the credit check and reserves stock.

keyActions.how: Cancel order, then type a reason of at least three characters.
keyActions.note: Available on a draft, a confirmed order or a fully allocated one — never once anything has shipped. The reason goes on the audit trail.

keyActions.action: See what is reserved and what is short
keyActions.how: The Allocation panel below the lines, which appears once the order is no longer a draft.
keyActions.note: It shows, per line, what was ordered, what is reserved, what has been despatched, what is still short, and how much free stock there is at the order's warehouse right now.

keyActions.how: Run MRP to plan the balance, in the amber box at the top of the Allocation panel.
Open an order, choose Dispatch, review the prefilled order lines and lower quantities if needed. Record vehicle/LR/tracking evidence, then create the consignment.
For a confirmed or partially dispatched order with a shortage, choose Allocate available stock on Allocation. The scheduled sweep also checks waiting orders every fifteen minutes.
Order detail lists its dispatches and invoices. Once the order is INVOICED, Close order completes it.

flow: Open the order and check the lines, the discounts and the totals.
If an amber banner says the order is waiting for a pricing approval, get it signed — the Confirm button stays greyed until then.
Press Confirm and read what comes back: either the order is fully allocated, or it says how many lines are short.
Read the Allocation panel line by line. A line marked Covered is fully reserved; a line with a shortfall is demand nothing can meet from stock today.
For any shortfall, follow the link to planning and let a run propose how to cover it.
rules: A draft reserves nothing. It is a quotation the customer has not committed to, and holding stock against it would starve an order that is real.

Confirming runs the credit check first, against the customer's account as it stands at that instant. If the account is blocked, inactive, or the order would take the account past its credit limit, the confirmation is refused and the message states the numbers — what is outstanding, what this order adds, and what the limit is. To proceed: settle or write off part of the balance, raise the limit on the customer record, or release the credit hold.

Confirming reserves stock; it does not move it. The goods stay physically where they are and stay in the stock total. What changes is that they stop being available to any other order. Nothing leaves the warehouse until a despatch is made.

Reserving less than was ordered is the normal outcome, not a failure. Refusing the whole order because one line is short would hide the shortage until somebody tried to pick it. The shortfall reported here is exactly the number planning exists to cover.

A line priced below the item's cost, or discounted above the company approval threshold, holds the order at draft until a second person approves it. A discount above the threshold without the discount-override right is refused when the order is saved, not queued. The approver may not be the person who raised the order — an approval signed by the salesperson who granted the discount is not evidence of anything. Discounts that come from a dealer scheme skip the threshold but still face the below-cost check.
Prices come from the price list that belongs to the customer's channel. Typing a price over the top is an override and needs the right to manage prices.

When no discount is typed on a line, the order takes the best dealer scheme that applies — one percentage off, never stacked — and records which scheme it came from. A typed discount always wins and keeps today's approval rules.

Tax is decided once and then frozen on the order: the same state as the seller means CGST plus SGST, a different state (or an export) means IGST. The place of supply comes from the ship-to address. If the selling company or branch has no state code recorded, a taxed order cannot be raised at all — fix the state code on the company or branch first.
The required date cannot be earlier than the order date, and a line quantity must be more than zero. A discount cannot be larger than the line it is discounting.

Once an order is confirmed this screen offers no edits at all except cancellation. The warehouse, the branch and the two addresses are frozen because the order already holds reservations against that warehouse and the tax was settled from those addresses. If something material has to change, cancel and raise a replacement.

Cancelling releases every reservation the order held back to free stock, in the same step. A cancelled order cannot be reopened, and it cannot be cancelled once anything has shipped — a document that moved stock cannot claim never to have existed.
screens.permission: Opening the order needs the right to see sales orders. Edit, Add line, and Confirm all need the right to change sales orders — the same right, so anyone who can edit an order can confirm one. Approve pricing needs the separate right to approve sales orders. Cancel order needs the right to cancel them. The standard Sales Executive role can view, create and update but cannot approve or cancel — those sit with a manager.
screens.notes: Two honest gaps worth knowing before the deck is written. First, there is no Delete button for a draft, even though a draft can technically be removed; in practice anything past draft must be cancelled anyway, so cancellation is the only path this screen offers. Second, the system will accept a quantity or delivery-date change on a confirmed order and will move the reservation to match, but this screen does not offer it — a confirmed order is read-only here. Also: a line shows the description that was keyed against it plus the item's reference, not an item code, because the line record does not carry one. For the screenshot, use a confirmed order with at least one short line so the Allocation panel and its amber banner are both visible; on a draft the panel is replaced by a one-line notice. Reserved / Dispatchable now / Short are live figures. Closed reservations do not permit shipment; short confirmed orders may dispatch their reserved part.

screens.title: Customers
screens.purpose: The account master — everybody the business sells to, whether a direct customer, an OEM buyer, a dealer or a distributor. Each account carries the two facts that govern order entry: which price list it is quoted from, and what credit it has been granted. This screen is where accounts are opened, amended, put on hold, released and eventually retired, and where the addresses and contact people behind each one are kept.
screens.whoUses: The sales desk for day-to-day account work; the owner or accounts for credit limits, holds and retirement.

keyActions.how: New customer, top right. A dialog with three tabs — Details, Addresses, Contacts.
keyActions.note: Addresses and contacts can only be added once the account has been saved, because they hang off it. The dialog says so rather than collecting rows it cannot store.

keyActions.how: Click anywhere on the row, or the pencil icon at the end of it.

keyActions.action: Put an account on credit hold
keyActions.how: Open the account, then Block in the Standing box at the foot of the Details tab. A reason of at least three characters is required.
keyActions.note: A blocked account is refused at order confirmation and the reason is shown to whoever tries. Orders already in flight are not withdrawn.

keyActions.how: Same place — the button reads Unblock once the account is blocked.

keyActions.action: Stop offering an account on new orders
keyActions.how: Deactivate, in the same Standing box, with a reason.
keyActions.note: An inactive account cannot take new orders. Existing documents are unaffected.

keyActions.how: Addresses tab. Add, edit, remove, and set which one is the default for billing or for shipping.
keyActions.note: An address is either billing or shipping, never both. The shipping address is what decides the place of supply, and therefore the GST treatment, on every order.

keyActions.how: Contacts tab. Add, edit, remove, and mark one as primary.
The bin icon at the end of the row, then a reason.
keyActions.note: Greyed out, with the amount named, while the account still owes money.

keyActions.how: Standing dropdown — Blocked only, Not blocked, or Over credit limit.
Search box — matches code, name and GSTIN.

flow: Filter or search to the account.
Click the row to open it.
On Details, set the trading name, the legal name printed on the invoice, GSTIN and PAN, the customer type, the price list, the credit limit and the credit days.
Move to Addresses and record at least the ship-to address, with its state code — the tax on every order depends on it.
Move to Contacts and record who to speak to.
Use the Standing box to block, unblock, activate or deactivate; each of those is recorded with your reason.
rules: A blank credit limit ticked as Unlimited means no ceiling has been agreed — the account can order any value. A limit of zero means the opposite: no credit at all, everything against payment. These two must never be confused, which is why the form makes Unlimited an explicit tick rather than an empty box.

The Outstanding figure is the account's unpaid invoiced value. It turns red when it is past the limit. The system, not the screen, decides who is over their limit, so the Over credit limit filter is right on every page of the list.

Blocking, unblocking, activating and deactivating are separate recorded actions with their own reasons, not tick boxes on the save. A change to an account's standing is a decision somebody made and it belongs on the audit trail with a reason attached.

An account that owes anything — even a credit balance left by an overpayment — cannot be retired. Retiring it would hide a live receivable behind a closed record. Settle or write off the balance first.

Retiring an account removes it from every list and every picker in the system, and retires its addresses and contacts with it. Orders and invoices already issued keep their reference to it; nothing is erased. Bringing an account back is a separate, permissioned action that this screen does not offer.
The account code cannot be changed once the account exists, because it is quoted on orders and invoices already issued.

A GSTIN encodes its state in its first two digits. If that disagrees with the state code on the address, the save is refused — the resulting invoice would be rejected by the GST portal, and one of the two numbers is simply wrong.

Dealer and distributor accounts are the channel team's. Opening one, amending one, blocking one or retiring one needs the dealer-management right on top of the ordinary customer right. Without it those two channels are not even offered in the customer type list, and on an existing dealer account Save, Block and Deactivate are withheld with a note saying who to ask.
screens.permission: Seeing the list needs the right to view customers. New customer needs the right to create; editing and every standing change need the right to update. Retiring needs the right to delete a customer — and, on a dealer or distributor account, the dealer-management right as well. The standard Sales Executive role can view, create and update, but cannot retire an account and cannot touch the dealer channel.
screens.notes: There is no separate customer page — everything, including addresses and contacts, happens in the dialog that opens from the row. The dialog is where the screenshots have to come from. Two things the system knows but this screen does not display: the account's remaining credit headroom, and a live check of whether a particular order value would be accepted. Both are available; neither is on this screen. And there is no way back from retirement here.

screens.title: Dealers
screens.purpose: The dealer and distributor channel seen on its own, and seen read-only. It is the same set of accounts as the Customers screen filtered to the two channel types, with one thing added that Customers does not show: how much credit each account has left. It exists so somebody responsible for the channel can look at its credit position in one place without going account by account.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns the dealer network — a channel or sales manager reviewing exposure, and the owner.

keyActions.how: Channel dropdown — Dealer or Distributor.
keyActions.note: Only those two are offered. Direct and OEM accounts are not part of this list at all.

keyActions.how: Price list dropdown.
keyActions.note: The channel and the price list are separate facts on the account, so a dealer quoted at sale prices is a real situation and is shown as one.

keyActions.action: Find who is blocked or over their limit
keyActions.how: Standing dropdown — Blocked only, Not blocked, or Over credit limit.
State box — two digits of the GST state code, for example 27.
keyActions.note: It filters on the addresses held against the account, so it answers "dealers in Maharashtra" rather than "dealers whose record happens to mention 27".

keyActions.how: Tick Assigned to me.
Status dropdown — Active only, Inactive only, or Any status.
Search box — matches code, name, legal name and GSTIN.

flow: Choose the channel, or leave it on both.
Set Standing to Over credit limit to see the accounts that need a conversation.
Read the Outstanding column: the figure underneath it says how much room is left, or how far over the account is.
Note the Opened date next to it — a week-old dealer at its limit is a different conversation from a five-year-old one.
rules: This screen is read-only, and deliberately so. There is nothing to create, edit, block or retire here. Dealer and distributor accounts are opened and amended on the Customers screen, where the extra dealer-management right is enforced. Nobody should go looking for missing buttons: they do not exist, they are not hidden by a permission.
An account appears here the moment it is opened on Customers with the Dealer or Distributor channel.
An unlimited credit limit reads as Unlimited, never as zero, and no headroom figure is shown against it — there is no ceiling to have room inside.
Retired accounts never appear, whichever status filter is chosen.
screens.permission: Needs the right to see dealers, which is what puts the menu entry there and opens the page. The Sales Executive role has it.
screens.notes: This is genuinely the Customers list seen through one filter — the deck should say so rather than describing the columns twice. The one thing it adds is the remaining-credit figure under Outstanding. The salesperson an account is assigned to is not shown as a column (the row carries the reference, not the name), so "Assigned to me" is the only owner filter available. Because there is no actions column at all, the screenshot will read as a pure report, which is correct.

screens.title: Material requirements planning
screens.purpose: Planning answers one question: given everything customers have actually committed to buy, what do we not have, and when do we have to act to get it. A run reads the confirmed order book out to a horizon you choose, looks at what is in stock, at what is already spoken for, at purchase orders already placed with suppliers and at work already on the shop floor, explodes the bill of materials for anything that has to be manufactured, and adds up every demand for the same part into one number. What comes out is a list of proposals. This screen is where a run is started and where the history of past runs lives.
screens.whoUses: The production planner. The purchase manager also runs it, because most of what comes out is something to buy.

keyActions.action: Set how far ahead to plan
keyActions.how: Horizon (days) box in the Run MRP card. Anything from 1 to 1095 days; 90 is the starting value.
keyActions.note: Only demand due on or before the end of that window is picked up.

keyActions.action: Restrict the run to certain warehouses
keyActions.how: Warehouses box — tick as many as apply, up to fifty. Leave everything unticked to plan across all of them.
keyActions.note: Stock and incoming quantities are then read from those warehouses only, so a plant planner does not see the other plant's shortages or net against its stock.

keyActions.action: Decide whether to protect the safety buffer
keyActions.how: Protect safety stock tick box, on by default.
keyActions.note: Left on, the buffer is held back from the arithmetic and the plan will not propose running it down to zero. Untick it deliberately when you intend to draw the buffer down.

keyActions.how: Run MRP.
keyActions.note: Only appears for someone with the right to run planning.

keyActions.how: Nothing to do — an amber panel appears with the run's status and a running clock. You can leave the page and keep working; the run opens by itself when it finishes.
Click the run code, or the row, in the Run history table below.
Status dropdown in the history toolbar.

flow: Set the horizon — how far into the future the plan should look.
Pick the warehouses, or leave it on all of them.
Decide about safety stock; leave it protected unless you mean otherwise.
Press Run MRP.

A small run comes back in a moment and the screen opens it. A large one is queued and calculated in the background, with the elapsed time on screen; you can carry on working and it opens when it is done.
Read the run.
rules: Only confirmed, allocated and part-despatched orders are demand. A draft order is invisible to planning. This is the single most important thing to know about this screen: if the plan is missing something, check that the order behind it has actually been confirmed.

What is planned for each line is what was ordered, less what has been despatched, less what is already reserved for it. Stock already held for an order is neither counted as free nor planned for a second time.

The demand is photographed at the instant the run starts, and the run plans against that photograph — not against whatever the sales desk enters while it is calculating. That is what makes the plan defensible a week later when the orders behind it have been amended.

The system decides whether a run is calculated immediately or in the background, based on how much demand it has to chew through. It is not a choice on the form, because no screen should sit holding a connection open through a four-minute calculation.

Only one run at a time per company. A second is refused while one is still going — two plans running at once would each propose orders for shortages the other had already covered. And there is a budget on top of that: five starts per company in any five minutes, so a run cannot be restarted the instant the last one ends.

A run that would cover more than twenty thousand demand lines is refused outright. That is almost always an unintentionally huge horizon rather than a real order book — narrow the horizon or the warehouses.
A run whose calculation dies is closed off automatically after two hours, so planning is never blocked forever by a process that no longer exists.
screens.permission: Seeing this screen and the run history needs the right to view planning. The Run MRP card only appears for someone with the right to start a run — the Production Planner and the Purchase Manager have it; a purchase executive can read runs and act on them but not start one.
screens.notes: The system will accept extra demand lines typed in by hand alongside the order book ("plan for 200 of this as well"), but this screen has no field for them — a run here plans the order book only. There is also no way to cancel a run in progress from this screen, and no way to schedule runs to happen automatically. For the screenshot, catch the amber "Calculating" panel if possible; otherwise a history table with a mix of Immediate and Background runs shows the two modes well.

screens.title: Planning run
screens.purpose: What one run found, and what to do about it. The top half is the proposals — buy this, make this, send this out for job work, by this date. The bottom half is the arithmetic behind them, so a number can be checked rather than merely believed. Nothing on this screen has been ordered. Every proposal is exactly that until a person accepts it, and accepting is what creates a real document that other people will act on.
screens.whoUses: The production planner working through the list; the buyer, who converts the purchase proposals into requisitions.

keyActions.how: The amber "Read these before acting on the suggestions" box at the top, when it is present.
keyActions.note: It names anything the run could not do properly and, most often, the parts whose incoming supply lands too late to count.

keyActions.action: See the shape of the run at a glance
keyActions.how: The six tiles — demand lines, items short, and how many proposals are to purchase, to manufacture, to send for job work, plus how many items have supply arriving too late.
Click the arrow in the Source demands column, or click the row.
keyActions.note: It lists every order that contributed and, for a component, which parent product it came through. A merge icon means more than one source — the run has combined them into one order rather than several.

keyActions.how: Tick the box at the start of each row, or the box in the header to take every open row on the page.
keyActions.note: Only open proposals can be ticked. Ones already converted or ignored are locked.

keyActions.how: Convert selected, in the blue bar that appears once something is ticked. A confirmation lists exactly what will be created before anything is written.
keyActions.note: A purchase proposal becomes a purchase requisition, a manufacture proposal becomes a production order, a job work proposal becomes a job work order. Each is converted separately, so one being refused does not undo the rest.

keyActions.action: Dismiss proposals you are not acting on
keyActions.how: Ignore selected, then type a reason of at least three characters.
keyActions.note: Up to five hundred at a time; anything beyond that stays ticked for a second go. The reason is recorded against every row.

keyActions.how: Tick "Already past the order date" in the toolbar.

keyActions.action: Work one kind at a time
keyActions.how: Type dropdown — Purchase, Manufacture, Job work or Transfer.

keyActions.action: Check the arithmetic behind a shortage
keyActions.how: The Shortages and late supply table at the foot of the page.
keyActions.note: It shows demand, free stock, what is on order, what is being made, and — in its own column — the supply that exists but arrives too late to count.

flow: Open the run and read the amber caveats box if there is one.
Glance at the tiles: how many items are short, how the proposals split between buying, making and job work, and how many items have supply that misses its date.
Sort or filter the list — by default it is ordered by the date the order should be placed, soonest first, so the most urgent work is at the top.
Expand any row you want to justify: it names the sales orders behind it and the products it was exploded through.
Tick the rows you accept and press Convert selected. Tick the rows you are not acting on and press Ignore selected with a reason.

Before assuming a shortage needs a new order, check the Arrives too late column at the foot of the page: if the stock is already on order and simply lands after it is needed, the right action is a call to the supplier, not another order.
rules: Suggested quantity is normally larger than the shortage, and that is correct: it has been rounded up to the supplier's minimum order quantity and then up again to their pack multiple. A fifty-piece minimum from a supplier who ships in packs of thirty means an order for sixty.

Order by is the required date less the lead time — the last day the order can be placed and still arrive on time. When that day has already passed the row is marked Late, and the required date will slip unless the lead time can be squeezed.

What kind of proposal a shortage becomes comes from the item master's own statement of how the part is obtained: made here becomes a manufacture proposal, bought becomes a purchase, job work becomes a job work order. An item marked "make or buy" becomes a manufacture proposal if it has an approved bill of materials and a purchase proposal if it does not.

A part that several orders and several products all need becomes one proposal for the summed quantity, not one per order. That is the single biggest thing planning does for a hardware business, and it is what the expandable Source demands column exists to prove.

Supply that arrives after the date it is needed is not counted as supply. So an item can show a shortage while a purchase order for it is open — that is not a mistake, it is the plan saying the delivery is too late to help. Those quantities are shown separately, with the dates they land, in the Arrives too late column, and named in the warnings at the top.

Converting is one-way. A converted or an ignored proposal cannot be reopened — reopening a converted one would invite a second order for a shortage already covered. If the shortage is still real, the next run raises it again from scratch.
Ignoring a proposal does not make the shortage go away. It records that somebody looked at it and decided not to act, and keeps it off this run's working list.
Transfer proposals can be ignored but not converted. There is no document for planning to raise for them — a stock transfer between warehouses is raised by hand.

If two people convert the same proposal at the same moment, the second is refused rather than creating a duplicate document. A bulk ignore reports back how many rows it skipped because somebody else had already dealt with them.

Occasionally a conversion closes the proposal without producing a document, because the part of the system that would own that document is not available. The screen says so plainly in that case rather than reporting a document that does not exist.
screens.permission: Reading a run needs the right to view planning. Convert selected and Ignore selected both need the right to convert planning suggestions — the Production Planner, the Purchase Manager and the Purchase Executive all hold it. Without it the tick boxes are inert and the run is a report.
screens.notes: Two capabilities the system has that this screen does not expose: overriding the quantity or the date on an individual proposal before converting it (Convert always uses the proposal's own figures), and cancelling a run. Also, a proposal carries the item's code but no item name, no unit of measure and no warehouse — planning works per item across the whole scope of the run, not per warehouse — so the deck should not promise those columns. For the screenshot, use a completed run that actually has shortages and, ideally, at least one late-supply warning; a run with nothing short shows an empty table and none of the machinery.

chapters.groupTitle: Buying: from a request for material to the goods on the shelf
chapters.groupIntro: This part of the system covers everything between somebody saying "we need this" and the material standing in the warehouse with the vendor's account settled. It runs as a chain of documents, each one raised from the one before it: a requisition asks for material, an RFQ puts those lines out to several vendors, the quotations that come back are compared side by side, a purchase order commits the money, a goods receipt turns the delivery into stock, and a purchase return sends back anything wrong. Approvals sit at two points in that chain — on the requisition and on the purchase order — and in both places the person who raised the document is not allowed to approve it, because an approval by the requester is not a second opinion. Behind all of it sit two master records: the vendor, who cannot be ordered from until somebody has approved them, and the transporter, the carrier a consignment travels with.

screens.title: Requisitions
screens.purpose: A requisition is the moment a need becomes a document. Somebody on the shop floor or in the stores writes down what they want, how much, when they need it by and what it is for, and asks for it to be bought. Nothing is committed and no vendor is involved yet — this is an internal request, and it exists so that the decision to spend money is taken by somebody other than the person who wants the material. An approved requisition is what a buyer sources against.
screens.whoUses: Whoever runs out of material — a storekeeper, a production supervisor, a buyer raising work for themselves — and the purchase manager who approves what they ask for. The planning run also drops requisitions here on its own.

keyActions.how: Raise requisition, top right of the screen
keyActions.note: It is saved as a draft. It needs at least one line, a delivery warehouse and a required-by date, and only items marked as purchasable and still active can be asked for.

keyActions.how: The ... menu at the end of the row, then Edit draft
keyActions.note: Only while it is still a draft. Saving replaces the whole set of lines, so anything removed from the form is removed from the requisition.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Submit for approval
keyActions.note: A note is optional. Once submitted it can no longer be edited or deleted — only withdrawn.

keyActions.how: The ... menu on a row that is waiting for approval, then Approve
keyActions.note: You may add a note. The system refuses an approval by the person who raised it.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Reject
keyActions.note: A reason of at least three characters is required. The requester sees it.

keyActions.action: Raise purchase orders from one requisition
keyActions.how: The ... menu on an approved row that still has lines to order, then Raise purchase orders
keyActions.note: The system proposes one draft purchase order per vendor and item category, each handed to the vendor's manager for that category. Change a line's vendor, price or quantity, or leave it out, and the proposal is worked out again. Nothing is raised while any line has no vendor or no price.

keyActions.action: Raise purchase orders from several requisitions at once
keyActions.how: Raise POs from approved requisitions, top right, then tick the requisitions
keyActions.note: Up to 50 at a time - the planning run raises one small requisition per shortage, and this pools their lines so each vendor gets one order per category and delivery warehouse instead of one per requisition.

keyActions.how: The ... menu on an approved or converted row, then Close requisition
keyActions.note: A reason is required. Whatever is still unordered on it will not be ordered and it stops counting as open demand; orders already raised from it are not affected. Closing is final.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Cancel requisition
keyActions.note: A reason is required and cancelling is final. Available on a draft, one awaiting approval, or an approved one that is no longer wanted.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Delete draft
keyActions.note: A reason is required. The draft and its lines are gone and the document number does not come back; the audit entry with your reason is the only trace.

keyActions.how: Status box, the Required-from / Required-to date window, and the "Approved, still unmet" tick in the toolbar
keyActions.note: "Approved, still unmet" is the demand a buyer has not yet covered — approved or only partly ordered.

keyActions.how: Search box above the table
keyActions.note: Searches the requisition number and the purpose text.

flow: Click Raise requisition.
Set the raised date, the date the material is needed by, and the warehouse it is needed at.
Set the priority (1 to 9, 5 by default; the lower the number the more urgent) and write what it is for in Purpose — that sentence is usually what decides the approval.
Add a line for each item: pick the item, type the quantity, and optionally an estimated price.
Save the draft. The screen totals the estimates as an indicative value; nothing is committed by it.
From the row's ... menu, submit it for approval.
The approver filters the list to Pending approval and either approves it or rejects it with a reason.
An approved requisition can now be put out to vendors as an RFQ, or turned straight into purchase orders: open its ... menu and choose Raise purchase orders.
Read the proposal: one card per vendor and item category, with each line's price and where it came from, the vendor manager the order goes to, and any open order it would duplicate.

Correct anything that is wrong - another vendor, a different price or quantity, or leave a line out for later - and press Raise. The orders open as drafts on the Purchase orders screen, to be submitted, approved and sent like any other.
rules: Only a draft can be edited or deleted. Anything further along is cancelled instead, because somebody may already be deciding on it and a document must not change underneath them.
The person who raised a requisition cannot approve it. That is the whole point of the approval step.
A rejection, a cancellation and a deletion each need a written reason, because the requester reads it and the audit trail keeps it.
Only items flagged as purchasable, and still active, can be asked for. Whether an item can be bought is decided on the item record, not by which group it belongs to.
A requisition must name the warehouse the material is wanted at, because an order raised from it has to be delivered somewhere.
The required-by date cannot be earlier than the date the requisition is raised — that is nearly always a mistyped year.
The estimated price is indicative only. What will actually be paid is settled on the purchase order.

Once an RFQ or a purchase order has been raised against an approved requisition it becomes Converted, and from there the only move left is to close it — cancelling it would say nothing about the commitment already made to a vendor.
When a purchase order raised from a requisition is cancelled or rejected, the quantity goes back onto the requisition as unmet demand, so the shortage is not silently dropped.

Raising purchase orders picks each line's vendor in this order: the vendor chosen on the proposal, the vendor suggested on the requisition line, the item's preferred vendor, and the preferred vendor of the item's category or the nearest parent category that has one.

The price comes from the proposal, the requisition's estimated price, or the last price paid to that vendor for the item — never the item's standard cost, which is what the company values the item at, not what any vendor offered. A line with no vendor or no price stops the whole conversion until it is given one or left out; nothing is ever half-raised.

Lines are grouped into one order per vendor, item category and delivery warehouse. The category is the one the vendor is qualified to supply, so the order goes to that vendor's manager for it; when several managers cover the same category the order is left unassigned and the buyer chooses at Send.

At most 20 purchase orders are raised in one go. If an open order already covers the same demand the conversion stops and shows it; raising anyway needs the right to approve purchase orders and a written reason.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to see purchase requisitions can read this list. Raising, editing, submitting, cancelling and deleting are one right — the right to create requisitions — which both a Purchase Executive and a Purchase Manager carry. Approving and rejecting need a separate right to approve requisitions, which of the ready-made roles only a Purchase Manager and an administrator hold. Raising purchase orders from requisitions needs the right to create purchase orders, which buyers carry; closing a requisition needs the right to approve requisitions.
screens.notes: There is no separate page for one requisition — the list plus the raise/edit dialog is the whole screen, and the lines are only visible inside that dialog. The list carries no value column. A "To order" column counts the lines still to order on an approved or converted requisition, which is what decides whether purchase orders can be raised from it. A "Raised from" column shows Manual, or the planning source when the row was produced by an MRP run. The system also has a combined "waiting for your approval" queue covering requisitions and purchase orders together, but no screen uses it yet; approvers work this list with the status filter instead.

screens.title: Requests for quotation
screens.purpose: An RFQ is the enquiry you send to several vendors asking them all to price the same lines. This screen is the board a buyer works while prices are being gathered: what has gone out, to whom, and who has not answered by the date they were given. It exists so that a price is chosen against alternatives rather than out of habit.
screens.whoUses: The buyer.

keyActions.how: New RFQ, top right
keyActions.note: Saved as a draft, and the new RFQ then opens on its own screen so the lines and the vendor list can be checked before it goes out.

keyActions.action: Raise it against an approved requisition
keyActions.how: Inside the New RFQ dialog, the "Raised against" picker
keyActions.note: Leave the lines empty and every line on that requisition that has not already been ordered is copied onto the RFQ. Add a line yourself and the copying stops — what you typed is what is sent.

keyActions.how: Inside the dialog, the Vendors section
keyActions.note: Up to 50 on one enquiry. A vendor does not have to be approved to be asked for a price.

keyActions.how: The ... menu on the row, then Edit draft
keyActions.note: Only while it is a draft. Saving replaces the whole set of lines.

keyActions.how: The paper-plane button on the row
keyActions.note: Only appears once at least one vendor is invited. If nobody is invited the menu offers "Add vendors before sending" instead.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Close RFQ
keyActions.note: For when a vendor has been chosen. Closing is final and a closed RFQ takes no more quotations.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Cancel RFQ
keyActions.note: A reason is required. Cancelling is final.

keyActions.how: Toolbar: status, vendor, item, warehouse, and a "Replies due before" date
keyActions.note: The search box looks at the RFQ number only.

keyActions.how: Click anywhere on the row

flow: Click New RFQ.
Set the RFQ date, the date replies are due back, the date the material is needed, and the currency.
If the enquiry answers an approved requisition, pick it — its unordered lines come across on their own.
Invite the vendors you want a price from.
Check the lines: item, quantity, needed by, and the specification the vendor is quoting against (finish, grade, drawing revision).
Save. The RFQ opens on its own screen.
Send it to the vendors.
As each reply arrives, record it on the Quotations screen.
Once a vendor is chosen, come back and close the RFQ.
rules: A vendor need not be approved to be asked for a price — asking for a quotation is often how the evidence to approve a vendor is gathered. But a price from an unapproved vendor cannot be turned into a purchase order until they are approved, and the enquiry screen flags that.
