An RFQ that names no vendors cannot be sent. The fix is to edit it and invite somebody, not to try again.
Editing stops when the RFQ is sent, because from that moment the vendors are quoting against the lines as they were issued.

Quotations arriving do not change the RFQ's status. An RFQ with two replies of five is still an open, sent RFQ — which is why there is no "3 of 5 replied" column anywhere on this screen. The replies are read on the Quotations screen.
One currency per enquiry. Offers in another currency cannot be compared against these.
The overdue flag is only shown for an RFQ that has actually been sent. A missed reply date on a draft is a planning slip, not a late vendor.
Closed and cancelled are the end of the road; there is no way back out of either.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to view RFQs can read the board. Raising, editing, sending, closing and cancelling are all one right — the right to manage RFQs — held by both a Purchase Executive and a Purchase Manager. Picking a requisition to raise the RFQ against additionally needs the right to view requisitions, and the vendor and item pickers only appear for someone who may read those lists.
screens.notes: Vendors and warehouses show as short codes on the row because the underlying record carries only their references; the enquiry's own page names them in full.

screens.title: One request for quotation
screens.purpose: The whole of a single enquiry on one page: what was asked for, who it went to, and where the document has got to. It is the same task as the RFQ list seen from the other end — the list is for working through a queue, this page is for reading and acting on one enquiry with all of it in front of you.
screens.whoUses: The buyer, before sending an enquiry and while chasing replies.

keyActions.action: See where it has got to
keyActions.how: The Draft / Sent / Closed strip across the top
keyActions.note: A cancelled RFQ stops the strip and prints the cancellation reason underneath.

keyActions.how: The "Vendors asked" card on the right
keyActions.note: Each vendor shows their code, usual lead time, star rating and an Approved or Not approved badge. "Not approved" is a warning that an order cannot yet be raised on them.

keyActions.how: The Lines table at the bottom
keyActions.note: Line number, item, quantity, the date it is needed, the specification and any notes.

keyActions.how: Edit button in the page header
keyActions.note: Only appears while the RFQ is a draft.

keyActions.how: Send to vendors button in the page header
keyActions.note: Only appears once at least one vendor is named.

keyActions.how: Add vendors, on the empty "Nobody has been asked yet" panel
Close RFQ button in the page header
keyActions.note: Only on a sent RFQ.

keyActions.how: Cancel button in the page header
keyActions.note: A reason is required.

flow: Open the RFQ from the list.
Check the Enquiry card: reply-by date, the date the material is needed, the delivery warehouse, the currency, and whether it came from a requisition.
Check the vendor card — anyone marked Not approved can quote, but cannot be ordered from yet.
Check the lines and their specifications.
Send it, and come back later to close it once a vendor has been chosen.
rules: Only the commands the document can legally accept are shown at all. A button that could only be refused is simply not on the page.
An RFQ with nobody invited shows a warning saying so — it is the one thing standing between the enquiry and being sent.
A vendor suspended since the enquiry went out reads as "Vendor no longer listed". They were still asked, and that remains a fact of the document.
screens.permission: The right to view RFQs opens the page. Every command on it needs the right to manage RFQs.
screens.notes: The comparison of quotations is deliberately not on this page — it sits on the Quotations screen behind its own permission. The page says an RFQ was raised against "a purchase requisition" but does not link to it, because there is no page for a single requisition to open.

screens.title: Vendor quotations and the comparison
screens.purpose: Every offer a vendor has sent back, and the board on which they are compared. These are one screen rather than two because they are one job: the table is the register of what has been quoted, and narrowing it to a single RFQ turns the page into a side-by-side board with one column per vendor and one row per item, so the buying decision is taken from the column the price is on rather than several clicks away from it.
screens.whoUses: The buyer, and whoever signs off which vendor gets the work.

keyActions.how: Record quotation, top right
keyActions.note: Choose the RFQ and the vendor, then key the vendor's own quotation number, dates, currency, terms and the priced lines.

keyActions.how: The compare icon in the RFQ column of any row
keyActions.note: This narrows the list to that RFQ; the board appears above the table. A "Narrowed to one RFQ" chip in the toolbar shows it is on.

keyActions.how: Click the quotation number, or anywhere on the row
Select on the vendor's column of the board, or the ... menu on the row
keyActions.note: A written reason is required — even when you are following the recommendation.

keyActions.how: Reject on the board, or the ... menu on the row
keyActions.note: A written reason is required. The vendor has to requote to come back into contention.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Record revised offer
keyActions.note: Available on a rejected or lapsed offer. It reopens and replaces that vendor's quotation rather than adding a second one.

keyActions.how: Toolbar: status, vendor, and a "still valid on" date
keyActions.note: The search box looks at the vendor's quotation number.

flow: A vendor's quotation arrives on paper or by email.
Click Record quotation and pick the RFQ and the vendor.
Enter their quotation number, the quotation date, how long it stays valid, the currency, the payment terms in days, the lead time in days, and any freight.
Add a line per item: item, quantity, unit price, discount percentage, and a lead time for that line if it differs.
Repeat for each vendor that replies.
When enough have come in, click the compare icon on any row of that RFQ.

Read the board — each column shows the vendor's total, how much more it is than the cheapest offer still valid, lead time, payment terms, rating, validity and how many lines it wins; each cell shows the effective unit price after discount with Lowest and Fastest flags.
Read the recommendation at the top and the per-item reasons underneath each item.
Select the winning column and type why. Then close the RFQ and raise the purchase order.
rules: One live quotation per vendor per RFQ. A revised offer updates that vendor's existing quotation, so the board always shows one column per vendor and never two versions of the same piece of paper.
A rejected or lapsed offer can be brought back by recording the vendor's revised offer. A selected offer is final — it is the one an order is raised against.
A quotation cannot be selected once its validity date has passed. Ask the vendor to requote and record the revision.
The reason for selecting is required even when you agree with the recommendation, because the buyer's judgement is what goes on the record and the system's score is only an input to it.

The recommendation weighs price at 60%, delivery lead time at 20% and the vendor's rating at 20%, and it always states in words why the winner won. A vendor with no rating yet scores neutrally rather than badly, so a new supplier can win their first order.

A lapsed offer stays on the board, ranked last, rather than disappearing — so nobody is left wondering where the cheapest price went. Comparisons against "the cheapest" always mean the cheapest offer still valid.
When the offers are in different currencies no recommendation is made and no money comparison is shown; the board says so instead of subtracting one currency from another.
An item nobody quoted reads "Not quoted", never zero.
An RFQ that has been closed or cancelled will not take another quotation.
screens.permission: Reading the register and the comparison board needs the right to view quotations. Recording, revising, selecting and rejecting need the separate right to manage quotations — deliberately different, so that being allowed to look at prices does not hand somebody the buying decision. Choosing the RFQ when recording an offer needs the right to view RFQs, and the vendor search needs the right to view vendors.
screens.notes: There is no RFQ code on a table row — only the compare icon, which opens the board and names the RFQ itself. Selecting a quotation does not create the purchase order; that is keyed separately on the purchase orders screen, and because of that the "Ordered" marker on a quotation row will not appear for orders raised through the screens.

screens.title: Purchase orders
screens.purpose: The order book: what is on order, from whom, for how much, and where each order has got to. This is where an order is raised, and it is also the screen somebody opens to answer "is it late?" — an order past its promised delivery date that is still expecting goods is flagged in red.
screens.whoUses: The buyer who raises orders and the purchase manager who watches the book.

keyActions.how: New purchase order, top right
keyActions.note: Only vendors that have been approved can be chosen — the vendor search on this form is restricted to them.

keyActions.how: Click the order code, or anywhere on the row

keyActions.action: See only what is still coming
keyActions.how: The "Still expecting delivery" tick in the toolbar
The "Overdue only" tick in the toolbar

keyActions.action: Narrow by vendor or delivery window
keyActions.how: Toolbar: vendor picker, Expected-from and Expected-to dates, status box
keyActions.note: The date window is on the expected delivery date, not the order date.

keyActions.how: Click a category in the Category column, or choose one in the category box in the toolbar
keyActions.note: Includes the categories beneath it. The category box is there for whoever can read the category list; clicking a category works for everybody.

keyActions.how: Search box above the table
keyActions.note: Searches the order code, the vendor's own reference and the consignment tracking reference.

flow: Click New purchase order.
Choose the vendor — only approved ones appear.
Set the order date, the expected delivery date and the warehouse it is delivered to.
Set the priority, the payment terms in days (leave it blank to use the terms agreed on the vendor's record) and the vendor's own reference if they gave one.
Add a line per item: item, quantity, unit price.
Add the delivery address, terms and notes if they are needed.
Save. If the system finds an open order that already covers the same requirement it stops and shows you what it found.
The order opens on its own page as a draft. Submit it for approval from there.
rules: An order can only be raised on a vendor that is approved and not suspended. If the supplier you want is refused, get their record approved first on the Vendors screen.
Only items flagged as purchasable and still active can be ordered.
The expected delivery date cannot be earlier than the order date.

Before an order is saved the system looks for open orders covering the same requirement: same vendor, same item, same delivery warehouse, and a required date within seven days — or, strongest of all, raised from the same recorded demand. If it finds any, the order is not created; the screen lists them with how sure it is and what to do about each.

There are four ways out of a duplicate warning: merge the lines into the existing order, increase the quantity already on that order, cancel the existing order, or raise this one anyway. Only the last can be done from the dialog, and only by somebody who can approve purchase orders, with a written reason that stays on the order for anybody who opens it later. The other three are edits to the other document, which opens in a new tab so nothing typed here is lost.
Line totals shown while typing are indicative. Discounts, tax and freight are calculated by the system and the order value is what it comes back with.
The delay flag only appears on an order that is past its expected date and still expecting a delivery.
An order carries the item category it was raised for. An order raised from requisitions is one category by construction; an order whose lines span several categories has none and shows a dash.
screens.permission: The right to view purchase orders opens the list. The New purchase order button needs the right to create purchase orders, held by a Purchase Executive and a Purchase Manager. Overriding a duplicate warning additionally needs the right to approve purchase orders, which of the ready-made roles only a Purchase Manager and an administrator carry.
screens.notes: The list carries no received quantities and no percentage complete — those are on the order's own page. Vendors show as a name plus code resolved from the vendor list; a suspended vendor shows a dash here and is named properly on the order's own page.

screens.title: One purchase order
screens.purpose: The whole life of one order on one page. A strip across the top places the document in a ten-stage life from Draft to Paid, so what happens next needs no explanation. Below it are the order's terms, its priced lines with what has been received against each, the totals as the system calculated them, and a tracking panel that answers the question the buyer actually rang up about — where is it, is it late, and what is being held at the gate.
screens.whoUses: The buyer, the approver, and anyone chasing a delivery.

keyActions.how: Submit for approval, top right
keyActions.note: Only on a draft. Once submitted the order goes to whoever holds the approval right.

keyActions.how: Approve, top right
keyActions.note: Only on an order awaiting approval, and never by the person who raised it. A note may be added. Approval is the commitment — there is no way back from it.

keyActions.how: Reject, top right
keyActions.note: Only on an order awaiting approval. A written reason is required and the buyer sees it.

keyActions.how: Send to vendor, top right
keyActions.note: On an approved order, or on one the vendor declined once a new date or price is agreed. Choose who owns it at the vendor: the list offers the vendor's portal users whose categories cover the order (or who cover every category), with the one the system suggests already chosen. This is what starts the delivery clock against the expected date.

keyActions.how: Vendor acknowledged, top right
keyActions.note: Only on a sent order. Records that the vendor has accepted the order as issued.

keyActions.how: Cancel order, top right
keyActions.note: A written reason is required. Only available before anything has been received; after that the order is short-closed instead. Cancelling an order the vendor declined gives its quantity back to the requisition, so it can be ordered from somebody else.

keyActions.how: The Tracking panel at the foot of the page
keyActions.note: Ordered, received, still to come, accepted, rejected, and how many lines are held for inspection — plus every goods receipt booked against the order.

keyActions.how: The refresh button on the Tracking panel
keyActions.note: A consignment moves while the page is open.

keyActions.how: Click the description on a line

flow: Open the order from the list.
Read the strip at the top to see where it stands.
Check the lines: ordered, received, accepted, rejected, returned and still pending, with the unit price, discount, tax and line total.
Check the totals card — subtotal, discount, tax, freight and the order value.
Submit for approval; somebody else approves it; then send it to the vendor, choosing the person there who owns it.
When the vendor confirms, record the acknowledgement.
As deliveries arrive they are booked as goods receipts, and this page's tracking panel lists them and shows what is still outstanding.
rules: The order can only move the way the lifecycle allows, so only the legal commands are shown. An approved order cannot be approved again, and a received one cannot be cancelled.
The person who raised an order may not approve or reject it.

Cancelling is only possible before anything has been received. Once stock has moved against the order, cancelling it would leave the stock records describing a delivery against a document claiming never to have existed. A part-delivered order that will never be completed is short-closed instead — the undelivered balance stops being expected.
Approving or cancelling an order changes what the planning run treats as material on its way in.
An order raised over a duplicate warning shows that warning and the reason given for it, permanently, on this page.

The tax figure on this document is a single amount, not the CGST/SGST/IGST split. The statutory split lives on the vendor's invoice in the finance area, and putting a guess at it here would only give the accounts team a second number to reconcile.

The order's item category and its vendor assignee are shown on the Order card. The assignee is the vendor user who manages that category; if that person has been switched off or re-scoped since the order was raised, sending it hands it to whoever the system now suggests, or to the person you choose.

The vendor answers a sent order from its own portal: it accepts, optionally committing its own delivery date and reference, or declines with a reason. The vendor's committed date is kept beside the expected delivery date, never in place of it - the planning run keeps using the date the buyer set until a buyer adopts the vendor's.

An order the vendor declined shows Vendor declined, and the notification the buyer receives carries the vendor's reason. Nothing is expected against it any more, but it still holds the quantity it took from its requisition until it is cancelled or sent again, and its vendor cannot be retired while it is open.

Once a vendor has accepted, each consignment it records - courier or transporter, tracking and LR numbers, boxes, weight, freight - and each lorry receipt or dispatch photo it uploads is announced at once to the order's creator, its approvers and the administrators, as one notification per consignment that updates as the consignment moves.
screens.permission: The right to view purchase orders opens the page. Submit and Vendor acknowledged need the right to update purchase orders; Approve, Reject and Cancel each need their own separate right, and of the ready-made roles only a Purchase Manager and an administrator hold them. Sending to the vendor needs the right to send purchase orders.
screens.notes: Two things the system supports but no screen currently offers: editing an order that is still a draft or awaiting approval, and short-closing a part-delivered order. If a draft is wrong, cancel it and raise a new one. The courier and consignment details on the tracking panel are read-only here — they are written by the vendor's own dispatch side. Recording the vendor's acknowledgement does not capture a revised delivery date they may have committed to, even though the system can hold one. The vendor's name is a link to the vendor list; there is no page for a single vendor.

screens.title: Goods receipts
screens.purpose: This is where a delivery becomes stock. Everything a purchase order promises is only paperwork until a receipt is posted against it; posting is the moment the material enters the company's books, the order advances, and anything needing inspection is put on hold rather than made available. The fact this list leads with is whether a receipt has actually been posted — a receipt keyed but not posted means material physically in the building that the system does not yet own.
screens.whoUses: The storekeeper at the gate, and whoever is authorised to post.

keyActions.how: Receive against PO, top right
keyActions.note: Choose the order first, then count what arrived line by line. Only its outstanding lines are shown.

keyActions.how: The Post button at the end of a draft row
keyActions.note: This is what moves the stock. It cannot be undone.

keyActions.action: See what is waiting on inspection
keyActions.how: The "Waiting on QC" tick in the toolbar
Toolbar: status, vendor and a received-date window
Search box above the table
keyActions.note: Searches the receipt code, the vendor's delivery note number and their invoice number.

keyActions.action: Open the order behind a receipt
keyActions.how: The "Purchase order" link in the Against column

flow: Click Receive against PO and pick the order the lorry is delivering against. Orders that have not yet been sent to the vendor are listed but cannot be chosen.
Confirm the receipt date and record the vendor's delivery note number, their invoice number, the gate entry number and the vehicle number.
For each line, enter what was Received, how much of it you Accepted and how much you Rejected. The two must add up to what arrived.
If a quantity is rejected, say why — the field appears as soon as you type a rejected figure.
Enter the vendor's lot number in Batch number for any item that is batch tracked.
Look at the warnings: lines marked "Goes to QC hold" will not become available stock when this is posted.
Submit. If you hold posting rights the receipt is created and posted in one step; if you do not, it is saved as a draft for somebody who does.
Post it from the list if it was left as a draft.
rules: Nothing moves until the receipt is posted. Creating one only records the count.
Goods can only be received against an order that has been sent to the vendor. An order still in draft or awaiting approval will not take a delivery.

Accepted plus rejected must equal what was received. Splitting a delivery into the part you kept and the part you refused is the whole job of a receipt, and a line where the two do not add up cannot be reconciled against the vendor's challan.
A rejected quantity needs a written reason.

Rejected quantity is never taken into stock. Goods refused at the gate never entered the company's custody and leave on the lorry they arrived on. Material accepted and only later found defective goes back with a purchase return instead.

A line whose item requires incoming inspection does not become available stock. The accepted quantity is received into QC hold, an inspection is raised against it, and it can only be issued once quality has released it.
An item that is batch tracked will not post without the vendor's lot number on the line.
Serial-numbered items cannot be received here at all — serial numbers cannot be captured on a receipt line, so those units are registered through the inventory screens instead.
Posting also writes the price paid back onto the item-and-vendor record as the last purchase price, so the next buyer sees what this vendor last charged.
A short delivery leaves the order Partially received; a complete one moves it to Received and then straight on — to QC pending if any line is held for inspection, otherwise to receipt complete.
A posted receipt is final. It can never be edited, cancelled or retracted; the way to correct it is a purchase return, which posts the opposite movement.

A receipt does not create a bill. It is the delivery half of the check the accounts team runs when the vendor's invoice arrives: the invoice is recorded in the finance area against this order and this receipt, checked against both, and only then does the order move on to Invoiced and later Paid.
A receipt line requiring incoming inspection is received at warehouse level. After acceptance, put it away with a bin move. Other lines can receive directly into their selected bin.
screens.permission: The right to view goods receipts opens the list — a Store Keeper has it. Recording a receipt needs the right to create them, which a Store Keeper also has. Posting one is a separate right, and of the ready-made roles only an administrator carries it, so out of the box a storekeeper keys the delivery and somebody else posts it. That split is deliberate and can be changed by granting the posting right to a role.
screens.notes: There is no page for a single receipt — the register plus the receive dialog is the whole screen. The system can cancel an unposted draft receipt but no screen offers it. The receive form will not let you enter more than a line still has outstanding, so the 5% over-delivery tolerance the system allows cannot be used from this screen; a genuine over-delivery has to have the purchase order amended. The form does not record which transporter brought the goods, only the vehicle number, even though the underlying document can hold a carrier.

screens.title: Purchase returns
screens.purpose: Material going back to the vendor. Because a posted goods receipt can never be retracted, a return is the only way stock that was booked in comes back out — it posts the opposite movement rather than erasing the original. The fact this list leads with is whether the goods have actually left: a return raised but not posted is stock the vendor believes is coming back while it is still on your shelf.
screens.whoUses: The storekeeper sending material back, and the buyer raising the debit note against the vendor.

keyActions.how: New return, top right
keyActions.note: Raised against one posted goods receipt. The receipt picker only offers posted ones.

keyActions.how: The Post button at the end of the row
keyActions.note: This is the step that moves the goods. It cannot be undone.

keyActions.how: The circle-slash button at the end of the row
keyActions.note: A reason is required. The document is abandoned and nothing moves.

keyActions.how: Click the return code, or anywhere on the row
Toolbar: status, vendor, warehouse and a return-date window
Search box above the table
keyActions.note: Searches the return code, the debit note number and the reason text — "damaged in transit" is how most people find one again.

flow: Click New return and pick the posted goods receipt the material came in on.
Set the return date, the debit note number if one has been raised, and the reason — this is recorded on the document, on every stock movement it writes and in the audit trail.
For each line, enter how much is going back. The badge on the line shows how much of it is still returnable.
Add a line-level reason or note where a particular line differs from the rest.
Save. The return is a draft and the stock is still in the warehouse.
When the material is actually leaving, open the Post dialog, read what it will do, and post it.
rules: A return can only be raised against a goods receipt that has been posted — only material that was actually received can be sent back.
A line can only return what was accepted on that receipt line, less anything already returned. Quantity that was rejected at the gate never became stock, so there is nothing of it to return.
Material still sitting on QC hold cannot be returned. Quality has to decide on it first, because until they do the stock has no settled position to take it out of.

Posting takes the goods out against the very lot they arrived on, credits the goods receipt line and the purchase order line with what went back so it cannot be returned twice, and moves the document to a state it can never leave.
A posted return is final. It can never be cancelled, edited or reversed. If the vendor sends the goods back to you, that is a new receipt, not an undo.

The value of the return is calculated at the price the goods were received at, with tax added at the item's own rate. Posting it moves stock and records the debit against the vendor on this document; the debit note number you type is the reference the accounts team works from.

Posted and cancelled are never shown as the same thing. Posted means the material physically left; cancelled means the paperwork was abandoned and nothing moved. Collapsing the two would tell a storekeeper a shelf is empty when it is not.
screens.permission: The right to view purchase returns opens the list. Raising, posting and cancelling are all one right — the right to create purchase returns — held by a Purchase Executive and a Purchase Manager. Unlike a goods receipt, posting is not split off behind a separate right: anyone who may raise a return may also move the stock. Searching for the goods receipt to return against additionally needs the right to view goods receipts; without it the form says so rather than showing an empty picker.
screens.notes: The system decides which pool the goods leave from — rejected stock first, then available — rather than asking. If a quantity would need both pools it is refused and the line has to be split. The return names the goods receipt it reverses but does not link to it, because there is no page for a single receipt. No debit note document is produced; the number is a field you fill in.

screens.title: Vendors
screens.purpose: The supply base. Every firm you buy material from, send job work to, hire transport from or pay for a service sits here as one record, with its GST and MSME details, its agreed payment terms and lead time, its bank details, its people and the item categories it is qualified to supply. Two things make this more than an address book: a purchase order cannot be raised on a vendor until somebody has approved the record, and the vendor's rating is calculated from delivery and inspection history rather than typed in by anyone.
screens.whoUses: The buyer who maintains the supply base, and the purchase manager who approves a new supplier.

keyActions.how: New vendor, top right
keyActions.note: A new vendor is not approved. Approving is a separate, deliberate step.

keyActions.how: The pencil button at the end of the row
keyActions.note: Opens the record in three tabs: Details, Contacts and Categories. The code cannot be changed once orders quote it.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Approve vendor
keyActions.note: A reason is required. Purchase orders can be raised on the vendor from this point.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Withdraw approval
keyActions.note: A reason is required. New purchase orders are refused; orders already raised are unaffected.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Suspend vendor
keyActions.note: A reason is required. The vendor disappears from the pickers on new documents; existing orders and receipts are untouched.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Reactivate vendor
keyActions.note: Comes back with whatever approval state it already held — switching a vendor off and on again cannot promote an unapproved one.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Retire vendor
keyActions.note: A reason is required. It leaves the master and stops appearing in this list.

keyActions.how: Click the stars on the row, or the ... menu then Record a rating
keyActions.note: Choose the measurement window; the figures are computed and shown before anything is kept.

keyActions.how: Edit the vendor, then the Contacts tab
keyActions.note: Each contact carries a role — Owner, Manager, Dispatch, QC or Accounts. One of them is the primary contact.

keyActions.action: Qualify a vendor for a category
keyActions.how: Edit the vendor, then the Categories tab
keyActions.note: Tick "Preferred supplier for this category" to make them the one to approach first.

keyActions.how: Toolbar: vendor type, approval, and Active or Suspended
keyActions.note: The search box covers code, name, GSTIN and city.

flow: Click New vendor.
On Details, give the code and name, and the registered name as it appears on the GST certificate.
Tick every type that applies — the same firm can supply raw material and also do job work, so a vendor holds several types at once.
Record the GSTIN, PAN and the Udyam/MSME number.
Set the agreed payment terms in days, the credit limit if one is agreed, the usual lead time and the currency.
Fill in the address, including the GST state code — that is what decides whether a purchase attracts CGST and SGST or IGST.
Record the bank details the vendor is to be paid on.
Save. Then, on the Contacts tab, add the people, marking one as primary.
On the Categories tab, record which item categories the vendor is qualified for, and mark the preferred one where they are your first choice.
When the record is complete, somebody with approval rights approves it. Only then can an order be raised.
rules: A vendor cannot be approved by the person who created the record. Ask a second person to review it.

A vendor cannot be approved until either a GSTIN or an MSME/Udyam number is on file, and a bank account name and number are recorded. Approving without them only defers the problem to the first payment run, where it blocks a payment instead of a form.
A purchase order can only be raised on a vendor that is approved and not suspended. Withdrawing approval or suspending does not touch orders already raised.
Approval is recorded against the approver's account and dated; withdrawing it clears both, so an audit never reads as though a withdrawn approval is still standing.
Two live vendors cannot share a GSTIN — that is a duplicate record, and it is the mistake that produces two payment trails for one legal entity.

A vendor holds several types at once. The type is a classification that drives which vendors are proposed first on each kind of document; it is not a permission and no rule reads it to decide whether something is allowed.
At most one preferred supplier per item category, and at most one primary contact per vendor. Two "preferred" suppliers for one category would give sourcing no basis to choose.
A contact must have at least an email, a phone or a mobile — a name nobody can reach defeats the point of recording it.

The rating is computed, never typed. On-time delivery counts 60% and inspected quality 40%, on a scale of 0 to 5. A window with no inspections in it is scored on delivery alone rather than crediting the vendor with a quality result they have not earned.

A window with fewer than five measurable receipts is not enough evidence and nothing is recorded — the score the vendor already carries is left alone. A vendor rated 1.0 because their single delivery was a day late would be shut out of sourcing on noise.
An unrated vendor is unknown, not bad. That is why the list shows "Unrated" and never a zero.

A vendor cannot be retired while it still has an open purchase order, is named as a source on an item, or has an active portal login — close, unlink or deactivate those first. Retiring also retires its contacts and removes its category qualifications, and a restored vendor comes back suspended and unapproved without them.
Every change to the bank details is written to the audit trail with the account number masked. A diverted-payment fraud starts with a quiet edit here, and the audit trail is what catches it.
screens.permission: The right to view vendors opens the list and is needed by every screen that names a supplier. Adding needs the right to create vendors; editing, approving, withdrawing approval, suspending and reactivating all need the right to update them — a Purchase Executive and a Purchase Manager have all of these. Recording a rating is a separate right, so somebody may score their suppliers without being able to edit the master row. Retiring is a separate right again, and of the ready-made roles only an administrator holds it.
screens.notes: There is no page for a single vendor — everything is on the list and inside the three-tab dialog, and the contacts and categories tabs only open once the vendor has been saved. Approval and rating are deliberately absent from the edit form: a buyer who could type their own supplier's score into a form would make the rating worthless. Retired vendors do not appear in this list at all and there is no filter to bring them back into view.

screens.title: Transporters
screens.purpose: The carriers and couriers a consignment can be handed to. A transporter is deliberately not a vendor: it is named on a dispatch rather than on a purchase order, and keeping them apart stops every dispatch screen having to sift a vendor list. The one piece of real work this record does is the tracking link template — record the carrier's tracking address once with a placeholder for the consignment number, and every consignment turns into a link the customer can follow.
screens.whoUses: Whoever maintains master data, and the dispatch side that names a carrier on a consignment.

keyActions.how: New transporter, top right
keyActions.note: Choose Transport or Courier — the type drives the default tracking behaviour on a dispatch.

keyActions.how: The pencil button at the end of the row
keyActions.note: Not offered on a retired row.

keyActions.how: The Resolve button in the Tracking column
keyActions.note: Put a real LR or AWB number through the carrier's template and follow the link it produces. Nothing is saved.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Deactivate
keyActions.note: It disappears from the pickers on new dispatches. Nothing already booked to it moves, and its tracking links keep working.

keyActions.how: The ... menu, then Activate
The ... menu, then Retire
keyActions.note: A reason is required. The master row is withdrawn and its code is freed for reuse.

keyActions.how: Tick "Include retired", then the ... menu on the row, then Restore
keyActions.note: It comes back inactive — activating it is a separate step.

keyActions.how: Toolbar: carrier type, availability, and the "Include retired" tick
keyActions.note: "Include retired" widens the list rather than narrowing it. The search box covers code, name, GSTIN and city.

flow: Click New transporter.
Give the code and name and choose Transport or Courier.
Record the GSTIN and PAN — an e-way bill is raised against the transporter's GSTIN, so a carrier without one is worth knowing about.
Record the contact person, phone numbers and address.
If the carrier has an online tracking page, paste its address into the tracking link template and replace the consignment number in it with the placeholder shown on the form.
Save, then use Resolve with a real consignment number to check the link actually opens the carrier's page.
rules: A tracking link template must be an HTTPS address and must contain the consignment-number placeholder. Without the placeholder every consignment resolves to the same page — which looks like it is working and never is.
A carrier with no template is not a problem; plenty of local transporters are tracked by telephone, and a dispatch with one simply shows the consignment number on its own.

Two independent things decide where a row sits. Whether the carrier is active decides if it can be named on a new dispatch; whether it has been retired decides if the record exists at all. A retired carrier is always inactive too.
A carrier cannot be retired while it still holds an undelivered consignment — the goods are physically with them.
Restoring a retired carrier is refused if its code has since been taken by another transporter.
A retired row offers only Restore; a retired carrier's tracking link cannot be resolved from this screen even though the template is still on file.
screens.permission: The right to view transporters opens the list. Adding, editing, activating, deactivating, retiring and restoring are all one right — the right to manage transporters. Of the ready-made roles, a Dispatch Manager can see the list; the management right belongs to an administrator.
screens.notes: This master exists mainly for the dispatch side of the business, not for buying. The goods receipt screen does not record which carrier brought an inbound delivery — only the vehicle number — so a transporter will not appear anywhere in the purchasing chain today. The screen will look sparse on a fresh system: a manufacturer typically has a handful of carriers, and the list does not default to hiding inactive ones because that is how somebody concludes a carrier has vanished when it was only switched off.

chapters.groupIntro: This is the part of the system where things get made. A production order is one job: an item, a quantity, the bill of materials it is built from and the route it takes through the plant. Under each order sit work orders, one for every operation on the routing, which is how the floor knows what is queued at which machine. Alongside them, assembly orders cover kits built at a bench from issued components, and job work covers everything sent outside the factory for polishing, plating, PVD, laser marking or machining. The thread running through all four is stock: at every step the system knows what has left the store, what is on the floor, what is at a vendor and what has come back as finished goods.

screens.title: Production orders
screens.purpose: The register of everything the plant is making or has made. Each row is one job, and the columns are the questions a planner asks while walking the list: how much was planned, how much has come off, how far along it is, when it was promised and how urgent it is. This is where a new job is raised and where you come to find an existing one. The list is held on the server and paged fifty at a time, so a plant running hundreds of orders a month never waits for the browser to catch up.
screens.whoUses: The production planner and the production supervisor. Anyone else who needs to look up a job - a storekeeper, an accountant - reaches it from here too.

keyActions.how: New order, at the top right of the screen
keyActions.note: The order is saved as a draft. Nothing is reserved and no material moves. The screen then takes you straight to the new order's own page. Someone who may see cost centres can name the cost centre the job is charged to - material issued to it is charged there too - and the order's page shows it; for anyone else the order is raised unallocated. Quality inspection is automatic by default - the order holds its output when the item or the routing asks for it - or choose always-hold or straight-to-stock explicitly.

keyActions.how: Click the order code, or anywhere on its row
The toolbar above the table: status, item, plant, how the order was raised, and a planned-date window
keyActions.note: The plant selector only appears once plants have been set up. Clear removes every filter in one go.

keyActions.action: Find an order by its number
keyActions.how: Type into the search box above the list
keyActions.note: The search matches the order number. It does not search the item, despite what the placeholder text suggests.

keyActions.how: The Progress column, which shows produced against planned as a bar and a percentage
Click a column heading
keyActions.note: Order code, planned quantity, planned start, planned end and priority can be sorted on. Produced quantity, progress and status cannot, and their headings deliberately do not offer to.

keyActions.action: Book a whole day across every open order
keyActions.how: The Daily bookings tab: pick the date and shift, read what each live job booked, and press Record on a row to book against that job
keyActions.note: Only jobs that have started take bookings; a released job that has not started reads Not started until it is issued and started.

flow: Press New order.
Search the item master and choose the item to be made.
Enter the quantity to make.
Leave Bill of materials blank to use the item's own default approved structure, or pick a particular approved version of it.
Set the planned start and the planned end. Both are required.
Set the priority - a whole number, where a lower number is more urgent.
Choose the warehouse the finished goods will be received into.
Add notes if there is anything the floor should know, then press Raise order.
The new order opens on its own page as a draft, waiting for approval.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to see production orders can open this screen and read the list. The New order button only appears for someone with the right to raise production orders; everyone else sees the list without it.
rules: Only an item flagged on the item master as manufacturable, and still active, can be put on a production order. The capability flag on the item decides what the item may be used for - not its category or its reporting group.
The planned finish cannot be earlier than the planned start. The form refuses it before it is sent.
The quantity must be more than zero, to four decimal places at most.
Only an approved bill of materials may be chosen. Draft and superseded structures are not offered, because a job may only be built against a structure someone has signed off.
A new order is always a draft. It holds no stock and commits nothing until it is approved and then released.
The list opens in priority order, most urgent first, then by the earliest promise date - the order a planner actually works down.
screens.notes: The Item column shows a link reading 'Open item' rather than the item's code, because the list the server returns carries the item's identity but not its code or name. The same is true on several screens in this chapter, and it is worth a line in the deck rather than a surprise in a demo. The screen has no delete and no edit: both live on the order's own page.

screens.title: The production order
screens.purpose: One job, from the plan to the closed cost. The header carries the buttons that move it forward, and it only shows the ones that are legal from where the order stands right now - a released order cannot be approved again, so that button is simply not there. Below it, four tabs answer the four questions asked about a job in progress: what does it need, who is making it, what came off the machine, and what did it cost. This is the screen a supervisor lives on.
screens.whoUses: The production supervisor drives it. The storekeeper uses the material buttons, and the accountant reads the Costing tab.

keyActions.how: Approve, in the header, while the order is a draft
keyActions.note: The person who raised the order cannot approve it. Someone else has to, unless they hold the Super Admin role - approval commits material and capacity, and an order approved by its own author is not a second person's judgement.

keyActions.action: Release the job to the floor
keyActions.how: Release, in the header, once the order is approved
keyActions.note: This is the big one. It explodes the bill of materials into a fixed kit list, turns the routing into work orders, and holds the free stock it can find. It cannot be undone - only cancelled.

keyActions.how: Issue material, in the header, or from the Components tab
keyActions.note: The picking document is created and posted in one press, so stock really does leave the store here. Quantities are pre-filled with what is still outstanding; clear a line to leave it for later.

keyActions.action: Return unused material to the store
keyActions.how: Return material, in the header
keyActions.note: Only appears when the job is actually holding something it has not consumed. It is a separate right from issuing, because taking stock off a shelf and putting it back are different decisions.

keyActions.how: Start, in the header, once the material has been issued
keyActions.note: Do not skip this. Booking output does not move the order on by itself, and a job can only be completed from In process. Once started it can no longer be cancelled.

keyActions.how: Record production, in the header, or from the Production entries tab
keyActions.note: Date, shift, operator, machine, good quantity, rejected quantity with its reason, and downtime in minutes. Good output is received into stock - or onto QC hold with an inspection when the order holds output for quality; rejected output is not received.

keyActions.how: Complete, in the header, while the order is in process
keyActions.note: The dialog shows planned against booked good, rejected and scrap quantities. Capture any final good output, rejects with their reason, scrap, actual end date, shift and note. Return anything still issued but unused first. Refused while any booked output is still held for QC: decide the inspections first.

keyActions.how: Close, in the header, once the order is completed
keyActions.note: Review planned against booked quantities and enter the closure note. Closing works out the final cost and freezes it, and gives back anything the job was still holding. A closed order cannot be reopened.

keyActions.how: Cancel, in the header, with a written reason of at least three characters
keyActions.note: Refused outright while the job is still holding material. Post a material return first, then cancel.

keyActions.action: Read the kit list and what is short
keyActions.how: The Components tab
keyActions.note: Shows required, issued net of returns, consumed, still to issue, reserved for this job, free stock, and the shortage. A warning banner appears above the table when anything is short, with a link into MRP to plan it.

keyActions.how: The Work orders tab
keyActions.note: One row per routing step: planned setup and run minutes, actual minutes once clocked, quantity booked, rejects, and the hourly rate the job will be costed at.

keyActions.how: The Production entries tab
keyActions.note: Every booking with its date, shift, produced, rejected, rejection reason, downtime, and whether it put stock into the warehouse.

keyActions.action: Read what the job has cost
keyActions.how: The Costing tab
keyActions.note: Only visible to someone with the right to see production costs. It is marked Provisional until the job is closed.

flow: DRAFT. The order is a plan. It can still be edited or deleted, and it holds nothing.
APPROVED. Someone other than the author has confirmed the plan and the quantity. Still no stock movement, but the order can no longer be edited - cancel it and raise a new one if the plan changes.

RELEASED. Press Release. The bill of materials is exploded once and written onto the order as a fixed kit list; a change to the BOM tomorrow belongs to tomorrow's jobs, not this one. The routing becomes one work order per operation. Free stock is reserved against each component - not moved, just held, so nothing else can be promised it. Anything that could not be held is reported back as a shortage and the job is released anyway.

MATERIAL ISSUED. The storekeeper presses Issue material and posts the pick. Now stock genuinely leaves the store: the components come off the shelf and off the available balance. When every component that has to be picked has been fully issued, the order moves to Material issued by itself.
IN PROCESS. Press Start. The actual start date is recorded and the job can no longer be cancelled.

Bookings. Press Record production at the end of each shift. Good output booked at the last operation - or on a job with no routing at all - is received into the output warehouse. Rejected quantity is counted for the yield but never received, because it was never good stock.

COMPLETED. Press Complete. Review the quantities already booked against the plan, then capture any final good output, rejects and their reason, scrap, actual end date, shift and note. No more can be booked or issued. Every component's consumed quantity is set to what the job was holding; this posts nothing, because that stock already left the store when it was issued.

CLOSED. Press Close, review planned against booked quantities and record a closure note. The material cost and the operation cost are worked out and stored on the order, and anything the job was still holding is released. The figures are frozen at that moment, because work centre rates and stock valuations both move afterwards.
screens.permission: Reading the order needs the right to see production orders; the Costing tab additionally needs the right to see production costs. Every button asks for its own right, and they are deliberately not the same one: Approve needs approval of production orders, Release needs release, Start needs the right to manage work orders, Issue material needs the right to issue material, Return material a separate return right, Record production and Complete both need the right to book production, Close needs the close right, and Cancel needs the cancel right. A button you do not hold the right for is simply absent.
rules: A production order can only be edited while it is a draft. After approval it is a commitment, not a plan - cancel it and raise a new one.
Only a draft can be deleted. Anything further along is cancelled instead, so the trail survives.
The person who raised an order cannot approve it, unless they hold the Super Admin role. Approval commits material and capacity and needs a second person's judgement.
A job may only be released against an approved bill of materials, and against an approved routing if one was named. If no BOM is named, the item's single default approved structure is used.
Release freezes the structure. The kit list written at release is what the job is built from for the rest of its life, whatever the engineering department does afterwards.

Releasing does not guarantee the parts are held. Whatever is free is reserved and the rest is reported as a shortage, because a planner releasing a twenty-component job needs to know that three parts are short - not that the first one was, with the other seventeen left unheld.
A component may be issued up to 10% above its requirement, and no further. Beyond that the order's structure is wrong and should be corrected rather than over-issued.
Only the balance the job is actually holding can be returned. You cannot hand back more than went out.
A job may book up to 10% more good output than it planned. More than that is a decimal point in the wrong place, and it would put the stock into the warehouse before anyone noticed.
A rejection has to carry a reason. It is the only chance to capture it while the operator still remembers, and it is what the quality team reads later.

Finished goods that are batch or serial tracked cannot be received through a production booking, because a booking has nowhere to record the lot. Receive that output through inventory once the lot has been registered.

A job that is still holding issued material cannot be cancelled at all. That material is physically on the floor; cancelling around it would leave the books saying it was consumed by an order that no longer exists. Return it to the store first.
Booking output does not advance the order. Only Start moves a kitted job into process, and only from there can it be completed.
A completed order no longer accepts a return, so sweep the leftovers back to the store before completing.

The costing is calculated by the system from the issues and bookings actually posted - material at what the movements were valued at, operations at the time actually clocked at the work centre's rate. The screen never re-adds them, so the figures always reconcile with the stock ledger. The Costing tab also shows the material quantities and movement cost by component, and charged time, rate and time/setup/process cost by work order.
An operation with no rate behind it is flagged: its work centre carries no cost per hour, so the operation cost is an understatement rather than a complete figure.
screens.notes: Two things to be careful about in the deck. First, the Record production dialog carries a line saying the first booking moves the order from material issued to in process. It does not - only the Start button does that, and the header's own confirmation text says so correctly. Do not repeat the dialog's wording. Second, backflushed components (issued automatically at completion rather than picked) exist in the system, and the kit list will label them, but the Release button on this screen never nominates any - so on orders released through the screen the kit list is always fully picked. The item and the bill of materials appear as links ('Open item master', 'View BOM') rather than as codes, because the order carries their identity but not their names. Shift selects use the company shift master. Operators come from the active internal directory; choose a work order for per-operation output or leave it blank for final output. Downtime-only bookings are accepted. Legacy shift codes remain visible read-only.

screens.title: Work orders
screens.purpose: The shop floor's own queue: every operation of every live job, across all jobs at once. It answers what is next, who has it, when it is planned for and how long it should take. A second tab turns the same work into a load board grouped by work centre, which is how a bottleneck is found. Operations appear here when a production order is released - the release is what turns a routing into one work order per step.
screens.whoUses: The production supervisor and the cell leader. An operator uses it to start and finish the operation in front of them.

keyActions.how: The Queue tab, which opens in planned-start order
keyActions.note: Work with no planned start sorts to the bottom, which is where unscheduled work belongs.

keyActions.action: Narrow to one cell, machine, operator or status
keyActions.how: The toolbar selectors
keyActions.note: The machine selector only appears once a work centre has been chosen, because a machine only means anything inside its own cell. Changing the work centre clears the machine with it.

keyActions.action: Show only work that is still open
keyActions.how: The 'Still open' tick box in the toolbar
The pencil icon at the end of the row
keyActions.note: Sets the operator, the machine, the shift, the planned start and finish, and notes. It never touches a quantity - quantities are booked against the job, not typed in here.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu at the end of the row, then Start operation
keyActions.note: Stamps a start time. If work actually began earlier, put the real time into 'Happened at' - these timestamps are what the job is costed on.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Complete operation
keyActions.note: Stamps an end time. A completed operation cannot be reopened. An operation whose routing step demands quality inspection cannot complete until that inspection is accepted - raise a work-order inspection from Quality and decide it if none exists.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Cancel operation, with a reason
keyActions.note: The reason is kept on the audit trail against the operation. The screen insists on one even though the system would accept the change without it, because 'cancelled' on its own tells the next reader nothing.

keyActions.how: The 'Load by work centre' tab
keyActions.note: One row per cell: how many operations are queued, how many are running, and the chargeable minutes still to run. Busiest first.

keyActions.how: Click a cell on the load board
keyActions.note: It brings you back to the Queue tab with that work centre already selected.

keyActions.action: Open the job behind an operation
keyActions.how: The 'Production order' link in the Job column

flow: Filter the queue to your cell, or open the load board and click the busiest cell.
Find the operation and press the pencil to assign an operator, a machine and a shift.
When the operator starts, open the '...' menu and press Start operation. If they started an hour ago, set 'Happened at' to when they really began.
Output is booked on the production order, not here - the Booked / planned column fills in from those bookings.
When the operation is finished, open the '...' menu and press Complete operation.
screens.permission: The screen needs the right to view work orders. Both write paths - assigning and changing status - need the right to manage work orders, and neither is offered without it. Note that this is not the same as any of the production-order rights: someone who can approve production orders does not automatically get these controls.
rules: Quantities are never typed in against an operation. What came off the machine is recorded as a booking on the production order; this screen only reflects it.
An operation belonging to a closed or cancelled job can no longer be changed, because the job's cost was frozen from these very rows.
A completed or cancelled operation cannot be edited or reopened. The row shows 'Closed' where its buttons would be.
An operation cannot be recorded as finishing before it started. The screen checks it and so does the system.
The first booking against an operation starts it automatically and stamps the time.

An operation that was completed but never clocked is costed at its planned setup plus run time; one that never happened is costed at nothing. Time that was actually clocked is charged as it was measured, including any downtime recorded against it - the machine was occupied by this job while it stood idle.
The hourly rate is frozen onto the operation when the job is released, so a later change to the work centre's rate does not silently restate what an old job cost.
screens.notes: There is no search box, because the underlying list does not offer one, and only Sequence, Status and Planned start can be sorted. There is no machine column in the grid - a row knows its machine but the grid would need one lookup per row to name it, so machines are resolved in the assignment dialog and in the machine filter instead. The load board carries no work centre names of its own; it borrows them from the work centre master, and shows 'Name unavailable' if that cannot be read. A cell with nothing on it disappears from the board rather than showing zeroes, which is worth saying out loud in the deck. Shift selects use the company shift master. Operators come from the active internal directory; choose a work order for per-operation output or leave it blank for final output. Downtime-only bookings are accepted. Legacy shift codes remain visible read-only.

screens.title: Production planning
screens.purpose: One week of work per work centre and machine. The load strip answers whether the plan fits - remaining planned minutes per centre per day against rostered capacity where a roster exists, standard hours elsewhere, with the days that do not fit flagged. The timeline answers what runs where, and an operation is rescheduled through the same assignment dialog the queue uses.
screens.whoUses: The production planner, laying the week out before releasing it to the floor.

keyActions.how: The Previous week, This week and Next week controls above the board
The work centre selector
keyActions.note: The machine view then lists that cell’s seats plus the operations not yet on any machine.

keyActions.how: The Over badge on a load-strip day
keyActions.note: A day marked Over holds more planned minutes than the centre’s capacity for it.

keyActions.how: Select the operation on the timeline
keyActions.note: The new window is re-validated on save, and a machine double-booking is reported - or refused, where the plant blocks overlaps.

keyActions.how: The Without a planned window list at the foot of the board

screens.permission: Anyone with the right to see production orders can open this screen and read the board. Moving an operation needs the work-order management right.
rules: Releases plan operations inside rostered shift windows where a roster exists, and round the clock where none does.
A machine clash badge compares the operations loaded for the visible week; the assignment itself checks everything.

screens.title: Assembly orders
screens.purpose: Kits put together at a bench rather than run through a routing - the lock set built from a handle, a cylinder, a lock body, a set of keys and a screw kit. An assembly order names the finished item, the quantity, the components it eats and where the finished units are received. The order opens in a panel over the list rather than on a page of its own, because an assembly is a short document and an operator working down twenty of them should not lose their place. Where a component is serial tracked, the serials that went into each build are recorded against the order, which is what answers a warranty claim years later.
screens.whoUses: The assembly line supervisor and the bench operator.

keyActions.how: Click the order code, the row, or the Open button at the end of the row
The toolbar: status, item, and a planned-start date window
keyActions.note: A QC badge next to the status marks an order whose output has to be inspected and has not been.

keyActions.how: The search box above the list
New assembly order, top right
keyActions.note: Choose a manufacturable item - the search only offers those - optionally pick one of its approved assembly or production recipes, the quantity, the component and output warehouses, the bench, the plan, and a priority. A draft reserves and consumes nothing.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Edit draft or Delete, with a reason for the deletion
keyActions.note: Only while it is a draft. The item and the recipe cannot be changed - that is a different order, not an edit. A deleted draft leaves no trail; anything further along is cancelled instead.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Approve, with a reason
keyActions.note: Approval confirms the plan so the order can be scheduled and released.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Release, with a reason
keyActions.note: Takes a hard reservation for every component. The dialog shows what is still short before anything is promised - a short line refuses the whole release. Each reservation carries the order's priority and its planned start as the required date.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Start, with a reason
keyActions.note: Stamps when the bench actually began. Kitting and building are separate events, often hours apart, so issuing does not start the clock.

keyActions.action: Record the components handed to the bench
keyActions.how: Open the order, then Issue components
keyActions.note: No stock moves here. The parts are still owned and still reserved to this order; the ledger is written when the assembly is completed. Each figure is the running total handed over for that line, not an addition to it.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Complete
keyActions.note: Only offered while the order is in progress. This is the step that consumes the components and creates the finished stock. When the order needs inspection the output goes onto QC hold and an inspection is raised with it.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Record QC verdict
keyActions.note: When an inspection holds the output, this opens that inspection's own sheet in Quality and the verdict is decided there - deciding it releases the stock and completes the order in one step. When no inspection covers the hold, the accepted and rejected quantities are recorded here and must account for everything held.

keyActions.how: Open the order, then Close order or Cancel, with a reason
keyActions.note: Close once a completed order is done with. Cancel only before the components have been handed to the bench; its reservations are given back in the same step.

keyActions.how: The Board tab on the register
keyActions.note: Open work grouped by assembly line, planned against actual, with a lateness badge where the plan has slipped - days past the planned end, or a start that never happened.

keyActions.action: Name the serials that went into the build
keyActions.how: The serial pickers inside the Complete dialog, one per serial-tracked component line
keyActions.note: One serial per unit consumed. The system works out how many that should be and refuses the completion if the count does not match.

keyActions.action: Read the components and the serial trail
keyActions.how: The Components table and the Serial traceability section inside the order panel

flow: Raise the order: the item, the recipe when it is not the default, the quantity, the warehouses, the bench, the plan and the priority.
Approve it, then Release it to the bench - the release shows any shortage first and reserves every component.
Press Issue components and enter what was actually kitted to the bench, line by line, with a reason. Nothing moves in stock - this records the hand-over. Further hand-overs top the totals up.
Press Start when the build begins, so the plan and the reality can be compared on the board.
Press Complete. Enter the assembled quantity and, if any failed, the rejected quantity.
For every serial-tracked component, pick the exact serial numbers that went into these units.

Enter a reason and confirm. In one step the components are consumed and the finished units are received - into the output store, or onto QC hold with an inspection when the order needs one - and the serials are written against the order.
When the output is on hold, record the verdict: on the linked inspection's sheet, or on the order itself when no inspection covers it. Accepted output becomes saleable; the order completes.
Close the order when it is done with. A completed assembly can be packed from the Packing screen.
screens.permission: Reading the register needs the right to view assembly orders. Approve, release, issue, start, close, cancel, amend and delete all need the right to manage assembly orders; Complete needs a separate right to complete an assembly, and recording a verdict needs the right to decide inspections, so the three are asked for independently and one does not stand in for another. Searching for serial numbers inside the Complete dialog additionally needs the right to view inventory.
rules: Components are committed when the order is released, handed over when they are issued, and only eaten when the assembly is completed. Nothing is written to the stock ledger until then, because only then is it known what was actually built.

A line may be issued short of its requirement but never above it. Nothing beyond the requirement was ever reserved for this order, so issuing more would put unreserved stock on the bench that another document could still be promised.

Consumption is scaled by what was produced. A run planned for 100 that yielded 90 good and 5 rejected consumed 95/100 of every component - a rejected lock set ate its cylinder exactly as a good one did.

Rejected output is never received into stock. It is not a saleable unit, and receiving it would put scrap into the finished goods balance. It still consumed its components, which is why it is reported at completion rather than written off later.
More than the planned quantity cannot be reported. Components were only drawn for the plan; raise a second order for the excess.
A serial identifies one physical unit, so exactly one serial is named per unit consumed. A serial another assembly has already swallowed is refused.
Completing is one indivisible step. Either the components are consumed and the finished units created, or nothing happens at all - there is no path that eats a cylinder without producing a lock set.
When the order is marked as needing inspection, the finished units are received onto QC hold rather than into the available pool, and an inspection is raised with them. The stock is held either way.

The verdict on held output has exactly one release path. When an inspection holds it, deciding that inspection in Quality releases the stock and completes the order in the same step; recording a different verdict over it is refused. Only a hold no inspection covers is settled on the order itself, and then the accepted and rejected quantities must account for everything held.
A completed assembly cannot be reopened.

An assembly can only be cancelled before its components have been handed to the bench. Past that the parts are physically gone from the store and the order has to be completed or closed, so the trail survives.

A completed assembly whose output is packed nowhere yet is offered on the Packing screen. Packing it raises its packing order and marks it packed in one step, so it leaves the ready list the moment its order exists.
screens.notes: The item is shown as the first eight characters of its identifier with a link to the item master, not as its code, because the list does not carry the code.

screens.title: Job work
screens.purpose: Processing done outside the factory: handles going out for PVD, castings to a machinist, finished parts out for laser marking. The single most important thing this screen exists to make visible is that material sent to a job worker is still yours. It leaves the factory on a challan but it never leaves the books - it is company stock held in a job-work state, still counted in valuation, still attributable to a vendor, a challan and an order line. What it stops being is available, so nobody can be promised it. The second tab, Pending at vendor, is where you see how much of your working capital is currently sitting outside the factory and how long it has been there. The third tab, Invoices, is where the vendor's bills for that work are raised and tracked against what each receipt earned.
screens.whoUses: The planner raises and approves the order, the storekeeper issues the material and receives it back, and the plant manager approves and closes.

keyActions.how: New job work order, top right, on the Orders tab
keyActions.note: It is saved as a draft. Nothing is reserved and no material moves. Someone who may see cost centres can name the cost centre the processing charges belong to - typically the job-worked process, such as plating; an amendment by anyone else keeps it as it was.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu at the end of the row, then Amend draft
keyActions.note: Only while it is a draft, and the vendor cannot be changed - sending the same material to a different processor is a different order, because the challan would name the wrong party.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Approve, with a reason
keyActions.note: Approval confirms the vendor, the process and the rate, and takes hard reservations on the material so no other document can be promised it.

keyActions.action: Issue the material and raise the challan
keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Issue to vendor
keyActions.note: This is the step that moves the stock into the job-work state and produces the outward challan, with the declared values taken from what the books actually carry the material at.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Receive output
keyActions.note: Three separate figures per line - good output received, output the vendor spoiled, and material that came back untouched - because those three post to three different places.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Close order, with a reason
keyActions.note: Close only once the balance has been received or written off. Anything still recorded as at the vendor stays on the books as company stock.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Cancel order, with a reason
keyActions.note: Only before the material has left. Every reservation it holds is released in the same step, so the material becomes available to other documents immediately. It stays on the list as cancelled - the trail is kept.

keyActions.how: The '...' menu, then Delete draft, with a reason
keyActions.note: The draft and its lines are gone and the number is not reused. Cancel it instead if the order should stay visible.

keyActions.action: See what is out at vendors right now
keyActions.how: The 'Pending at vendor' tab
keyActions.note: Grouped by vendor and item, with the number of orders behind each figure, the oldest issue date, the earliest date it is due back, how many days it has been out, and an Overdue badge.

keyActions.how: The 'Overdue only' button on the Pending at vendor tab

keyActions.action: See only orders with material currently at a vendor
keyActions.how: The 'At a vendor now' button on the Orders tab

keyActions.action: Record the vendor's bill for the work
keyActions.how: The 'Invoices' tab, then Record job-work invoice: choose the vendor, then the order, tick the receipt lines and check the prefilled amounts, enter the vendor's invoice number and date, and save
keyActions.note: Each line is prefilled from what that receipt line still has unbilled, at the order's rate. Saving submits the bill, so the approver sees the match straight away. Approval is on the row, through the same match dialog the purchase bills use.

keyActions.action: Read what has been billed against what was earned
keyActions.how: The 'Invoices' tab
keyActions.note: Every job-work bill with its order, its match result and its status. A bill can never charge more than the receipt lines earned - billing beyond the unbilled charges is refused, not overridden.

flow: Press New job work order. Choose the vendor, the process (polishing, coating, PVD, laser marking, machining or other), and the date the material is due back - that date is what the ageing and the overdue flag are measured against.
Choose the store the material leaves from and, if different, the store the processed output returns to.
Set the rate basis - per piece, per kilo, or a flat rate for the lot - and the rate. The rate is frozen on the order, so a later rate-card change does not restate what was approved.
Set the GST rate and the SAC for the processing service - 18% and 9988 unless the vendor's paperwork says otherwise.
Tick 'Output must be inspected' if the returned goods have to go through QC.

Add the lines: the item going out, the quantity, what it comes back as (leave blank if the same item comes back), the expected output quantity if the yield is not one for one, and the agreed loss percentage.
Save the draft, then Approve it. Approval reserves the material.

Press Issue to vendor. Enter the challan date, the expected return, the vehicle number and the quantities going out. The challan is raised and the stock moves into the job-work state - still yours, no longer available.
The material sits at the vendor. Watch it on the Pending at vendor tab.
When a lot comes back, press Receive output. Split it across Received (good processed output), Rejected (what the vendor spoiled) and Returned unworked (material that came back exactly as it went).
Repeat for each lot until everything is back. Then Close the order.
screens.permission: The screen needs the right to view job work. The actions are split across four different rights on purpose: raising, amending, cancelling and deleting a draft all need the right to create job work orders; issuing needs the right to issue; receiving needs the right to receive; and approving and closing both need the senior job-work right that the plant manager holds and the planner who raises orders does not. That separation is deliberate - the person who raises an order is not the person who approves it.
rules: Material at a vendor is still company property. Issuing does not remove it from the books - it moves it into a job-work pool where it is still owned, still valued and still countable. It is simply not available to promise to anyone else.

The order can only be amended while it is a draft. Once approved it holds reservations that other documents have been refused material because of, and once issued it holds company stock on somebody else's premises. Neither can be quietly restated by a line edit.

An order can only be cancelled before the material has left. Once a challan exists, the order is the only record of where company stock went - a consignment that never comes back is settled by a final receipt that writes the loss off, so the loss is stated rather than implied.
A line cannot issue more than was ordered on it, because only that much was reserved.
Material that came back untouched cannot exceed what is at the vendor. It is the same item that went out, so there is no yield to argue about.
