Getting back more output than the order expected is refused, not quietly accepted - beyond a 2% allowance for the odd extra piece a plating line runs to fill a rack. More than that is a mis-keyed quantity or somebody else's goods, and both need a person.

Loss inside the agreed allowance on the line is written off as scrap with the receipt's reason. Loss beyond the allowance refuses the receipt until someone with the senior job-work right accepts it, and the value of the material lost is charged back to the vendor at what the company was carrying it at - not at a price list, and not as a penalty.
Rejected output the vendor is going to rework keeps the material where it is: nothing moves, the order line stays open, and the quantity keeps appearing as pending at the vendor with its true ageing.

The vendor's charge accrues on good output received, at the agreed rate, on the receipt date. A short or rejected delivery therefore costs less without anyone raising a credit note. A flat lot rate is charged once, on the first receipt that brings any output back.
Give the order its GST rate and SAC when raising it - 18% and 9988 unless the vendor's paperwork says otherwise. Both are copied onto the vendor-invoice lines when the work is billed.

A job-work bill charges receipt lines, never the order in the abstract. Approving one books the processing charge to the job-work expense account, moves what each receipt line has billed, and recovers the chargeback for material the vendor lost beyond allowance against the same bill. Cancelling a posted bill reverses both postings.
Where an order requires inspection, the returned output is received onto QC hold rather than into the available pool, and an inspection is raised with it.

Batch-tracked and serial-tracked items cannot be sent for job work, in either direction. There is no way to name a batch or a serial on the challan, so it is refused at order entry rather than after the material has left the building.
Only items flagged for job work on the item master, and still active, can be put on a line.
screens.notes: Two gaps worth flagging to whoever assembles the deck. First, there is no detail page for a job work order: the challans it travelled under, the history of lots received against it, and the issued-versus-received reconciliation report all exist in the system but have no screen. The order's lines are only visible inside the Issue and Receive dialogs. Second, the Receive dialog has no control for approving loss beyond the agreed allowance and no control for closing a line and writing off the shortfall - so a receipt where the vendor lost more than the allowance will be refused on this screen with a message saying it needs approval, and there is nowhere here to give it. Also: the row menu offers 'Issue to vendor' on orders that have already been issued, but the system only accepts an issue against an approved order, so a second challan raised from that menu will be refused. Vendor names come from the vendor master and fall back to a dash; items are shown as the first eight characters of their identifier, since the list carries no item code.

screens.title: Shift roster
screens.purpose: Plan operators against local shift windows, cells and machines. Day board shows each cell and machine under active shifts; Week shows operators across seven days; Shifts maintains immutable codes and wall-clock times.
screens.whoUses: Production supervisors and plant managers plan staffing; planners read it.

keyActions.how: Day board, choose date and work centre, then Assign or Bulk assign
keyActions.note: Bulk planning is atomic. Every overlap is named; none of the batch is saved on conflict.

keyActions.how: Copy day, source date and target date range
keyActions.note: Limit the work centre when a copy exceeds the bounded batch.

keyActions.how: Shifts tab, New shift or Edit; activate, deactivate or retire with a reason
keyActions.note: The company timezone supplies the local times. Future planned assignments must be cancelled before re-timing or retirement.

flow: Maintain shifts with their start/end times, break and ordering.
Choose the local start date, cell, optional machine and internal operator.
Check the day or week board. Cancel with a reason when the plan changes.
Choose a shift on work-order assignment or production booking. The booking pre-fills from the operator roster and can differ from the plan.
rules: Night shifts belong to the date they start. Adjacent windows do not overlap.
An operator cannot hold overlapping planned windows; each machine permits one operator at a time. Use a cell assignment when tending several machines.
Maintenance and breakdown warn rather than refuse a staffing plan.
Legacy production shift text is shown read-only and retained.
screens.permission: shift_roster.view opens the board; shift_roster.manage plans and cancels. shift.view opens the shift register; shift.manage changes the master. Administrators must grant new rights to existing non-system roles.
screens.notes: Rostered capacity is displayed beside calendar capacity in Machine utilisation. Daily production by shift reports output, rejections, downtime and yield.

chapters.groupIntro: This part of the system covers everything that happens between "the goods exist" and "the goods have left". It starts with the check sheets you write yourself, which state what good means for each of your products; goes on to the inspections that judge material against those sheets and decide where held stock goes; then to the packing bench, where boxes are opened, filled, weighed and sealed; and finishes at the gate, where a consignment is loaded, released and followed until the customer confirms it arrived. The thread running through all four screens is accountability: every lot inspected accounts for every piece, every serialised unit is named into the carton and onto the lorry, and every movement carries a reason recorded against the person who made it. The specification screen is described first, because the inspection screen cannot be understood without it.

screens.title: Inspection specifications
screens.purpose: This is where you write down what "good" means for your own products, in your own words. A specification lists the characteristics an inspector has to check, what each one is measured against, and how much of a delivered lot to look at. Every inspection anywhere in the plant is judged against one of these sheets, so this is the single place your quality standard is stated rather than remembered. It is also the clearest example of the system being configured by you rather than by a developer.
screens.whoUses: Whoever owns quality standards - a quality engineer, a plant manager or the proprietor. Inspectors read these sheets constantly and write them never.

keyActions.how: New specification, top right
keyActions.note: It is created as version 1. The button only appears for an account allowed to author specifications.

keyActions.action: List the characteristics to be measured
keyActions.how: Inside the form, Add characteristic, then name it and choose its type
keyActions.note: Four types: a measured value with a minimum, maximum, target and unit; a pass-or-fail; a free-text observation; or a chosen value picked from a list of answers you supply, one per line.

keyActions.how: Tick "Critical - one failure condemns the lot" on that characteristic
keyActions.note: A critical characteristic can never be optional, so "Must be recorded" ticks itself and locks.

keyActions.action: Set the order the sheet is worked in
keyActions.how: The up and down arrows on each characteristic
keyActions.note: This is the order the inspector sees it on the shop floor.

keyActions.how: Applies to: one item, an item category, or the stage default
keyActions.note: An item specification beats a category one, which beats the stage default.

keyActions.how: Inspection stage: Incoming, Job work, In process, Assembly, Final or Return
keyActions.note: This is when the check happens, and it is how the specification is found for an arriving lot.

keyActions.action: Choose how much of a lot to measure
keyActions.how: Sampling plan: Every piece, Percentage of the lot, Fixed sample, or AQL (ISO 2859-1)
keyActions.note: A percentage plan needs its percentage, a fixed sample needs a whole number of pieces. A percentage always rounds up and never falls below one piece.

keyActions.action: Stage a specification without putting it in force
keyActions.how: Untick "Selected for new inspections"
keyActions.note: Useful for preparing the next revision without displacing the one currently used.

keyActions.action: Read a whole sheet and its history
keyActions.how: Click any row
keyActions.note: Shows the characteristics as a table, warns how many of them can condemn a lot on their own, and lists every revision of that code.

keyActions.how: The pencil on the row, or Amend this version in the detail
keyActions.note: Refused once an inspection has been judged against it; the screen then offers "Raise a new version instead".

keyActions.how: The ... menu on the row, or New version in the detail
keyActions.note: The current check sheet is carried over so changing one tolerance is not forty rows retyped. A reason of 3 to 255 characters is required and is kept against both versions.

keyActions.how: The ... menu on the row, Retire this version, with a reason
keyActions.note: It stops being used for new inspections and drops out of every list. It is not deleted.

keyActions.how: Filters for stage, sampling, item, category, and In force / Superseded only / Every version; the search box takes a code or a name
keyActions.note: The list shows what is in force by default; superseded versions are hidden until you ask for them.

flow: New specification.
Give it a code and a name.
Choose the stage the check happens at.
Choose what it applies to: one item, an item category, or every item at that stage.
Choose the sampling plan and fill in its figure.
Add each characteristic: what is measured, its type, its limits or its permitted answers, and whether a failure condemns the lot.
Order the characteristics the way they are worked on the floor.
Create specification. It is version 1, and in force immediately unless you unticked "Selected for new inspections".
rules: Only one specification may be in force for a given scope and stage. Two competing sheets would mean the answer depended on which was found first, so an arriving lot always resolves to exactly one.

A version that has already judged an inspection is frozen. Its name, description and whether it is selected stay editable; its scope, stage, sampling and characteristics do not, because a past pass or fail has to stay reproducible against the sheet it was judged by. The way to change those is to raise a new version, which retires the old one and moves nothing already recorded.
A critical characteristic is always mandatory. One that could be skipped would never condemn anything, so the combination is refused outright.
A chosen-value characteristic must list the answers it accepts, and the answers cannot repeat.
Limits belong only to a measured value. A pass-or-fail or a free-text question cannot carry a minimum and maximum, because nothing would ever read them and the sheet would only look configured.
A specification needs at least one characteristic and may hold at most 200. Two characteristics cannot ask the same thing - names are compared ignoring case.
Retiring is not deleting. The row survives so an inspection carried out six months ago still says what it followed.
screens.permission: Anyone who can see quality may read the specifications. Writing, amending, versioning and retiring all need a separate right to author inspection specifications - deliberately not the same right as measuring or deciding, because the person who measures a part is not the person who decides what it has to measure. The standard QC Inspector role does not carry it; administrators do, and it can be granted to a custom role.
screens.notes: The list and detail show the item and category a specification governs as short identifiers rather than names - an item is an eight-character link into the item master, and a category name appears only for a reader who can also read the category list. Screenshots will show that rather than an item code, which is worth knowing before the deck is laid out. There is nothing on this screen that lists which inspections used a given version.

screens.title: Quality control
screens.purpose: This is where material waits for a verdict and where the verdict is given. Goods arriving on a receipt, coming back from a job worker, finished on an assembly, booked out of production or packed for a customer are inspected here - most lots arrive automatically from the document that raised them, and a supervisor can also raise one by hand. The screen has four tabs: the queue of what is waiting, the full history of what has been decided, the rework bench, and two reports on what those decisions say about your items and your vendors.
screens.whoUses: The QC inspector lives on the pending tab. Whoever is authorised to release material takes the decision. Buyers and the owner read the reports.

keyActions.how: Raise inspection, at the top of the screen
keyActions.note: For a supervisor pulling a lot off the shelf: name the stage, the item, the store and the quantity, and whether raising it moves the quantity into QC hold. Leave the hold off when an upstream document has already held the stock.

keyActions.how: Click the row, at any status
keyActions.note: Readings per characteristic with their photo thumbnails, the rejection reason, the decided quantities, every earlier verdict and the rework cycles. Lots still owed a verdict keep their Inspect action beside it.

keyActions.action: See what is waiting for a decision
keyActions.how: Pending inspections, the tab the screen opens on
keyActions.note: Oldest first, because the oldest hold is the one blocking a delivery. A lot waiting three days is badged, seven days is badged in red.

keyActions.how: The stage selector above the queue
keyActions.note: The queue has no search box and no sortable columns on purpose - it is ordered oldest first by the system. Searching lives on the next tab.

keyActions.action: Open the check sheet for a lot
keyActions.how: Inspect on the row
keyActions.note: Available to an account that can record measurements or decide, or both.

keyActions.how: Type into the box on each characteristic
keyActions.note: A measured value that leaves its limits turns red as you type and states the allowed range. A pass-or-fail is two buttons; a chosen value is a list of the permitted answers.

keyActions.action: Attach a photograph to a reading
keyActions.how: Photo, on the characteristic
keyActions.note: Shown only to an account that can both record measurements and upload documents.

keyActions.action: Add a note against one characteristic
keyActions.how: The Remark box beside the reading
keyActions.note: For the detail that a number cannot carry.

keyActions.how: The five boxes: Accepted, Rejected, Rework, Hold, Scrap
keyActions.note: A running line says how much is still to allocate, and the form will not submit until it reads that everything is accounted for.

keyActions.how: Fill Reason, then Submit inspection
keyActions.note: Reason is required on every decision and is kept in the audit trail. The system works out the verdict from how you split the quantity - there is no result to choose.

keyActions.how: Save readings (this is what the button says for an account that cannot decide)
keyActions.note: The system replies with what the readings so far imply - accepted, rework or rejected - and what is still to be measured.

keyActions.how: All inspections tab
keyActions.note: Search by inspection, item or reference, sort, and filter by stage and outcome. Accepted, rejected, rework and scrapped quantities are all columns, and rejected material owed back to a vendor is flagged "To vendor".

keyActions.action: Re-decide a lot on hold or in rework
keyActions.how: Inspect, on a row still showing pending, in progress, rework or hold
keyActions.note: Quantity in those two buckets is still sitting in QC hold and still owes somebody a verdict.

keyActions.how: Rework tab, then Open a cycle on the lot
keyActions.note: Name the quantity and who does it. Starting puts it on the bench; completing it with an outcome hands the lot back for re-decision. A scrapped or returned outcome is the bench's recommendation - the inspector still dispositions it.

keyActions.action: Chart an item's quality over time
keyActions.how: Reports tab, Item quality history, choose an item and a window of 90, 180 or 365 days
keyActions.note: Accepted, rework and rejected quantity by month, with the same figures repeated as a table beneath the chart.

keyActions.how: Reports tab, Vendor quality record, choose a vendor
keyActions.note: Inspections, quantity inspected, quantity rejected and the rejection rate for the window, then the rate broken down by item.

flow: Open Quality. The pending queue is the tab you land on.
Take the oldest lot for your stage and press Inspect.
Work down the check sheet in order, entering each reading and attaching a photograph where a defect needs one.
Split the inspected quantity across Accepted, Rejected, Rework, Hold and Scrap until nothing is left to allocate.
Type the reason for the decision. If anything is being rejected or scrapped, fill in the rejection reason and the inspection remarks as well.
Submit inspection. The stock moves as you split it, and the confirmation tells you what actually moved.
rules: Material on QC hold is in the building and on the books, but nothing can issue it, sell it or promise it to a customer. That is the entire point of the hold.

A decision moves the stock in the same breath as it records the verdict, and the two commit together or not at all. Accepted quantity is released into free stock; rejected quantity moves to the damaged pool, where it is counted but unusable; scrapped quantity is written off and does not come back; rework and hold quantities deliberately stay in QC hold to be decided again later.

Deciding the inspection also settles the document that raised it, in the same step: the receipt line passes or fails and the purchase order moves on, the assembly order completes, the job-work lot is released - with no second movement and no second verdict for the same hold.

The five quantities must add up to exactly the quantity inspected. Anything left over would be stock sitting in QC hold that no decision explains - which on the floor is unexplained material on a shelf.

A critical characteristic that fails condemns the whole lot. None of it may be accepted or sent for rework; reject it or scrap it. The screen says so before anything is entered, and stops offering acceptance the moment a critical reading fails.

Every characteristic marked as must-be-recorded needs a reading before a decision can be taken - unless a critical failure has already settled the answer, in which case no further measurement could change it and the rest of the sheet is not demanded.

Rejecting or scrapping anything requires a stated cause. It is what feeds the vendor's rating, what a debit note is written from, and what a corrective action starts with, so the decision is refused without it.

A lot can be decided again while quantity is still on hold, but accepted, rejected and scrapped quantities can only ever grow. Material already released may have been issued or sold, so it cannot be pulled back by editing the inspection.

Rejected material from a named vendor is flagged as owing a return and the buyers are notified. The return itself is raised in procurement - quality states that one is owed, it does not raise it, because the return is procurement's document, numbering and approval.

Whether a reading passes is decided by the system against the specification, never asserted by whoever typed it, and the result is stored as it was judged at the time. A later change to the specification therefore cannot rewrite the past.

An item for which nobody has written a specification is still put forward for inspection. It simply arrives with no characteristics to measure, and the inspector dispositions it on judgement with a remark - refusing to raise it would mean the goods were never inspected at all.

A finished rework cycle hands the lot back for re-decision rather than dispositioning it. Every verdict stays in the lot's history, so re-deciding a reworked lot never erases how it was decided before.
screens.permission: Reading the queue, the history and the reports needs the right to see quality. Recording measurements and deciding a lot are two separate rights on purpose: the person who measures a part is usually not the person authorised to release a consignment on the strength of it. An account that may only measure sees the readings and no disposition section at all, and is told so; an account that may only decide sees the readings as recorded and sends only the decision. Attaching a photograph additionally needs the right to upload documents.
screens.notes: Most inspections arrive automatically from goods receipts, job-work returns, assembly completions, production bookings and packing starts - and a supervisor can raise one by hand with Raise inspection. There is also no Close action anywhere on the screen: a fully dispositioned inspection stays on the record as decided. Rows carry the item, batch and vendor as identifiers rather than names, so the Item column is an eight-character link into the item master; a screenshot will show that rather than an item code. Both report cards are empty until an item or a vendor is chosen, so a screenshot needs a selection made first.

screens.title: Packing
screens.purpose: This is the bench. A packing order says what has to be boxed for one customer; opening one gives you the carton builder, where each box is opened, filled, weighed and sealed. What comes out of it is the carton count and gross weight the freight is priced on, the packing list that travels with the goods, and the record of exactly which serialised unit went into which box - the answer to a customer complaint months later.
screens.whoUses: The packing supervisor and the packers. The despatch bay reads it too, through the "Awaiting dispatch" filter.

keyActions.action: See what is on the bench and what is finished
keyActions.how: The list, with the "Still on the bench" and "Awaiting dispatch" tick boxes
keyActions.note: A packed order that no consignment has claimed shows "Awaiting dispatch" in amber. That is the despatch bay's queue.

keyActions.how: Status, customer, and a planned-date range; the search box takes a packing order code
Click the row, or the Pack button at the end of it
keyActions.note: The button reads View instead of Pack for an account that cannot change anything.

keyActions.how: The Ready from assembly panel above the list, then Pack on the row
keyActions.note: Lists completed assemblies whose output is packed nowhere yet. Packing one raises its packing order - the assembled item, from the warehouse it was received into - and marks the assembly packed against it in the same step, so it leaves the list the moment its order exists. The customer comes from the sales order when the assembly was raised for one; otherwise name it here. Nothing here is created automatically.

keyActions.how: Start packing, at the top of the open order
keyActions.note: A draft has no bench: cartons can only be opened once the order is in progress. Starting raises a final inspection per line whose item requires final quality control, and the order cannot complete or hand over until each is accepted.

keyActions.how: Add a carton, at the foot of the cartons list
keyActions.note: Name the box being used and how many of it, its type (box, carton, crate, pallet, bag, drum or shrink wrap), its dimensions and its empty weight. The box list shows only packing material actually in stock at that warehouse, with the free quantity beside each.

keyActions.how: Choose a line, the quantity and the net weight, then Pack
keyActions.note: The line list offers only what is still unpacked and shows the balance left on each.

keyActions.action: Name the batch or the individual units
keyActions.how: The batch selector, or the serial picker, appears under the line when the item is tracked
keyActions.note: One serial per unit, chosen from stock at that warehouse; the count must equal the quantity being packed.

keyActions.action: Take something back out of an open carton
keyActions.how: The bin icon on the content row
keyActions.note: The quantity goes straight back to the order's line.

keyActions.how: Seal carton, with a reason
keyActions.note: One way. The net weight is totalled from the contents, the gross adds the empty box, and the box itself is issued from stock at that moment.

keyActions.how: The bin icon in the carton header, with a reason
keyActions.note: Only while it is unsealed. Its contents go back to the order's lines, and the carton number is not reused.

keyActions.how: Complete, with a reason
keyActions.note: Every carton must be sealed first. If a line is not fully packed, tick "Allow a short pack" to complete anyway; the lines that went out short are named in the confirmation. Refused while a line's final inspection is anything short of accepted: decide it, or repack the rejected goods and re-inspect the line.

keyActions.action: Hand the boxes to a consignment
keyActions.how: Hand to dispatch, then choose one of that customer's consignments that has not left
keyActions.note: This needs the right to create dispatches, not the packing right - handing goods over is a despatch act. The consignment has to exist already; it is created on the Dispatch screen.

keyActions.how: Generate packing list, above the cartons
keyActions.note: It is built in the background so nothing waits; the button turns into Download when it is ready. Watching the build needs the right to see reports - without it the document is still built, but somebody else has to fetch it.

keyActions.how: Close, once it has been handed over
keyActions.note: Nothing further can be recorded against it.

keyActions.how: Cancel order, with a reason
keyActions.note: Only before it is packed. Unsealed cartons are emptied back to the lines.

flow: Open the packing order and press Start packing.
Add a carton: name the box, its type and its empty weight.
Pack lines into it - quantity, net weight, and the batch or the individual serials where the item is tracked.
Seal the carton. Its gross weight is settled and the box is issued from stock.
Repeat until every line reads Complete.
Complete the order. It becomes packed and appears to the despatch bay.
Generate the packing list, then hand the order to the consignment that will take it.
rules: Packing moves no finished goods. The only stock it consumes is the packing material itself, and only when a carton is sealed - a carton is a real box somebody paid for. The goods leave the building on dispatch, and taking them out here as well would decrement the same stock twice.

Sealing is one way. A sealed carton is a taped box on a pallet: its contents cannot be changed, it cannot be removed from the order, and it cannot be unsealed - undoing it would mean putting a box that has already been used back on the shelf.
An empty carton cannot be sealed, because that would consume a box for nothing.

You cannot pack more of a line than the order asked for. Over-packing is refused rather than trimmed, because the difference is either a mis-keyed quantity or goods nobody ordered, and both need a person to look at them.
A batch-tracked item must name its batch, and a serial-tracked item must name one serial per unit, before the box is closed. Once the tape is on, "which carton held that unit" has to be answerable.
An order cannot be completed with an open carton on the bench, or with no cartons at all. It can be completed short only if you say so deliberately.
An order that has been packed can no longer be cancelled - packing material has been consumed against it. It is closed instead. Cancelling is offered only before that point.

A completed assembly is packed from the Ready from assembly panel, not from the order list: raising its packing order and marking it packed happen in one step, so two packers cannot plan around the same output.
A packed order can be claimed by one consignment only. A second, different consignment is refused, so two dispatchers cannot plan around the same boxes.
Sealing needs the named packing material to be in stock at that warehouse. If none is, the form says so plainly, and no carton on that order can be sealed until some is.
screens.permission: Seeing packing orders needs the packing view right. Starting an order, opening and filling cartons, sealing, completing, closing and cancelling all need the packing management right. Handing an order over to a consignment is the one exception: it needs the right to create dispatches, because that is a despatch decision rather than a packing one.
screens.notes: There is no way to raise a packing order from this screen - there is no New button, and no other screen in the application creates one either; the empty state says they come from allocated sales orders. It is worth confirming with the client how their packing orders will be raised in practice before this page is presented. Lines and carton contents display the item as a long identifier rather than a code or a name, and the order header says "Against a sales order" rather than showing the order number, so a screenshot of a real order will read thinner than the client expects.

screens.title: Dispatch
screens.purpose: This is the gate, and the board for everything still on the road. One tab lists the consignments themselves and walks each one from staged, to released, to in transit, to delivered. The other is a tracking board showing both directions at once - what has gone out to customers and what is still coming in from vendors - with the carrier reference, the promised date and whether it has been missed. Anything past its promised delivery date is flagged here before anywhere else, because that is the call you get from the customer.
screens.whoUses: The despatch manager and the gate. The tracking board is what the owner or a customer-facing person leaves open all day.

keyActions.how: Create dispatch, top right
keyActions.note: The type, the counterparty, the warehouse it leaves, the whole carrier record and the lines it carries are all captured at once. Nothing moves in stock.

keyActions.action: Say what kind of consignment it is
keyActions.how: Dispatch type: Sales, Purchase return, Job work or Transfer
keyActions.note: A sales consignment must name the customer; a purchase return or a job-work consignment must name the vendor. Only a sales consignment may be attached to a sales order.

keyActions.action: Record how it can be traced
keyActions.how: Transporter, courier name, transport name, tracking id, LR number, vehicle number, driver name and mobile, e-way bill number
keyActions.note: At least one of tracking id, LR number or vehicle number is required. A consignment with none of them cannot be chased when the customer rings.

keyActions.how: Boxes, weight in kilograms, freight amount, and who pays the freight
keyActions.note: Freight paid by the consignor is you, by the consignee is the receiver. It is captured per consignment because it decides whether the freight is recoverable.

keyActions.how: Item, quantity, and the batch or the serials, then Add
keyActions.note: A serial-tracked item needs one serial per unit, picked from stock at that warehouse; a batch-tracked item needs its batch named. A consignment cannot be created with no lines.

keyActions.how: Actions, Mark ready, with a reason
keyActions.note: The consignment is packed and standing at the gate. Nothing has left and no stock has moved.

keyActions.how: Actions, Dispatch, with a reason
keyActions.note: The only action on this screen that moves stock, and it is offered only on a consignment already marked ready.

keyActions.how: Actions, Mark in transit, with a reason
keyActions.note: Records that the carrier has picked it up.

keyActions.how: Actions, Confirm delivery
keyActions.note: The delivery note is optional. If the consignment arrived after its promised date, the screen asks for the delay reason first, because the system will not confirm it without one.

keyActions.how: Actions, Cancel dispatch, with a reason
keyActions.note: Only before it leaves. Nothing has moved out, so nothing comes back, but the document stays on the record.

keyActions.action: See the whole story of one consignment
keyActions.how: Actions, Tracking timeline
keyActions.note: Transport detail, LR number, vehicle, driver and e-way bill, the exact serial numbers that went out, and every reported movement newest first.

keyActions.how: Inside the timeline: what happened, when, where, and a remark
keyActions.note: In transit, Delivered, QC pending or Received. An event whose status differs from the consignment's own also moves the consignment itself.

keyActions.how: The "Delayed only" tick box on either tab, or the Delay column
keyActions.note: A late row is accented in red with the number of days spelled out, on the leading cell where the eye lands first.

keyActions.action: Watch inbound as well as outbound
keyActions.how: The Tracking board tab
keyActions.note: Both directions in one list: the party, the purchase or sales order reference, the carrier, the tracking id, the promised date, the delay and its stated reason, and whether inspection or a goods receipt is still owed at the far end.

keyActions.how: On a linked SALES dispatch that is ready or later, choose Raise invoice, review the preview and optional date, then Confirm and issue. View invoice opens its stored record.

flow: Create dispatch. Choose the type and the counterparty it is going to.
Choose the warehouse it leaves from, the dispatch date and the expected delivery date.
Fill in the carrier: transporter or courier, and at least a tracking id, an LR number or a vehicle number.
Add each line, naming the batch or the individual serials where the item is tracked.
Create dispatch. It is staged, and nothing has moved.
Actions, Mark ready once it is loaded at the gate.
Actions, Dispatch to release it. This is where the stock leaves.
Actions, Mark in transit as the carrier reports it, and Confirm delivery when it arrives.
rules: Releasing a consignment is the only step that moves stock, and it does everything at once: the promise the sales order was holding is consumed, the goods are posted out of the warehouse, each order line's dispatched quantity is advanced and the order moves to partly dispatched or fully dispatched. Either all of that happens or none of it does - there is no state in which the stock has gone and the order does not know.

The customer's order is answered when the consignment is released, not when it arrives. Releasing it is what reduces what the order still owes. Confirming delivery afterwards records the arrival date, who confirmed it and the receiver's note; it moves nothing in stock and changes nothing on the order.
A sales order must be fully allocated before a consignment against it can leave. If it is not, the release is refused and names allocation as the missing step.
Shipping more than was ordered is refused rather than trimmed, and the refusal states how much of the line actually remains. A short shipment is normal and leaves the balance open.
A serial-tracked item ships the exact units named on its line. Each one must be in stock, belong to that item, and be held at the warehouse the consignment leaves from.
A consignment can only be cancelled before it leaves. Once it has gone there is nothing to call off, and the record stays.
A consignment that arrived after its promised date must state why before the delivery will be confirmed. An on-time-delivery figure whose late rows carry no explanation is a number nobody can act on.
A consignment cannot be recorded as arriving before the day it left.
Tracking events are never edited or deleted. A correction is a later event, and the two together are the truth - a delivery history somebody can rewrite answers no question worth asking.

Anything past its promised delivery date is picked up by an automatic sweep that raises one notification for the company - not one per consignment and not one per hour - and the tracking board is where the full list is read.
screens.permission: Seeing the dispatch list and the tracking board needs the dispatch view right. Raising a consignment and releasing it need the right to create dispatches - releasing is the act that moves stock, so it is held to the stronger right. Staging, marking in transit, cancelling and adding a tracking event need the right to update dispatches. Confirming a delivery is a right of its own again, because it is the sentence that closes a customer's expectation.
screens.notes: Three gaps worth knowing before the deck is assembled. First, the screen offers no way to amend a consignment after it is created and no way to delete one; the only route back is Cancel, and only before it leaves. Second, lines added on this screen are not tied to a particular sales-order line: the consignment names the order, and releasing it does mark the order partly dispatched, but the outstanding quantity on each individual order line is not reduced by a consignment raised here, and the stock comes out of free stock rather than out of what that order had reserved. Third, boxes and weight on the create form are typed by hand - they are not carried across from the packing order's own carton totals, and there is no packing-order or carton field on this form at all; the link between a packed order and a consignment is made from the Packing screen's "Hand to dispatch", not from here. Also minor: the delivery confirmation dialog says that anything requiring inspection on arrival moves to QC pending, but in the system that state is reached by recording a tracking event of that kind rather than automatically on confirmation, so do not repeat the claim in the caption. The delay notification points at a "delayed" view that is not a page in the application; the board's "Delayed only" filter is the equivalent. The dispatch list shows the counterparty as "Sales order" or "Vendor consignment" rather than a name - the tracking board does show party names, so it is the better screenshot for a client audience. An order-linked line must name its order line and fit the live reservation; a live invoice blocks dispatch cancellation or amendment.

chapters.groupIntro: Everything the business promises to a customer, buys from a vendor or issues to the shop floor rests on one question: how much of a part do we actually have, and how much of it is already spoken for. This part of the system answers it with three numbers that are easy to confuse and expensive to confuse. **On hand** is what is physically standing in the warehouse. **Reserved** is the part of that same stock already promised to a particular order — it has not moved anywhere, it is simply no longer yours to give away. **Available** is what is left to promise to somebody new, and the system works it out for you: on hand, less reserved, less anything held for QC inspection, less anything marked damaged. Behind those numbers is the stock ledger — a permanent, dated line for every movement that ever happened, which is never edited and never deleted; a mistake is corrected by posting a further entry, exactly the way an accountant corrects a book. These screens show you the balances, the ledger behind them, the promises made against them, the paperwork that moves stock, and the warehouses and bins it all lives in.
chapters.groupTitle: Stock: what you hold, what is promised, and where it lives

screens.title: Stock balances
screens.purpose: This is the screen that answers "can we promise it?". Each line is one item in one warehouse (and, where the item is tracked by lot, one batch), with what is physically on hand, how much of it is already promised, how much is held for inspection, how much is on a lorry between two of your own warehouses, and what is genuinely free. The free figure — Available — is calculated by the system from the others and can never be typed over, so it cannot quietly disagree with the numbers it is made from. Nothing on this screen is remembered from a previous visit: it is read afresh every time the page opens and every time you come back to the browser tab, because a stale "yes, we have it" is how a delivery date gets promised that the plant cannot meet.
screens.whoUses: The storekeeper, the planner and the buyer. In practice it is the most-opened screen in the system.

keyActions.action: See stock for one warehouse only
keyActions.how: Choose the warehouse from the box above the grid. Leave it on "All warehouses" to see every site at once.
keyActions.note: The list covers every warehouse the person is assigned to. A user restricted to particular warehouses does not see the others.

keyActions.action: Find everything that has run low
keyActions.how: Tick "Below reorder level".
keyActions.note: A line qualifies when its free stock has fallen under the reorder level recorded on the item master. Items with no reorder level set never appear here.

keyActions.how: Tick "Has stock".
keyActions.note: Useful after a warehouse has been in use for a while: positions that once held stock stay on the list at zero.

keyActions.how: Type the item code or part of its name into the search box above the grid.
Click the heading of On hand, Available, Stock value, Last movement or Last changed.
keyActions.note: Only those five columns sort. The rest are deliberately fixed, because the sorting is done by the server and it accepts only those.

keyActions.action: Open the item behind a line
keyActions.how: Click the item code in the first column.
The Stock value column appears on the right for those entitled to see it, and is simply absent for everyone else.
keyActions.note: Not hidden — genuinely not sent to the browser. A storekeeper counts stock; a controller values it.

keyActions.how: Page controls at the foot of the table; the page size can be changed there too.

flow: Open Stock balances.
Pick the warehouse, or leave it on all warehouses.
Search for the item code.
Read the Available column — that is what can be promised today.
If Available is low but On hand is not, look across the row: the difference is sitting in Reserved, QC hold, or Damaged.
If a quantity shows under In transit, it is already yours and already on its way to this warehouse — it will become available when the transfer is received.
rules: Available is on hand less reserved, less QC hold, less damaged. The database calculates it; no one can key it. This is what makes it impossible for the free figure to drift away from the figures it is made of.
Reserved stock has not moved and has not left the shelf. It is present, counted in On hand, and simply promised to a named document.
Stock put on QC hold does not come off On hand. The goods have not gone anywhere — they have only stopped being usable — so they stay in On hand and are subtracted from Available.

In-transit stock is counted at the warehouse it is travelling to, not the one it left. That is where the question gets asked: a receiving storekeeper and a planner both want to know what is coming to them.
A red mark against a line means nothing is left to promise. An amber mark means free stock has fallen below the item's reorder level.
Availability is never cached anywhere in the system, on purpose. It costs a moment more to read and it is the number the whole promise chain depends on.

The Bin column identifies a location within the warehouse. Choose a warehouse and then its bin to filter a position. Scrap is shown separately from on-hand and available stock; it stays owned until disposed of.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to view stock can open this screen. The Stock value column needs the separate right to see stock valuation — the standard Store Keeper role deliberately does not carry it, so a storekeeper sees quantities and not money.
screens.notes: Two honest gaps worth knowing before the screenshot is taken. (1) The **Allocated** column will show 0.0000 on every line: the figure exists in the database but nothing in the system currently writes it, so it is always zero. Consider cropping it out of the screenshot or captioning it. (2) There is **no Location column**, although stock can be held down to bin level and the server can filter by bin — so a warehouse that racks its stock will show several lines for the same item and warehouse with no visible reason. The server also accepts filters by item and by batch that this screen does not offer.

screens.title: Stock ledger
screens.purpose: The ledger is the permanent record of why every balance is the number it is. One dated line per movement — every receipt, issue, transfer, adjustment, QC decision, dispatch and count correction — with the quantity, the resulting balance, the document it came from and the reason that was recorded at the time. Nothing here is ever edited and nothing is ever deleted; if a movement was posted wrongly, the fix is to post a further movement that corrects it, exactly as an accountant passes a correcting entry rather than rubbing out an old one. That is a feature, not an inconvenience: it means the balance on the shelf can always be explained back to the paperwork that produced it, and no one can quietly make an awkward month disappear.
screens.whoUses: The storekeeper tracing a discrepancy, the accountant reconciling stock, the owner asking "where did those forty pieces go?".

keyActions.how: Choose the item in the Item box at the top.
Choose it in the Warehouse box.

keyActions.action: See only one kind of movement
keyActions.how: Choose from the movement-type list — goods receipt, material issue, dispatch, transfer in or out, adjustment up or down, scrap, QC hold, QC release, customer return, and the rest.
Set the From and To dates. The screen opens on the last thirty days.
keyActions.note: A ledger with no date limit means reading the whole history, which only gets slower as the company trades. Widen it deliberately when you need to.

keyActions.how: Click "Load more" at the foot. Each click adds the next slice; the running count of what is loaded is shown beside it.
keyActions.note: There are no page numbers here. The ledger only ever grows, and reading it forward in slices stays fast whatever its size.

keyActions.action: Open the document behind a movement
keyActions.how: Click the reference code in the Reference column.
keyActions.note: Where the system can point at the exact document it does. Where it cannot, the link goes to the audit trail searched on that document number — a slower route to the same story, never a dead end.

keyActions.action: Read the pool a movement landed in
keyActions.how: The Stock state column on the right — Available, QC hold, Damaged, In transit, Job work, Scrap, Return.
keyActions.note: A QC hold and a goods issue both reduce what can be promised, but only one of them has left the building. This column is what tells them apart.

flow: Open Stock ledger.
Choose the item, and the warehouse if you know it.
Widen the date range back to when the stock was last known to be right.
Read down the Quantity column: green with a plus is stock coming in, red is stock going out.
Check Balance after against what you expected at each step — the line where they part company is the movement to investigate.
Click that line's reference to open the document that caused it, and read the Reason recorded against it.
rules: A ledger line is never changed and never removed. A mistake is corrected by posting another movement, so both the error and the correction stay on the record with their reasons and their dates.
Every movement carries a reason, and the reason is kept forever. Six months later it is the only answer to why the stock changed.
The direction is fixed by the type of movement, not by whoever keys it. A receipt adds and an issue removes; a receipt keyed as a negative number is treated as a mis-keyed document and refused.
Balance after is the position's balance immediately after that movement posted, recorded at the time. It is not recalculated later.
Entries are ordered by when the movement happened, with the newest first, and cannot be re-sorted. The order of events is the point of the record.
screens.permission: Reading the ledger is a separate right from seeing stock balances, and someone can be given one without the other. It is normally given alongside stock view — the standard Store Keeper, Plant Manager and Accountant roles all carry it.
screens.notes: Straightforward, dense screen. There is no export or download button on it; stock reporting lives on the Reports screen. The screen offers filters by item, warehouse, movement type and date only — the server can also filter by batch, by serial number and by source document, and those are not exposed here. For a screenshot, filter to one busy item so the trail reads as a story rather than a wall.

screens.title: Reservations
screens.purpose: A reservation is a promise made against stock that is standing on your shelf. It does not move anything — the units stay exactly where they are and stay in On hand — it simply stops that quantity being available to anybody else. This screen lists every live promise: how much, of what, at which warehouse, for which order, how firm the promise is, and how much of it has already been used up. It is the screen to open when a planner asks why an item shows plenty on hand but nothing free to sell.
screens.whoUses: The planner and the sales or production person who has to decide whose order gets the stock when there is not enough for everyone.

keyActions.how: Read the grid: Item, Warehouse, Demand (the order the stock is held for), Type, Priority, Reserved, Consumed, Released, Remaining, Required date, Status.
Boxes above the grid for warehouse, kind of demand (sales order, production order, assembly order, job work order, spare, transfer), firmness (hard or soft) and status.
keyActions.note: There is no free-text search on this screen. Narrow with the filters instead.

keyActions.action: Open the order behind a promise
keyActions.how: Click the document number in the Demand column, where the system can point at that document's screen.

"Reserve stock" button above the grid, then fill the form: item, warehouse, quantity, firmness, what it is held for, the document's id, priority, an optional required date, and a reason of at least ten characters.
keyActions.note: Most reservations are not made here — confirming a sales order or releasing a production order creates them automatically. This form is the manual route.

keyActions.how: The actions menu at the end of a row, then Release. A reason is required.
keyActions.note: Releasing hands the whole remaining quantity back to free stock. That order loses its claim and may not get it back if somebody else takes the stock first.

keyActions.action: Ask for stock somebody else is holding
keyActions.how: The actions menu, then "Suggest reallocation". Say how much more this demand needs and why.
keyActions.note: You do not choose the donor. The system ranks every reservation that could give stock up and raises the request against the best one, then shows you what it chose, why, and what else it considered.

flow: A customer needs stock the balances screen says is not free.
Open Reservations and filter to that item's warehouse.
Read who is holding it, how urgent each holder is (lower priority number is more urgent) and when each needs it.
If a holder no longer needs it — the order was cancelled — use Release, and record why.
If it is a genuine contest, use Suggest reallocation on the row of the demand that needs helping, state the shortfall and the reason.
Read what the system decided: which reservation it proposes to take from, whether that donor's promise was firm, and whether the request now needs an approver.
rules: Reserving does not move stock. The quantity stays on hand and stays where it is; only the free figure falls. This is why a reservation writes nothing to the stock ledger — nothing moved.

You cannot reserve more than is free. The system locks the position, re-reads it and refuses if the claim is bigger than what is available. The availability figure shown in the form while you type is a courtesy; the check at the moment of saving is what counts.

A hard reservation is a real commitment and cannot be taken away by a reallocation without somebody approving the loss. A soft reservation is a plan, and gives way more easily. A reservation created without saying which is treated as hard — the conservative reading.
Priority is a whole number where lower means more urgent, and 100 is the default. It is what the system ranks donors against.

A reservation needed within three days is protected and will never be suggested as a donor. Material for a job starting this week has usually already been kitted, and taking it back causes a second problem rather than solving the first.
Releasing needs a written reason, because it takes stock away from an order that was promised it.
A required date that has passed while the promise is still live is shown in red.
screens.permission: Seeing the list needs the right to view reservations. Making one needs the right to create reservations, releasing one needs the right to release them, and asking for a reallocation needs the right to reallocate — three separate rights, deliberately. The live availability figure inside the Reserve form needs the allocation view right; without it the form still works and simply says that availability will be checked when the reservation is saved.
screens.notes: Three things the deck should be honest about. (1) The Reserve stock form asks for the **demand id to be pasted by hand** — there is no picker for it, because the six kinds of demand live in six other parts of the system. Reservations raised from a sales or production order carry it automatically; this form is genuinely the manual fallback and is fiddly. (2) **There is no screen anywhere in the application that lists or approves reallocation requests.** A request raised against a soft donor goes through; one raised against a hard donor is created and waits for an approver, and nothing in the interface can sign it. Worth flagging to the client as a gap rather than showing a flow that dead-ends. (3) Release here is all-or-nothing, although the system underneath can take back part of a reservation and leave the rest standing.

screens.title: Transfers, adjustments, counts, putaway, scrap and internal issues
screens.purpose: Record why stock moved. Transfers move it between warehouses; bin moves put it away within one warehouse. Adjustments correct the book quantity and stock counts reconcile the shelves. Scrap disposals clear stock already set aside as scrap. Internal issues record what a department or cost centre consumes.
screens.whoUses: Storekeepers record and move stock. Separate approvers review larger adjustments and internal issues. The person who accepts a physical count needs the separate reconciliation right.

keyActions.how: Use Transfers, Adjustments, Physical counts, Bin moves, Scrap disposals or Internal issues.
keyActions.note: Each tab has its own searchable, paginated register.

keyActions.how: New transfer: choose source and destination warehouses, a reason and item quantities. Batch-tracked items require a batch. Choose source and destination bins when the stock occupies them.
keyActions.note: Nothing moves on creation. The transfer is a draft waiting for approval.

keyActions.action: Approve, dispatch and receive a transfer
keyActions.how: The button at the end of the row changes with the document's stage: Approve on a draft, Dispatch once approved, Receive once it is in transit.
keyActions.note: Dispatch is the moment the stock actually leaves the source warehouse. Between dispatch and receipt it shows as In transit at the destination.

keyActions.how: New adjustment: choose the warehouse, reason code and explanation, then enter signed quantities. Choose the batch and bin for each position. A positive quantity adds stock; a negative quantity removes it. With cost-view rights you can enter the write-up unit cost; otherwise the server uses its fallback cost.
keyActions.note: The reason code says what kind of loss it was; the description says what happened. Both are kept on the ledger forever. Someone who may see cost centres can also name the cost centre that bears the write-off; for anyone else the adjustment is raised unallocated.

keyActions.how: Edit a draft, submit a larger adjustment, approve or reject it with a reason, then post it. Cancel a draft or other cancellable document with a reason. The cost centre is shown in the register and approval dialog when you may view it.
keyActions.note: Posting is what changes stock. Everything before it is paperwork.

keyActions.how: Physical counts tab, "New count": choose the warehouse and date, say why the count is being run, and optionally note the scope ("Aisles A to C only, night shift").
keyActions.note: Opening the sheet takes a snapshot of what the system believes about every position in the warehouse that holds stock. That snapshot is what the counter compares against.

keyActions.how: Start on the draft sheet, then "Key counts": type what was found on the shelf against each line. The book figure is shown beside it. Save as often as you like.
keyActions.note: A line left blank stays uncounted — it is never treated as zero. The sheet only becomes ready to confirm once every line has a figure. Save at most 500 lines at a time; the screen tells you if you have keyed more.

keyActions.action: Confirm a count and post the difference
keyActions.how: Confirm on a counted sheet. The dialog shows how many lines differ, the net value, what is written off against what is written on, and a line-by-line list — before you agree.
keyActions.note: This is the end of the road. It writes to the ledger, and a ledger line cannot be deleted. A mistake afterwards is corrected by a further adjustment.

keyActions.how: Recount on a counted sheet, with a reason. Figures already keyed stay in place to be corrected and the snapshot is not retaken.
Cancel on a sheet that has not been confirmed, with a reason. Nothing is posted; the figures stay on record and never reach the ledger, and the warehouse is free to open a new count.
Bin moves: choose one warehouse, the item, batch, source bin and destination bin, quantity and reason. Leave a bin empty for the unbinned position.
keyActions.note: Saving posts both sides immediately. Quantity and original stock cost move together.

keyActions.how: Scrap disposals: choose the warehouse and scrap position, quantity, Sale, Write off or Recycle, and the reason. Add the buyer or reference and any realised amount.
keyActions.note: Saving permanently removes that quantity from scrap. A write-off realises zero. It cannot remove usable stock.

keyActions.action: Issue to a department or cost centre
keyActions.how: Internal issues: name the receiving department and/or cost centre and enter the materials, positions, quantities and reason. Save the draft, then Post a smaller issue or Submit one requiring approval.
keyActions.note: Above 25,000 in company currency, another approver reviews and approves the issue. Approval posts the stock. A pending issue can be rejected with a reason; a draft or pending issue can be cancelled.

flow: Moving stock between warehouses: open the Transfers tab, click New transfer, name the two warehouses and the lines, save.
A colleague clicks Approve. Nothing has moved yet, and the transfer can still be abandoned at this point.
The storekeeper clicks Dispatch when the stock physically leaves. It comes off the source warehouse and shows as In transit at the destination.
The receiving storekeeper clicks Receive when it arrives. The stock lands on hand at the destination and becomes available to promise.
Counting a warehouse: Physical counts tab, New count, then Start, then Key counts as each aisle is walked, saving as you go.
When every line has a figure the sheet turns to Counted. Somebody with the right to accept a count clicks Confirm, reads the variance, and posts it.
rules: An adjustment worth more than ₹25,000 cannot be posted by the person who raised it. It must be submitted, approved by somebody else, and only then posted. Below that figure a draft posts straight away. The limit is one setting and can be changed deliberately.
An adjustment may not be approved by the person who raised it. That is the whole point of the approval.

The value the approval is measured against is the real cost of the stock being written off — the oldest stock at what it actually cost, not a blended average. If a document is posted and turns out to cost more than the limit after all, the posting is refused and nothing reaches the ledger. The gate and the write-off are measured with the same ruler.
A posted adjustment cannot be un-posted. Correct it with a further adjustment.

Only a draft transfer can be edited, and a transfer can only be abandoned before it is dispatched. Once the stock is on a vehicle there is no way back except receiving it — cancelling would leave the goods owned by nobody.

A transfer cannot carry a serial-tracked item at all. A transfer line has nowhere to record which individual units were shipped, so the system refuses it when the line is keyed rather than failing later. Move serialised stock with an issue and a receipt instead.
Only one stock count can be open per warehouse at a time. Finish or cancel the current one first, otherwise two sheets each snapshot the other's corrections.
A count sheet covering more than 5,000 positions is refused. Count a narrower scope — which is what cycle counting means.

Confirming a count posts the difference between what was counted and what the system says at that moment, not the difference from the snapshot taken when the sheet was opened. Otherwise every receipt and issue made while the count was running would be silently reversed and booked as shrinkage.
A line nobody counted is left alone. It is not written down to zero.
A transfer, adjustment or count involving a warehouse you are not assigned to is refused, whatever rights you hold. Rights say whether you may adjust stock; your warehouse assignment says where.
New scrap is refused for an item whose Can scrap capability is off. Record unusable inspected stock as damaged instead. Existing scrap can still be disposed of after the capability is disabled.
Scrap disposal uses what that scrap originally cost. A later, more expensive receipt does not reprice it. FIFO cost columns are visible only with cost-view rights.
Bin moves and scrap disposals post when saved. Review the positions and quantities before saving; a posted document is corrected with a further stock document.
Internal issue approval is measured against the actual oldest stock consumed. If its value rises beyond the limit at posting, nothing moves until it has approval.
The consumables warehouse is a classification. Internal issues may consume permitted stock from any warehouse you are allowed to operate.
screens.permission: Seeing all three lists needs only the right to view stock. Raising, approving, dispatching and receiving transfers all need the right to transfer stock. Raising, submitting and posting an adjustment need the right to adjust stock; approving or rejecting one needs the separate right to approve adjustments. Opening, starting, keying and cancelling a count need the right to run a stock count; confirming it and posting the variance needs the different right to reconcile stock — whoever walks the aisles is not automatically the person who accepts what they wrote down. Bin moves use the transfer right. Scrap disposal has its own disposal right. Internal issue creation and approval have separate rights. Existing customised roles may need the administrator to grant the new rights.
screens.notes: The six tabs share the stock register. Batch and bin are part of the stock position: selecting the wrong position is not corrected by having enough total stock in the warehouse. Serial-tracked transfers and these new operation documents remain unavailable until the serial identity workflow can record the units.

screens.title: Warehouses
screens.purpose: The register of every place the company holds stock: the raw-material store, the component store, work in progress, assembly, finished goods, packing, scrap, returns, the QC hold area, the job-work store and goods in transit. Every stock figure in the system hangs off one of these, so this screen is where a new store is set up, an old one is switched off, and the racks and bins inside each one are added. Expanding a row shows that warehouse's storage locations underneath the table.
screens.whoUses: The owner or whoever administers the masters. Storekeepers read it; they rarely change it.

keyActions.action: See the bins inside a warehouse
keyActions.how: Click the arrow at the start of the row, or the row itself. The storage locations appear in a panel under the table, with their code, name, type, capacity, barcode and status.
keyActions.note: The Locations column on each row shows how many live locations that warehouse has.

keyActions.how: "New warehouse" at the top right. Code, name and type are required; branch, parent warehouse, address, GST state code, phone, email and notes are optional.
keyActions.note: The code must start with a letter or a digit and may use letters, digits, dot, dash, slash, underscore and space, up to 32 characters. It must be unique within the company.

keyActions.how: The actions menu at the end of the row, then Edit.
keyActions.note: The code cannot be changed once the warehouse exists — it is printed on bin labels and quoted on documents already issued. The field is greyed out.

keyActions.how: Actions menu, "Set as default". Offered only on an active warehouse that is not already the default.
keyActions.note: Receipts and issues propose the default warehouse when a document does not name one. There is exactly one, and nominating a new one demotes the old one in the same step.

keyActions.action: Switch a warehouse off or back on
keyActions.how: Actions menu, Deactivate or Activate. A reason is required and is kept in the audit trail.
keyActions.note: Deactivating stops documents proposing the warehouse. Stock already in it is untouched and still shows in reports.

keyActions.action: Allow issues before receipts, for one warehouse
keyActions.how: The "Allow issues before receipts" tick box on the warehouse form.
keyActions.note: Relaxes the availability check for that warehouse only — intended for line-side work in progress where material is consumed before the paperwork catches up. Stock still cannot go below zero; the database refuses that everywhere. It is not a way round a shortage.

keyActions.action: Add a rack, bin, shelf, floor space or staging area
keyActions.how: Expand the warehouse, then "Add location" in the panel. Code, name and type are required; barcode, capacity, capacity unit and notes are optional.
keyActions.note: Location codes are unique within their warehouse, not across the company — A-01 can legitimately exist in four warehouses.

keyActions.how: Type and status boxes above the table, plus search on code, name or city. Clear resets them.

flow: Setting up a new store: click New warehouse.
Give it a code and a name, and choose the type that describes what it holds.
Fill in the address and GST state code if invoices or e-way bills will reference it.
Leave "Allow issues before receipts" unticked unless it is a line-side work-in-progress store.
Save, then expand the new row and add its racks and bins with Add location.
If it is to be the site everything defaults to, use Set as default from its actions menu.
rules: A warehouse code is unique within the company and cannot be changed afterwards, because it is printed on labels and quoted on documents already issued.
The default warehouse cannot be deactivated. Nominate another default first — otherwise documents that do not name a warehouse have nowhere to propose.
An inactive warehouse cannot be made the company default, and cannot take new storage locations.
A deactivated warehouse may still give its stock up but may not take any in. Refusing outbound movements too would strand whatever is still on its shelves behind the flag.
Warehouses can be nested — plant, store, sub-store — up to five levels. Deeper than that is treated as a data-entry mistake.
Switching a warehouse on or off needs a written reason. Six months from now that reason is the only answer to why it was switched off.
screens.permission: The right to view warehouses opens the screen. Creating, editing, setting the default and changing the status all need the right to manage warehouses. Adding a storage location in the panel needs the separate right to manage locations — a storekeeper typically has that one and not the other.
screens.notes: There is **no way to retire or delete a warehouse from this screen** — only deactivate. The system does support retiring one, but it refuses while the warehouse still holds any stock or still has sub-stores, and no button offers it. Likewise the locations panel is **add-only**: a bin can be created there but not edited, deactivated or retired anywhere in the interface. There is also no warehouse detail page — expanding the row is the whole of it — so the screenshot should show one row expanded with its bins visible.

screens.title: Storage locations
screens.purpose: Every rack, bin, shelf, floor space and staging area in the company, across all warehouses, in one list. The warehouses screen answers "what is inside this warehouse"; this screen answers the question that one cannot — find bin A-14 wherever it lives, or put the racking of six plants side by side and see whether they are labelled to the same standard. It is the same information as the panel on the warehouses screen, seen the other way round, and it is read-only: bins are created inside the warehouse they belong to, which is where the warehouses screen puts them.
screens.whoUses: Whoever maintains the racking standard, and anyone chasing a bin code or a barcode they have scanned and cannot place.

keyActions.how: The search box matches the location code, the name and the barcode. When a match came from the barcode, the barcode is shown under the code so you can see why.
Boxes for warehouse, type (rack, bin, shelf, floor, staging) and status, plus a "Include retired" tick box. The Clear button says how many filters are applied and removes them all at once.
Click its code. A panel shows the warehouse, type, what it sits inside, barcode, capacity, maximum weight and volume, status, when it was created and when it last changed, and any notes.

keyActions.action: See what is nested inside a location
keyActions.how: "Show sub-locations" in that panel, or click the parent's name in it. The list narrows to what sits inside; a button in the toolbar says which location you are inside and clears it.
Click the warehouse in the row or in the detail panel — it opens the warehouses screen narrowed to that code.
Tick "Include retired". Retired rows are badged as such, with the date they were withdrawn.
keyActions.note: Retiring also deactivates, so asking for retired rows automatically drops an "Active only" filter, which could otherwise only ever return nothing.

flow: Somebody scans a barcode on a shelf and cannot place it.
Open Storage locations and paste the barcode into the search box.
Click the code that comes back to see which warehouse it is in and what it sits inside.
Use "Show sub-locations" to see everything nested under it.
To change or add anything, follow the warehouse link and work in that warehouse's panel.
rules: Location codes are unique within a warehouse, not across the company. Seeing A-01 four times in this list is correct — and it is exactly how an inconsistent labelling standard becomes visible.
A location's parent must be in the same warehouse. A bin nested under a bin in another building is a data-entry accident, not a hierarchy. Nesting is limited to five levels.
Capacity, maximum weight and maximum volume are recorded for planning only. No stock movement is refused for exceeding one, and the screen says so rather than implying a control that does not exist.
A capacity that has not been recorded is shown as "Not set", never as zero. "Nobody has measured this bin" and "this bin takes nothing" are different claims.
A retired bin may still give its stock up but may not take any in — the same rule an inactive warehouse follows, so that whatever is still in it can be moved out.
A location cannot be retired while it still holds stock or still has live sub-locations. Move the balance out, or retire the sub-locations, first.
screens.permission: The right to view locations opens the screen. The warehouse column, the warehouse filter and every link out of it need the right to view warehouses as well — without that right the column is left out entirely rather than filled with unusable references. Nothing on this screen changes anything, so no management right is needed to read it.
screens.notes: This is deliberately a read-only screen and there is **nothing to click that creates or changes a location** — it offers a link to the warehouses screen instead. If the deck already has a warehouses screenshot showing an expanded locations panel, say plainly that this is the same information organised by bin rather than by building, and use the screenshot to show the cross-warehouse search or the retired-locations view, which the panel cannot do. The warehouse list it draws names from covers active warehouses only, so a bin left behind in a deactivated warehouse shows a "Not an active warehouse" badge — which in an audit is itself the finding.

chapters.groupIntro: This part of the system is where money, evidence and control live. Finance is where you see what you owe your suppliers and what your customers owe you, where supplier bills are checked line by line against the order and the goods actually received before anyone approves them for payment, where payments and receipts are recorded and posted, and where the stock on hand is valued and the month's GST position is read. Reports answer the questions the owner asks on a Monday morning — what is late, what is not moving, which vendor is letting you down. The audit trail is the memory of the business: every change, who made it, when, and what the value was before and after, in a record that nobody can edit or delete. Documents holds the drawings, certificates and generated files; Users and roles decides who may do any of it. Together these screens are what make the ERP defensible in front of a customer, a supplier, an auditor or a tax officer — the rest of the system produces the work, and this part produces the proof.

screens.title: Finance — Ledgers and Outstanding
screens.purpose: This is the finance overview: what is owed, how old it is, what the stock is worth, and where GST stands for the month. It gathers five separate questions into one screen with five tabs, so a controller can move from "who has not paid us" to "what do we owe" to "what is the closing stock worth" without leaving the page. Nothing here is edited — every tab is a reading of figures the system has already posted. The tab you are on is carried in the address, so you can send a colleague a link that opens on the ageing of payables rather than telling them which tab to click.
screens.whoUses: The accountant and the owner. The Ledger, Inventory valuation and GST tabs each need their own right, so a junior clerk may see only Outstanding and Ageing.

keyActions.action: See every supplier bill that still owes money, oldest due first
keyActions.how: Finance → Outstanding tab
keyActions.note: This tab is payables only. There is no customer invoice document in this system, so what customers owe is read on the Ageing tab instead.

keyActions.action: Narrow the open bills to one supplier
keyActions.how: Finance → Outstanding → Vendor picker

keyActions.action: Restate the open bills as at a chosen date
keyActions.how: Finance → Outstanding → "As on" date box
keyActions.note: The days-late figure and the age bucket are worked out by the system against that date, never by your computer's clock.

keyActions.action: Show only bills that are past their due date
keyActions.how: Finance → Outstanding → tick "Overdue only"
Finance → Ageing tab → Receivables
Finance → Ageing tab → Payables

keyActions.action: See one customer's or supplier's ageing on its own
keyActions.how: Finance → Ageing → choose the party in the picker

keyActions.action: Read a full account statement for one customer or supplier
keyActions.how: Finance → Ledger tab → choose Customer or Vendor, pick the party, set a date range
keyActions.note: Shows the opening balance, every posting with its debit or credit, and the running balance after each one.

keyActions.how: Finance → Inventory valuation tab
keyActions.note: Valued at what the open cost layers actually cost, first-in-first-out, as things stand now. There is no "as on" date.

keyActions.action: Narrow the valuation to one warehouse
keyActions.how: Finance → Inventory valuation → Warehouse box

keyActions.action: Get the whole valuation as a spreadsheet
keyActions.how: Finance → Inventory valuation → "Export full valuation"
keyActions.note: Only for someone with the right to export reports. It is prepared in the background and a download appears on the screen when it is ready — you can carry on working.

keyActions.action: Read the GST position for a month
keyActions.how: Finance → GST summary tab → Return period box
keyActions.note: Output tax, input credit, the net figure, and a table for each side broken down by HSN code and rate.

keyActions.action: Go to the supplier bill register
keyActions.how: Finance → "Vendor invoices" button, top right

flow: Open Finance from the left menu.
Start on Outstanding to see the supplier bills still owing money, oldest due first.
Set "As on" to the date you are reporting for, or leave it for today.
Tick "Overdue only" to reduce the list to what is actually late.
Move to Ageing and choose Receivables or Payables.
Read the tiles across the top — not due, 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days — and the chart of the ten worst parties.
Move to Ledger and pick a party to see the postings behind their balance.
Move to Inventory valuation for the closing stock value, and to GST summary for the month's return figures.
screens.notes: Deliberately read-only: nothing on this screen creates or changes a document. Screenshot advice — take the Outstanding tab and the Ageing tab separately, since the Ageing tab is the only one with a chart. Three tabs (Ledger, Inventory valuation, GST summary) are hidden from an account that lacks their right, so a screenshot taken as a limited user will show only two tabs. Thin spots worth knowing: the Outstanding tab has no sort or search box, because the system always returns those bills oldest-due-first and offers no other order; and it has no currency selector even though rows carry their own currency.
