The Ageing report returns party-by-party detail for at most five currencies at a time and up to 200 parties in each, though the totals for every currency are always shown. Receivable ageing uses sales-invoice due dates and legacy posting dates, FIFO within each customer/currency. GST output uses issued invoice HSN snapshots by invoice date; uninvoiced dispatch GST is shown separately.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to view finance can open the page and use Outstanding and Ageing. The Ledger tab needs the right to view the general ledger; Inventory valuation needs the right to view stock valuation; GST summary needs the right to view GST reports. Exporting the full valuation additionally needs the right to export reports.
rules: Amounts in two different currencies are never added together, and no total spans them. There is no exchange-rate table in this system, so a combined figure would be a number with no meaning. Each currency is reported in its own block, and the screen tells you plainly when money is outstanding in a currency other than the one you are looking at.

Ageing buckets are 0-30, 31-60, 61-90 and 90+ days, with anything still inside its terms shown as "not due". The same boundaries are used everywhere in the system, so the Outstanding list and the Ageing report can never disagree.
Payables are aged from the invoice due date. Receivables are aged from the date the entry was posted, because there is no customer invoice document in this system to carry a due date.

The inventory valuation shows two value columns — the value written on each stock position, and the same total recomputed from the underlying cost layers. They are an independent check on each other. A few paise of difference is ordinary rounding; a material difference means that position needs reconciling.
Cost per unit in the valuation is shown to six decimal places, not two, because a washer that genuinely costs four-tenths of a paisa each would otherwise appear to cost nothing.

The GST figures come from what actually happened, not from what was ordered: output tax is taken from consignments dispatched in the period, and input credit from purchase invoices approved in the period. Document counts in the HSN tables are per rate slab and are never added up, because one invoice spanning two rates is counted under both.

screens.title: Sales invoices
screens.purpose: The issued GST invoice register, its fixed seller/buyer and line snapshots, receipt allocations, due dates and permanent PDFs.
screens.whoUses: Accounts and sales staff who hold sales_invoice.view.

keyActions.how: Search by number/customer or filter status, customer, date range and overdue only.
Open an invoice row to read its lines, tax totals and allocated receipts. Generate PDF queues a job; Download opens its permanent document.
An unpaid ISSUED invoice with no credits or allocations offers Cancel invoice for twenty-four hours. Enter the reason; the journal and fulfilment counters reverse together.

flow: Open Sales invoices under Finance.
Filter and open an issued invoice.
Review tax and receipts, then download its PDF.
rules: Issue starts from a priced SALES dispatch in READY_FOR_DISPATCH or later. Preview allocates no number; Confirm and issue allocates an SI number and posts receivables.
Due date follows customer credit days. A live invoice prevents the dispatch from being cancelled or amended.
Paid invoices and invoices outside the cancellation window need a credit note.
screens.permission: View: sales_invoice.view. Issue: sales_invoice.create. Cancel: sales_invoice.cancel. Receipt allocation: payment.record. Report polling and document download retain their existing read rights.
screens.notes: Totals round to the nearest rupee HALF_UP. Flat discounts across partial consignments reconcile on the final invoice. Issued invoice PDFs never expire.

screens.title: Vendor Invoices
screens.purpose: This is the payables desk: every bill a supplier has sent you, recorded here and then checked against two other documents before anyone agrees to pay it. The check is the three-way match — what you ordered, what you actually accepted at the gate, and what the vendor has billed — and it is the single most valuable thing on this screen, because a quiet price increase or a bill for material that never arrived is how money leaves a manufacturer by mistake. The list is a queue you work down; opening a row shows the match line by line and is where the bill is approved. Bills for job work done on your own material carry their own type: they are matched against the job-work order's rate and the receipt lines instead of against a purchase order, and they are raised from the job-work screen rather than here.
screens.whoUses: The accounts clerk who keys the bills, and the accounts manager or owner who approves them. These are deliberately two different people.

keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → "Record invoice" button, top right
keyActions.note: Needs the right to record vendor invoices. A bill can be recorded with or without a purchase order, but only one linked to an order and a goods receipt can be matched cleanly.

keyActions.action: Copy the lines from the purchase order or goods receipt instead of retyping them
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → Record invoice → name the goods receipt or purchase order → "Copy lines"
keyActions.note: From a goods receipt the quantity copied is what was accepted at the gate; from an order alone it is what was ordered. The unit price copied is the agreed price after discount, which is exactly what the match compares against.

keyActions.action: Charge a bill, or one of its lines, to a cost centre
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → Record invoice (or Amend) → the Cost centre box under the bill's details, and the cost centre box on any line that belongs somewhere else
keyActions.note: Shown only to someone who may see cost centres. A line left on "As the invoice" follows the bill's cost centre, decided when the bill is approved; approval then posts the purchase cost to the ledger split by cost centre, which is what the Cost centre statement reads. A bill whose cost centre was switched off after it was keyed is refused at approval until it is changed.

keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click the row → "Submit"
keyActions.note: The three-way match is run again on the way in. A note may be added but is not required.

keyActions.action: Amend a bill nobody has approved
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click the row → "Amend"

keyActions.action: Delete a draft keyed in error
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click the row → "Delete", giving a reason
keyActions.note: Only a draft. The row goes for good and the reason is kept in the audit trail.

keyActions.action: Read the three-way match line by line
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click any row
keyActions.note: Shows, per line: the order price against the invoice price, the accepted quantity against the invoiced quantity, and the money difference each produces.

keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click the row → "Approve"
keyActions.note: Needs the right to approve vendor invoices. Approving posts the purchase, the input tax and the amount owed to the supplier into the ledger.

keyActions.action: Approve a bill that failed the match, on your own authority
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → click the row → type a reason in the box → "Approve"
keyActions.note: The reason is stored on the invoice and written to the audit trail, and the bill is thereafter marked "approved over a variance" rather than "matched".

keyActions.action: Find the bills that failed the match
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → "Match result" filter → Variance

keyActions.action: Find bills still unpaid, or past their due date
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → tick "Unpaid only" or "Overdue only"

keyActions.action: Show only purchase bills or only job-work bills
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → "Invoice type" filter → Purchase or Job work
keyActions.note: Job-work bills are matched against the job-work order's rate and the receipt lines. The match dialog shows the agreed rate where it shows the order price on a purchase bill, and the good output where it shows the accepted quantity.

keyActions.action: Search by the supplier's own invoice number
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → search box

keyActions.action: Open the purchase order behind a bill
keyActions.how: Vendor invoices → "Purchase order" link in the Order / receipt column

flow: Open Vendor invoices from the left menu.
Press "Record invoice" and choose the supplier.
Name the goods receipt if there is one — the purchase order is filled in with it.
Press "Copy lines" to bring in the lines from that receipt, then correct anything the paper bill says differently.
Enter the supplier's own invoice number, the invoice date and the due date, and save.
Press "Submit" to send it for approval. The match runs.
The approver opens the bill from the queue and reads the match panel: green if it agrees, red with a list of reasons if it does not.
If it agrees, press "Approve". If it does not, either send the discrepancy back to the vendor, or type a reason and approve over the variance.
screens.notes: One screen doing two jobs: the list is the queue, the dialog behind a row is both the bill's detail view and the approval desk. A screenshot of the dialog on a bill that failed the match is far more useful to the reader than one that matched cleanly. Two things exist in the system but have no button on this screen: marking a bill as disputed, and cancelling a bill that has already been approved. A dispute reason is displayed if one was recorded, but there is no control here to raise or resolve one, and no control to cancel an approved bill. If the client needs those, they are a small addition rather than new machinery. Also note the list cannot show a supplier's name against each row — only the bill number and the ERP document number — so use the vendor filter when you want one supplier's bills.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to view vendor invoices can open the list and read the match. Recording, amending, submitting and deleting a draft all need the right to record vendor invoices. Approving — and approving over a variance — needs the separate right to approve vendor invoices. That separation is the point: whoever keys a bill must not be the person who clears it for payment.
rules: A bill outside tolerance cannot be approved without a written reason, because the whole purpose of the match is to stop an overbilling passing unnoticed. Supplying that reason is the exercise of the approver's authority, and it is stored against the invoice and in the audit trail with their name on it.
The price tolerance is two per cent against the ordered price. Anything further out is reported as a finding on that line.
The quantity tolerance is zero — the invoiced quantity must equal what was accepted at the gate. A supplier billing for more than was taken in is never a rounding matter.

A line billed against no purchase order line is a finding, and a bill with no purchase order at all is reported as unmatched. Freight, packing and handling a vendor adds after the fact are exactly what this check exists to surface; approving them is a deliberate act, not a default.
A line with nothing received against it yet is a finding, because there is nothing to prove the goods arrived.

The match is re-run at the moment of approval, never taken from what was stored earlier. The order or the receipt may have moved since the bill was submitted, and approving against a stale verdict would defeat the check.
Only a bill awaiting approval can be approved. Approving one twice is refused outright, because it would post the amount owed to the supplier a second time.
Only a draft can be deleted, and it is deleted outright. A draft never reached the ledger, so there is nothing to correct with an offsetting entry; anything past draft leaves a trail instead.

Cancelling a bill that reached the ledger reverses the journals it posted - the bill and, on a job-work bill, the excess-loss recovery posted beside it - and rolls the job-work billing back, in the same step. Cancelling before approval moves nothing.
A job-work bill can never charge more than its receipt lines earned. Billing beyond the still-unbilled charges is refused outright, and no override reason can approve it.
Each bill is shown and totalled in its own currency. Two currencies are never added together.

screens.title: Payments and Receipts
screens.purpose: This is where money out to suppliers and money in from customers is recorded, approved and matched to the bills it settled. The system keeps two things carefully apart: the payment itself — a sum of money that left or entered the bank on a date — and the settlement, which decides which invoices that money paid. Recording a payment moves nothing; approving it posts the journal and moves the balance; deciding which bills it settled happens afterwards and can be corrected without ever changing the amount that left the bank.
screens.whoUses: The accounts clerk who records payments and matches them to bills, and the accounts manager or owner who approves the money going out.

keyActions.action: Record a payment to a supplier or a receipt from a customer
keyActions.how: Payments → "Record payment" button, top right
keyActions.note: It is created as a draft. Nothing has moved yet.

keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ menu on the row → "Amend draft"
keyActions.note: The party, the direction and the currency are fixed once the document exists and are shown as facts rather than editable boxes.

keyActions.action: Approve a payment and post it
keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ menu on the row → "Approve - post the money"
keyActions.note: Needs the right to approve payments. This is the moment the journal is written and, for a receipt, the customer's outstanding balance falls.

keyActions.action: Decide which bills a payment settled
keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ menu on the row → "Settle invoices"
keyActions.note: Needs only the right to record payments — matching is a clerk's job, not an approval.

keyActions.action: Release a settlement made in error
keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ → Settle invoices → remove the line → save
keyActions.note: What you see in the table is exactly what the payment will settle after saving. A line taken out of it is released.

keyActions.action: Cancel and reverse an approved payment
keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ menu on the row → "Cancel and reverse", giving a reason
keyActions.note: Needs the right to approve payments. The original journal stays and its mirror image is posted beside it.

keyActions.how: Payments → ⋯ menu on the row → "Delete draft", giving a reason

keyActions.action: Read one payment and everything it settled
keyActions.how: Payments → click the row

keyActions.action: Find approved payments not yet matched to bills
keyActions.how: Payments → tick "Not fully settled", and set Direction to "Payment - money out"

keyActions.action: Narrow to one supplier or customer
keyActions.how: Payments → Party side → then the vendor or customer picker

keyActions.action: Narrow by how the money moved
keyActions.how: Payments → Method filter — cash, bank transfer, cheque, UPI, card, or a book adjustment

flow: Open Payments from the left menu.
Press "Record payment".
Choose the direction — money out to a vendor, or money in from a customer.
Choose the party, the date, the amount and the method; add the cheque or transfer reference and the bank if the method has one.
Save. The document sits in draft.
The approver opens the row menu and presses "Approve - post the money". The journal is posted.
Back on the row menu, press "Settle invoices", tick the supplier's open bills the money paid, put an amount against each, and save.
screens.notes: Customer receipts settle issued or partially paid sales invoices of the same customer and currency. Receipt approval already posts the money and reduces outstanding; allocation identifies which invoices were paid. Cancelling a receipt releases its allocations and reverses the journal. Vendor payments retain their existing settlement rules. Manual non-GST customer adjustments remain API-only.
screens.permission: Anyone with the right to view payments can see the register and open a payment. Recording, amending, deleting a draft and settling against invoices need the right to record payments. Approving and cancelling need the separate right to approve payments — the same authority in both directions, because a cancellation reverses a posting.
rules: A payment goes to a vendor and a receipt comes from a customer. The opposite pairing describes a refund, which is a different document with different accounting, and it is refused.
A payment can only be amended or deleted while it is a draft. Once approved the money has moved, and the only way back is to cancel it, which posts the reversal rather than erasing the record.
Approving twice is refused. A double-clicked button or a retried request would otherwise credit the bank twice for money that moved once.

A payment cannot be cancelled while it still settles a bill. Un-settling the invoices is a deliberate act, not something a cancellation should do behind your back — so release the settlement first, then cancel.
A settlement can never change the amount that left the bank. It only decides which bills that money paid.
A payment may only settle bills that have been approved or are part-paid. A bill nobody has approved cannot be paid, and settling a disputed bill would quietly concede the dispute.
Deleting a draft and cancelling an approved payment both require a written reason, which is kept in the audit trail.

screens.title: Chart of Accounts
screens.purpose: The chart of accounts is the list of every ledger account the company posts to, and this screen explains what each one is. It is a reference: you come here to find out where something posts, to check whether an account is one the system uses automatically, and to drill from a control account down to the parties who make up its balance. It is read-only on purpose — opening, renaming and retiring an account is a settings job rather than a finance document, so those controls are not shown here at all.
screens.whoUses: The accountant, and the owner when they want to understand how a figure was arrived at.

keyActions.action: Find an account by code or name
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → search box

keyActions.action: Narrow to one class of account
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → Class filter — asset, liability, income, expense or equity

keyActions.action: Show retired accounts as well as active ones
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → Status filter
keyActions.note: The default shows active accounts only, because the chart is usually read to find where something posts.

keyActions.action: Separate the accounts the system posts to automatically from the ones staff created
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → the system / custom filter
Chart of accounts → click the row
keyActions.note: Shows its code, name, class, which side increases it, its parent, its status, when it was opened and last amended, and — where it applies — that it is a control account.

keyActions.action: See the accounts sitting beneath one account
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → click a row → "Accounts beneath this one"

keyActions.action: See who makes up the Accounts Receivable or Accounts Payable balance
keyActions.how: Chart of accounts → click the control account → "Open a customer ledger" or "Open a vendor ledger" → choose the party
keyActions.note: This is the same statement as the Ledger tab on the Finance screen, reached from the account rather than from a party picker.

flow: Open Chart of accounts from the left menu under Finance.
Search for the account, or filter by class.
Click the row to read what it is.
If it is Accounts Receivable or Accounts Payable, press "Open a customer ledger" or "Open a vendor ledger" and choose the party to see the postings behind the balance.
To walk the structure, press "Accounts beneath this one" to list the accounts filed under it.
screens.notes: This screen and the Ledger tab on the Finance screen show the same party statement; the only difference is how you get to it. Do not describe them twice in the deck — cross-reference instead. The chart is shown as a flat, paged list rather than an indented tree, and you drill down one level at a time. A row does not name its parent account; the parent is named in the detail dialog. The company starts with eight accounts the system needs by name: Accounts Receivable (1100), Bank (1200), Cash (1210), Input GST Credit (1300), Accounts Payable (2100), Output GST Payable (2200), Purchases and Services (5100) and Rounding Differences (5900). That list is worth putting in the deck as a small table. Sales Revenue is an additional system income account, preferred code 4500; an occupied preferred code advances to the first free number.
screens.permission: Needs the right to view the general ledger, which also covers the party statement reached from here. Opening the party picker additionally needs the right to view customers or vendors, so the drill-down button is only offered to someone who can use it. Creating, editing or retiring an account is a settings-management right and is not done from this screen.
rules: The accounts the system posts to automatically are found by an internal system code, not by their number or name. That means you can safely rename one to suit your accountant — but you cannot retire it, because the automatic postings would then have nowhere to go.

Which side increases an account is a property of its class, not a setting: assets and expenses grow on the debit side, liabilities, income and equity on the credit side. That is what decides whether a figure on a report reads as a plus or a minus.

A party's statement covers every account their postings touch, not only the receivable or payable control account you arrived from. So a party's totals will not necessarily tie back to the control account, and the screen says so.

The running balance on a statement is computed by the system across the whole period, not added up as you page through. A balance that were only correct on the first page would be worse than showing none.

screens.title: Reports
screens.purpose: This is the report room. Every report the system can produce is listed here as a card, split into those that cover a period — sales, dispatch, rejection, efficiency — and those that read the position as it stands right now, such as stock availability and dead stock. You pick a report, set its dates and filters, and press Run; a small result appears as a table on the screen, and a large one is prepared in the background as an Excel file you download when it is ready. Nothing is fetched until you ask for it, so opening the page never sets a heavy query running.
screens.whoUses: The owner, and any manager reviewing their area — the buyer, the production supervisor, the QC lead, the dispatch manager, the accountant.

keyActions.how: Reports

Reports → Sales order status

flow: Open Reports from the left menu.
Pick the report you want from the cards.
If it is marked "Needs dates", set From and To — the last thirty days is offered by default.
Add any of the six filters that apply.
Press "Run report".
Read the table, page through it, or use the search box to find a row.
If the result was too large to show, wait for the download strip and press Download to open the spreadsheet.
screens.notes: Twenty-four reports exist and every one of them is listed above — this list is worth its own page in the deck. Two things to be accurate about. First, the six filters are the same on every report, so the screen offers a Customer filter on a machine-utilisation report where it does nothing; that is a known simplification, not a fault. Second, the filter set has no category picker even though the system would accept one, and the Status filter expects the exact status word rather than offering a dropdown. The management dashboard tiles (open orders, stock value, QC pending and so on) are a separate screen, not part of this one. The packing list PDF is produced from the Packing screen, not from here.
screens.permission: Needs the right to view reports — that one right opens every report in the catalogue. Producing a large report as a downloadable file additionally needs the right to export reports; without it, a report that returns too many rows is refused with a message asking you to narrow the dates or filters instead.
rules: A report period may cover at most 366 days. An unbounded query over years of history is how a reporting screen takes the whole system down, so the limit is enforced rather than suggested.
A result of up to 5,000 rows is shown on screen. Anything larger is prepared in the background as an Excel file, because no screen and no waiting user should sit on a query of that size.

A generated file is reused for 24 hours for the same report and the same parameters. Five people opening the same link do not queue five identical exports — the later ones simply collect the file the first one produced.

Stock availability is never served from a stored copy, because an allocation decision made on a five-minute-old availability figure is an allocation of stock that may already be gone. The same applies to the tracking board and the valuation.
The list of reports is served by the system itself rather than being written into the screen, so a report added later appears here without anything else changing.
Scrap register shows scrap entering and leaving by source, at its recorded cost, over a chosen period.
Consumption by department groups only posted internal issues by department, cost centre and item over a chosen period.

screens.title: Audit Trail
screens.purpose: The audit trail is the memory of the business. Every create, every edit, every approval, rejection, cancellation and status change anywhere in the system writes an entry here saying who did it, what they did it to, when, from which address, and — for an edit — what the value was before and what it became. It is written in the same breath as the change itself, so a change that was made is a change that was recorded. Nobody can edit an entry and nobody can delete one, not a manager, not an administrator, not the person who made the change. That is what makes it worth something in a dispute with a supplier, an argument with a customer, or an audit.
screens.whoUses: The owner, an internal or external auditor, and whoever is investigating a discrepancy — a stock difference, a price nobody remembers agreeing, an order somebody says they never approved.

keyActions.action: See everything that happened in a period
keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity tab
keyActions.note: The last thirty days by default. Widen or narrow it with the date boxes.

keyActions.action: Narrow to one kind of record
keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity → "All record types" filter
keyActions.note: Purchase orders, goods receipts, inspections, payments, users, stock adjustments and so on.

keyActions.action: Narrow to one kind of action
keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity → "All actions" filter
keyActions.note: Created, updated, deleted, approved, rejected, cancelled, status changed, sign-in, password changed, stock movement, QC decision, and others.

keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity → "All users" filter
keyActions.note: Staff who have since left the company still appear, because their name still needs to sit against what they did.

keyActions.action: See exactly what changed on one entry
keyActions.how: Audit trail → click the row, or the arrow at its left
keyActions.note: Opens a panel with a Field / Before / After table, plus who, when, the address it came from, and a link to the record itself.

keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity → the history icon at the right of a row
keyActions.note: Switches to the Entity history tab already filled in for that record — every action ever taken against it, newest first.

keyActions.action: Look up a record's history directly
keyActions.how: Audit trail → Entity history tab → choose the record type, paste its id → "Show trail"

keyActions.action: Trace one request across several records
keyActions.how: Audit trail → Activity → search box → paste the request id
Audit trail → "Load more" at the foot of the table

flow: Open Audit trail from the left menu.
Set the date range around the period you are investigating.
Filter by record type, action or user to cut the noise.
Click a row to open the before-and-after panel.
If you need the full story of one document, press the history icon on the row and read the Entity history tab.
Press "Load more" to walk further back.
screens.notes: The most valuable point for the deck is the immutability, and it should be stated plainly and confidently: the database itself refuses any attempt to change or remove an audit row, and nothing anywhere in the system deletes them, so the trail is complete for the life of the system. Two limits are worth mentioning honestly: an audit query must have a date range and may span at most 366 days, and the Entity history tab currently asks for the record's internal id pasted in by hand — the practical way in is the history icon on an activity row, which fills both boxes for you. There is no export button on this screen. Note also that the approvals queue — requests waiting for someone's decision — lives on the dashboard rather than here.
screens.permission: Needs the right to view the audit log. Filtering by user additionally needs the right to view users. The Auditor role in the system is exactly this: read-only across everything, plus the audit trail. Nobody has a right to edit or delete an audit entry, because no such right exists.
rules: Audit entries are written once and never changed. The database refuses an update or a delete on this table outright, so the guarantee does not depend on anybody's good behaviour or on the application being correct.
The audit entry is written inside the same transaction as the change it records. Either both happen or neither does — a change can never be made without its record.
Only the fields that actually changed are stored, with their before and after values. Whole-record snapshots on every edit would make the trail enormous without making a single investigation easier.
Some entries are events rather than edits — an approval, a sign-in, a stock movement — and those record no before-and-after. The screen says so rather than showing an empty table.
A date range is required, and it may span at most 366 days. The audit log keeps every action ever taken, and an unbounded query would read years of history to answer a question about last week.
An audit entry survives the deletion of the thing it describes. Deleting a draft does not delete the record that it existed and was deleted, and by whom.

screens.title: Documents
screens.purpose: This is the company's filing cabinet: drawings, test certificates, supplier documents and photographs uploaded by hand, alongside the packing lists and report spreadsheets the system generates for you. A file can be filed against a record — a certificate against an inspection, a packing list against a packing order — so it can be found again from either end. Files are never reachable by a web address alone: every download is an authenticated request made by someone signed in to your company, which is what stops a link forwarded outside the business from working.
screens.whoUses: Anyone who needs the paperwork: the QC inspector attaching a certificate, the design engineer filing a drawing, the storekeeper looking one up, the accountant retrieving a generated report.

keyActions.how: Documents → "Upload a file" button, top right
keyActions.note: PDF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, CSV or Excel, up to 25 MB. Your administrator may allow fewer types.

keyActions.action: File the upload against a record
keyActions.how: Documents → Upload a file → fill in "Attach to record type" and "Record id"
keyActions.note: Optional, but both boxes or neither. A file filed against half a reference can never be found again.

keyActions.action: Set a file to be removed automatically
keyActions.how: Documents → Upload a file → "Delete automatically after"
keyActions.note: Up to a year ahead. Leave it empty to keep the file indefinitely.

keyActions.action: Mark a file as not confidential within the company
keyActions.how: Documents → Upload a file → tick the visibility box
keyActions.note: A classification for colleagues, not a relaxation — every download still requires a signed-in account in your company.

keyActions.how: Documents → search box

keyActions.action: Narrow by what kind of file it is
keyActions.how: Documents → "Any file type" filter

keyActions.action: Narrow by how the file is being kept
keyActions.how: Documents → "Any category" filter
keyActions.note: Uploaded documents and attachments are kept until deleted; generated exports and temporary files are given an expiry automatically.

keyActions.action: See everything filed against the same record
keyActions.how: Documents → click the "Attached to" reference on a row

keyActions.action: Show files past their retention date
keyActions.how: Documents → tick "Include expired"
Documents → the download icon on the row, or open the row and press Download
Documents → click the row
keyActions.note: Shows its type, size, what it is attached to, its visibility, its retention, when it was uploaded, and its checksum.

keyActions.how: Documents → the bin icon on the row → give a reason → confirm
keyActions.note: Needs the right to delete documents. It cannot be undone.

flow: Open Documents from the left menu.
To store something: press "Upload a file", choose it, pick a category, and — if it belongs to a record — fill in both the record type and its id.
Press Upload.
To find something: type part of the file name into the search box, or filter by category, file type or who uploaded it.
Click a row to read its details, or press the download icon to open the file.
To clear something out, press the bin icon, give a reason, and confirm.
screens.notes: The clean route to attaching a certificate is from the QC inspection screen, which uploads the file already filed against the inspection. Uploading from this screen and filing it against a record requires pasting the record's internal id by hand, which is realistic for an administrator and awkward for anyone else — worth stating in the deck rather than glossing over. The record types the system files documents under today are QC inspections, packing orders and generated reports; any other record type can be typed in and will be accepted. Files past their retention date are still listed if you tick "Include expired", but they can no longer be downloaded — only deleted, which is how you clear a lapsed export. The details dialog shows a checksum; that is the only thing that can prove a restored backup copy is the file that was originally uploaded, and it is worth a sentence.
screens.permission: Viewing the list, reading a file's details and downloading it all need the right to view documents. Uploading needs the right to upload documents. Deleting needs the separate right to delete documents.
rules: The system checks the actual content of an uploaded file against the type it claims to be, and refuses it if they disagree. An extension can be renamed; the file's own leading bytes cannot.
The stored location of a file is generated by the system and never derives from the name you gave it, so a mischievously named file cannot reach anywhere it should not.

Deleting a file removes both the record and the file itself, together, and requires a written reason. There is no undelete: a record whose file was gone would advertise a document that cannot be opened, which is worse than an honest absence. The audit trail is what remembers the deletion.
A file is filed against a record with both its type and its id, or with neither. Half a reference points at nothing any search can find.
A retention date must be in the future and at most a year ahead. Beyond that, keep the file indefinitely and delete it deliberately when it is no longer needed.
Files marked as not confidential are still only visible to people signed in to your company. Nothing here is ever public on the internet.

screens.title: Users and Roles
screens.purpose: This screen answers three questions that are really one question: who can sign in, what does each role allow, and which roles does each person hold. A role is a named bundle of permissions — Store Keeper, Purchase Manager, QC Inspector — and you give a person a role rather than ticking permissions for them one by one, so that a new storekeeper gets exactly the same access as the last one. The system ships with a set of ready-made roles; apart from two administrator roles, they are yours to edit, and you can create your own.
screens.whoUses: The owner or whoever administers the system. In practice one or two people.

keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users tab → "New user"
keyActions.note: Needs the right to create users.

keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu on the row → "Edit details"
Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu → "Assign roles" → tick the roles → give a reason
keyActions.note: Needs the right to assign permissions. The tick list replaces what they held; unticking a role removes it.

keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu → "Reset password" → give a reason
keyActions.note: Needs the right to reset passwords. You may set a password yourself, or let the system issue a temporary one, which is shown once and never again.

keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu → "Deactivate" → give a reason
keyActions.note: Every session that account currently holds is revoked immediately. Everything it created keeps its name.

keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu → "Activate" → give a reason
keyActions.note: The account can sign in again with its existing password.

keyActions.action: See who holds a particular role
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → "All roles" filter

keyActions.action: Separate staff accounts from supplier portal accounts
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → "All accounts" filter

keyActions.action: Limit a supplier's manager to item categories
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → ⋯ menu → "Edit details" on a supplier portal account → Item categories
keyActions.note: Only the categories that supplier is qualified for are offered. Tick none and the account works with every category the supplier supplies. Purchase orders for a category are handed to the manager scoped to it.

keyActions.action: See every role and how much each grants
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Roles tab
keyActions.note: Each row shows whether it is a built-in role or one you created, and how many permissions it carries.

keyActions.action: Create a role of your own
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Roles → "New role"
keyActions.note: Needs the right to manage roles. It is created empty; you then grant it permissions on the Permission matrix.

keyActions.action: Rename a role or take it out of use
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Roles → ⋯ menu → "Edit"
keyActions.note: An inactive role grants nothing, even to accounts that still hold it.

keyActions.action: Change exactly what a role allows
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Roles → click a role → Permission matrix → tick or untick → Save
keyActions.note: Needs the right to manage roles.

keyActions.action: Find a permission in the matrix
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Permission matrix → search box
keyActions.note: The search narrows what is shown on the page; nothing is hidden from the saved set.

keyActions.action: See what a role grants from a person's row
keyActions.how: Users & roles → Users → click a role badge in the Roles column

flow: Open Users & roles from the left menu under Administration.
On the Users tab press "New user", enter their name, email and first password, and save.
Open the ⋯ menu on their row and press "Assign roles".
Tick the roles that describe their job — a storekeeper gets Store Keeper, a buyer gets Purchase Executive or Purchase Manager — give a reason, and save.
To check what a role actually allows before you hand it out, go to the Roles tab and click the role to open the Permission matrix.
To adjust a role, tick or untick permissions in the matrix and press Save.
When someone leaves, open their row's ⋯ menu, press Deactivate and give a reason.
screens.notes: Fourteen internal roles ship ready to use — Administrator, Plant Manager, Store Keeper, Purchase Manager, Purchase Executive, Production Supervisor, QC Inspector, Dispatch Manager, Sales Executive, Accounts, Production Planner, Design Engineer, Auditor and Super Administrator — plus five roles for supplier portal accounts. That list is worth a table in the deck, with the one-line description of each. Two administration roles (Super Administrator and Administrator) are marked as system roles; of these only Super Administrator is locked outright. Every other role, including the built-in Store Keeper or Accounts, can be renamed and have its permissions changed, which is the point: they are a sensible starting set, not a straitjacket. There is no delete button for a user or a role on this screen — deactivating is the intended route, and it is the right one, because a deleted user would leave their name missing from years of records.
screens.permission: The page opens for anyone with the right to view users or the right to view roles, and each tab checks its own. Creating, editing, deactivating and resetting passwords each need their own separate right, so a helpdesk account can be given the password reset alone. Editing roles and the permission matrix needs the right to manage roles; handing roles to a person needs the right to assign permissions.
rules: A role's code cannot be changed once the role exists, because it appears in historical audit entries — renaming it would make that history ambiguous. The display name can be changed freely.

The Super Administrator role cannot be edited or retired at all. It is the role the "you cannot remove the last administrator" protection is written in terms of, so emptying it of permissions would quietly defeat that protection.
A system role cannot be deleted, because it would simply be recreated on the next deployment. Take it out of use instead.

You cannot grant a permission you do not hold yourself, and equally you cannot take away one you do not hold. The first would be an escalation; the second is how a junior administrator would lock out the people able to stop them.
Deactivating an account, changing someone's roles and resetting a password all require a written reason. Six months from now that reason is the only answer to why it was done.
Deactivating an account revokes every session it currently holds, immediately. Signing someone out is the point of switching them off.
A resetting administrator sees a temporary password once and never again. Hand it over through a channel the account holder controls; the account must choose a new one at its next sign-in.

A role marked as a supplier portal role can only be given to an account tied to a supplier, and that marking cannot be changed after the role is created — one careless edit would otherwise either strip the portal boundary from everyone holding it, or make every holder invalid.

Hiding a button never grants or withholds authority. The system re-checks the signed-in person's permissions on every single request, so what a screen shows is a convenience and what the system allows is the rule.

A supplier portal account can be limited only to item categories its supplier is qualified for, and a category covers the categories beneath it. Qualify the supplier for a category on the Vendors screen first.
